Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
The Alphonsine Tables at the Technische Universität Wien (Tresor 7704 I), heavily annotated by Tycho and dedicated to him in 1590 by Lave Urne til Bæltebjærg, landsdommer in Skåne; formerly in the Prague Jesuit College (Mortensen 1955, p. 30). The volume is distinct from the Paris edition of 1553 of the Tables that Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho from Munich on 10 December 1600, a copy marked ‘No. 43’ (Opera omnia VIII, pp. 393–394: ‘mitto Alphonsinas Tabulas recognitas, Parisijs A° 53 impressas, No. 43 signatas’). Norlind (1970, p. 337) prints the title-page notes: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Iesu Pragae. I Bibl. min. Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ above the title, and below it ‘Hunc librum dono dedj singularj Amico meo Domino Tychoni Brahe de Knudstorp Amicitiae ergo Anno salutis 1590. Laue Vrne senior min hand’. Tycho’s notes and the Urne dedication are known from Teichl’s report to Mortensen and from the title-page inscriptions Norlind prints; neither describes the notes, and the library’s own record names no former owner. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Norlind 1970, p. 337
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
På titelbladet står skrivet över titeln: »Collegij Cæsarei Societatis Iesu Pragæ. / Bibl. min. / Anno 1642. / Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana.» Under titeln: »Hunc librum dono dedj singularj Amico meo / Domino Tychoni Brahe de Knudstorp Amicitiæ ergo / Anno salutis 1590. Laue urne senior / min hand.» – Lave (Lage) Urne till Bälteberga, som alltså skänkte exemplaret till Tycho, var något äldre än denne och blev landsdomare i Skåne 1589, död 1623. Han kallar sig »senior» till skillnad från sin yngre broder med samma namn (död 1629).
Open questions
  • What Tycho’s annotations in the volume contain: they are known only from Teichl’s report to Mortensen (1955, p. 30) and from the title-page inscriptions Norlind prints (1970, p. 337), neither of which describes them, and the library’s record of Tresor 7704 I names no former owner; an examination of the volume would settle it.

Note
Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 16; NK Clementinum Sign. 14 J 28, in the original brown binding with the initials ‘T. B. O. 1580’ (Kleinschnitzová; Norlind 1970, p. 337). Regiomontanus’s Oratio introductoria and Melanchthon’s prefatory letter, which Šolc 2002 (p. 330) lists for the volume, are the front matter of the Nuremberg edition of 1537, not separate works. Tycho owned this edition and wanted a better text: he complained in August 1598 that the Latin translation teemed with errors (Opera omnia VIII, 102), asked Scaliger for the Arabic in April 1599 (VIII, 152), heard in March 1600 that Scaliger had neither it nor another Latin version (VIII, 264), and in November 1600 was offered a copy of the edition of 1537 by Herwart von Hohenburg (VIII, 386) (Norlind 1970, p. 337).
Norlind 1970, p. 337
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Originalbd med initialerna »T. B. O. 1580». – Albategnius' skrift, som f.ö. också utgavs separat, innehåller endast texten till hans berömda tabeller, vilka bl.a. upptogo stjärnpositioner för epoken 879,0. Texten är översatt av Plato från Tivoli med tillägg av Regiomontanus. Den arabiska texten återutgavs med latinsk översättning först av Nallino 1903–07. – Tycho skriver till Scaliger i april 1599 (VIII, 152), att han önskade den arabiska texten. Redan i aug. 1598 (VIII, 102) hade han klagat över, att den latinska översättningen vimlade av fel. Som svar på Tychos brev från april 1599, meddelar Scaliger, mars 1600 (VIII, 264), att han inte kunnat komma över någon arabisk text och f.n. inte har någon latinsk översättning. Tycho hänvände sig tydligen därefter till Herwart von Hohenburg i München. I nov. 1600 (VIII, 386) svarar denne, att uppl. 1537 är svår att skaffa och f.ö. betingar ett högt pris; den är inkorrekt på flera ställen. Ett exemplar har han emellertid förvärvat från ett bibliotek och han erbjuder sig att skicka det. Tycho, som dock ägde denna uppl., synes ha trott, att det skulle ha funnits ytterligare en latinsk översättning. En sådan existerade emellertid icke vid denna tid.

Note

Norlind 1970, p. 337
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ett astronomiskt praktverk med rörliga pappskivor till åskådliggörande av planeternas rörelser. »Ouvrage très intéressant pour connaître l'état de l'astronomie vers le milieu du XVIe siècle» (Houzeau & Lancaster); »the most sumptuous scientific book ever printed» (D. J. Price, »The equatories of the planetis», Cambr. 1955, s. 132). Dåtidens omdöme om verket S. A. Ionides, »Caesar's Astronomy», i: »Osiris» 1936, s. 356–389. Ett astronomiskt praktverk med rörliga pappskivor till åskådliggörande av planeternas rörelser. »Ouvrage très intéressant pour connaître l'état de l'astronomie vers le milieu du XVIe siècle» (Houzeau & Lancaster); »the most sumptuous scientific book ever printed» (D. J. Price, »The equatories of the planetis», Cambr. 1955, s. 132). Dåtidens omdöme om verket var emellertid ganska kritiskt. Hagecius skriver sålunda till Tycho i nov. 1588 (VII, 147): »Hunc eruditum pulverem, in quo nos versamur, ille [sc. Apianus] ne somniavit quidem. Eius artem sæpe Rheticus, bonæ memoriæ, vocare solitus erat faden Dunst.» Kepler beklagar i sin »De motibus stellæ Martis», kap. 14, den »miserabilem industriam» som Apianus nedlagt på sitt verk, men han menar ändå, att Apianus »palmam ... inde famæ perennis est adeptus, quicquid operibus ipsis fortuna ista detrimenti attulerit». Tycho ägde i varje fall ett exemplar (till Hagecius nov. 1589; VII, 212). Längre fram i brevet (215) omtalar han ett annat exemplar, som han en gång köpte för 20 fl. och sedermera skänkte Paul Wittich vid dennes besök på Hven 1580. Tycho ber nu Hagecius att, eftersom Wittich avlidit, underhandla med systern i Tychos namn angående förvärvande av dennes bibliotek, som tydligen måste ha varit synnerligen värdefullt. Lyckas Hagecius i sina underhandlingar, skall han få det exemplar, som Wittich erhöll av Tycho. – I Landesbibliothek i Gotha finnes ett exemplar, däri Tycho på ett tomt blad i början gjort en del anteckningar (se Chr. Rausch i: Zeitschr. f. Bücherfreunde, N.F. 5: 2, 1914, s. 223–224). De utgöras av några verser ur Davids 19:e psalm (»Cœli enarrant Gloriam Dei et opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum») samt ett distikon: »Qui negat esse Deum cœlos et sidera spectet / Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum.» Därunder: »Tycho Brahe / scripsi / Anno 1599 / Junii die 14 / quo Viteberga / discessi / Pragam / a Cæsare vocatus.» Pr. upptager exemplaret som tillhörigt Tycho (nr 1 i hans förteckning). Att det skulle ha varit Tychos, synes dock knappast sannolikt. Den handskrivna anteckningen påminner snarare om en stamboksautograf. Exemplaret kan mycket väl ha tillhört någon annan, kanske rent av hertig Fredrik Wilhelm av Sachsen-Altenburg, med vilken Tycho vid denna tid stod i förbindelse. Ortroy, Apianus förtecknar under nr 112 ett 30-tal kända exemplar. Till denna förteckning kan ytterligare läggas dels Gotha-exemplaret dels ett i UUB. – Apianus' handexemplar ägdes av Mæstlin i Tübingen, som i ett brev till Kepler (april 1613; Caspar nr 651, s. 57) omtalar, att änkan efter Petrus Apianus' son Philippus Apianus utan Mæstlins vetskap låtit försälja hela restupplagan.
Open questions
  • Whether the book was Tycho's own before 14 June 1599 or Duke Friedrich Wilhelm's book in which he wrote; the basis of the Gotha copy record's naming of the duke as recipient (probably Gehrt 2013 on the duke's library); and the sense of Rauch's remark that the book came to Gotha from Munich.

Apianus, Petrus, Private hands · identification A · Period 3 (T.B.O. 1583; the binding is not otherwise described)
Binding stamped ‘T.B.O.’ above the date ‘1583’; Tycho's annotations in the comet section near the end of the Astronomicum Caesareum (Gingerich 2002, fig. 2: f. O1 verso, a marginal heading reading, in the reproduction, ‘Motus diurnus Cometae in suo circulo’ beside Apianus's table of the comet's daily motion)
No online catalogue record traced.
Bound with: Schöner, Johann, Aequatorium astronomicum (Nuremberg, 1521) — bound with Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum of 1540 in the T.B.O. 1583 volume (1521)
Road of dispersal
Road U, Route out of the library unknown. The French and Dutch/Flemish annotations place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; until about 1960 it was in a monastery library there. Gingerich's suggestion: it migrated to the Low Countries by the same Jesuit hands that carried the Wittich Copernicus now in Liège.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Tycho’s own retained Astronomicum Caesareum, bound for him in 1583 with Schöner’s equatorium of 1521 and stamped ‘T.B.O. 1583’; he gave a second copy to Paul Wittich (Chicago) and inscribed a third at Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 (Gotha, Prandtl Band VI). The volume surfaced about 2000 through an e-mail enquiry to Gingerich from its Belgian owner, who asked why books of 1521 and 1540 sat in a binding stamped 1583 with the initials TBO; Gingerich recognised the mark and learned of Tycho’s annotations in the comet section (2002, pp. 327–328, fig. 2 = f. O1 verso). Later annotations in French and in Dutch or Flemish place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a long period, in a monastery library until about 1960 — in Gingerich’s view carried there by the same Jesuit hands as the Wittich Copernicus now in Liège. It was sold about 2001–2002 to an anonymous American collector for, Gingerich reports, close to a million dollars. Gingerich (2002, p. 327) had known only the Wittich copy and presumed that Tycho had retained another, which he had not found among the more than a hundred copies he had examined.
Open questions
  • Which monastery in the Low Countries held the volume until about 1960, who the Belgian owner of about 2000 was, and who bought it in about 2001–2002: Gingerich names none of them, and the dealer’s or the owner’s records would.
  • Which edition of Schöner’s equatorium of 1521 is bound with the Apianus: Gingerich gives neither title nor imprint, and a description of the volume would settle it.

Apollonius of Perga, Conicorum libri IV (prob. Commandino, Bologna 1566; or Memmo, Venice 1537). Bologna, 1566

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-apollonius-conica
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Mathematics
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 338 (s.v. Apollonius Pergæus); Jardine & Segonds 2008
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 366
Note
Norlind (1970, pp. 338–339): ‘Vi veta, att biblioteket på Hven ägde ett exemplar av Apollonius’ verk (Bil. 6)’ — the library on Hven owned a copy, on the evidence of his Bilaga 6. Which of the two Latin translations it was, Memmo’s (Venice 1537) or Commandino’s (Bologna 1566, with Eutocius’s commentary), is not known; Norlind inclines to Commandino’s. The ‘Opera’ that Herwart von Hohenburg sent from Munich at Tycho’s request in September 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, 366) was a loan, its title that of the edition of 1537. Christian Hansen Riber’s deposition of 13/23 May 1598 adds the one witness to the shelf: the former students, ‘who examined your library whenever we liked’, attest that it never held any writing of Apollonius on hypotheses and that Tycho had no book of his but the Conics (Jardine & Segonds 2008, p. 169). The authors suppose that Kepler found the Commandino volume, which also carries Serenus, in Tycho’s library for the Contra Ursum, and conjecture that the ‘Apollonij Pergaei Opera’ Herwart sent on 23 September 1600 may be the copy Kepler used; their page prints the editions as Memmo 1527 and Commandino 1556, misprints for 1537 and 1566 (pp. 169–170 n. 4).
Norlind 1970, p. 338
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Av detta berömda verk funnos vid denna tid tvenne latinska översättningar (av bok I–IV, som äro de enda bevarade på grekiska; bok V–VII föreligga endast i arabisk övers.). Den ena översättningen av den venetianske patriciern Johannes Baptista Memus utgavs i Venedig 1537.2°. Den viktigaste var dock av Federicus Commandinus och den trycktes i Bologna 1566, 2°. Den innehåller bl.a. Eutocius' kommentar och var det första försöket att göra verket begripligt genom förklarande noter. Vi veta, att biblioteket på Hven ägde ett exemplar av Apollonius' verk (Bil. 6), men vilken upplaga det varit, är icke känt; man skulle emellertid med skäl kunna gissa på Commandinus' översättning. – I sept. 1600 (VIII, 366) skickade Herwart från München på Tychos begäran till låns Apollonius' »Opera», detta är titeln på den upplaga, som trycktes 1537. föreligga endast i arabisk övers.). Aslakssøn, Cort, De natura caeli triplicis libelli tres. Siegen, 1597, 4°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-aslaksson-denatura
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Cosmology
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 339 (s.v. Aslakssön, Cort); Zinner no. 3699; VD16 A 3899
Acquisition
the author’s dedication to Tycho; a presentation copy is presumed, none is documented (Norlind 1970, p. 339) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Dedication
dedicatee: Tycho Brahe de Knudstrup; incipit: Magnifico et amplissimo viro, virtute, eruditione, prudentia veré nobili Domino TYCHONI BRAHE de Knudstrup, fundatori Arcis Uraniburgicae in lectissima Hellesponti Danici Insula Huena; sideralis scientiae scrutatori, instauratori, conservatori unico, Domino & fautori meo summé colendo S.; place date: Basel (Basileae Rauracorum), 16 November 1596; signed: Tuae Excellentiae perpetuó studiosissimus Cunradus Aslachus Bergensis; content: Offers the book as 'primitiae' / a 'gratae recordationis symbolum' in return for Tycho's benefactions; hails him as 'indefessus ille Caeli scrutator & Atlas'; praises the Brahe family's nobility and Tycho's heroic-Herculean labours in sidereal science, his celestial Globe ('Globus ille caelestis, infinitis tuis lucubrationibus & vigiliis comparatus, Mundoque pridem concessus') and his astronomical instruments ('Machinae Astronomicae tua opera incredibili sumptu affabré elaboratae'). The preface (sig. A2v) thanks his Siegen/Herborn teachers Johannes Piscator and Johann Bisterfeld, and records submitting the work to Rudolph Goclenius the Elder at the Frankfurt fair; it defends views 'a communi scholarum opinione abhorrentia' (the cautiously-stated Copernican paradoxes). A separate epigram 'Ad authorem' by Johannes Piscator faces the title.; source: BSB Munich copy bsb10192622, sig. A2-A3 (pp. 3-6); read from the open MDZ/IIIF digitisation
English translation
title: The Description of Heaven. Or, A diuine and comfortable discourse of the nature of the eternall heaven, the habitation of God, and all the Elect.; translates: Book III only (De caelo perpetuo); by: composed in Latin by Cunradus Aslachus; converted into English by Raph (Ralph) Iennings; imprint: London: A[ugustine] Mathewes for John Brambridge, 1623; ref: STC; EEBO-TCP A22193; note: Dedicated by the translator to Richard Liggins, Gentleman; neither Tycho nor Copernicus is named in the English.
Note
Cort Aslakssøn (Cunradus Aslacus, Cort Axelsen; Bergen 1564–1624), Tycho’s famulus on Hven 1590–93 and later the first Norwegian professor at Copenhagen. Full title: De natura caeli triplicis libelli tres, quorum I. de caelo aëreo, II. de caelo sidereo, III. de caelo perpetuo, e sacrarum litterarum & praestantium philosophorum thesauris concinnati (Siegen [Sigenae Nassoviorum]: Christoph Rab, Christophorus Corvinus, 1597). VD16 A 3899; Zinner 3699; [7] leaves and 214 pages, octavo (VD16; the ‘4°’ at Norlind, p. 339, is an error). Written and printed while Aslakssøn was abroad as tutor to Otto Brahe (matriculated at Basel 1596/97). The book is dedicated to Tycho (Norlind, p. 339; Store norske leksikon), whence Norlind’s inference that it ‘har väl alltså befunnit sig i Tychos bibliotek’. The ownership rests on that inference alone: no copy with Tycho’s marks and no presentation copy is recorded in the inventories of Prandtl, Kleinschnitzová, Šolc or Mortensen, or in the trade. In the preface Aslakssøn declares for Copernicus, a position Tycho rejected, so that the dedication stands in tension with the book’s own position. The work is a ‘Mosaic physics’, a synthesis of astronomy and scripture on the three heavens (elemental or aerial, astronomical or sidereal, eternal or perpetual); Comenius later listed Aslakssøn among the Mosaic physicists who preceded him. Book III, De caelo perpetuo, was translated into English as ‘The Description of Heaven … Composed in Latine by Cunradus Aslachus, and conuerted into English by Raph [Ralph] Iennings’ (London 1623; EEBO A22193). Copies of the edition survive in Munich (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek), Vienna (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek) and Copenhagen (Royal Library); none is Tycho’s. The dedicatory epistle, read in the Munich copy, is addressed ‘Tychoni Brahe de Knudstrup, fundatori Arcis Uraniburgicae … sideralis scientiae scrutatori, instauratori, conservatori unico’, dated Basel, 16 November 1596, and signed ‘Cunradus Aslachus Bergensis’; it hails Tycho as ‘indefessus Caeli scrutator & Atlas’ and pays eyewitness homage to his celestial globe and astronomical instruments.
Copies of the edition examined
  • Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (BSB), Munich, see bsb10192622 — Siegen: Christoph Rab (Corvinus), 1597, 8° (VD16 A 3899; Zinner 3699). From an Augustinian Canons-Regular house ('Ex Bibliotheca... regularis... Augustanae... observantiae', ms. on title-page foot); to BSB after the 1803 Bavarian secularisation. Not Tycho's copy. Ms. provenance line on title-page foot; BSB classmarks on the pastedown.
  • Österreichische Nationalbibliothek (ÖNB), Vienna — Siegen: Christoph Rab (Corvinus), 1597, 8° (VD16 A 3899). Ordinary copy; not Tycho's.
  • Det Kongelige Bibliotek (Royal Library), Copenhagen — via ProQuest Early European Books, (EEB ‘Copenhagen’ collection) — Siegen: Christoph Rab (Corvinus), 1597, 8° (VD16 A 3899). Ordinary copy digitised in EEB from the Royal Library holdings; not Tycho's.
Norlind 1970, p. 339
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Detta verk var tillägnat Tycho. Det har väl alltså befunnit sig i Tychos bibliotek.

Opera omnia: III, 251–253; VI, 172
Note
Norlind 1970, p. 340: that Tycho owned a copy of some edition is probable, since the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, pp. 251–253) quote verbatim a letter of Benedetti to Raimondo of Verona against the view that the new star of 1572 was one of Cassiopeia’s stars; which edition cannot be settled (in the Turin edition of 1585 the letter stands at pp. 371–374). No copy, receipt or mark is recorded; no edition is specified, and no mark by which a copy of Tycho’s could be recognised is known.
Norlind 1970, p. 340
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Att Tycho ägt ett exemplar av någon upplaga av detta verk, är sannolikt. I »Prog.» (III, 251–253) citerar han ordagrant ett ställe härur, ur ett brev från Benedictus till Raimundus från Verona, vari denne polemiserar mot Raimundus' åsikt, att den nya stjärnan i Cassiopeia icke vore »ny» utan en av stjärnorna där. Av Tychos ord framgår, att boken varit sällsynt. Vilken upplaga det varit, kan icke fastslås med säkerhet. I upplagan, tryckt i Torino 1585, 2°, står brevet på s. 371–374 (jfr G. Bordiga, »Giovanni Battista Benedetti», i: »Atti del R. Ist. Veneto di scienze» etc., 85, 1925–26, s. 613). Riccardi, »Biblioteca matematica italiana» uppger första upplagan tryckt i Torino 1580 och känner ingen upplaga från 1585 (endast ett omtryck av uppl. 1580). I ett brev till Rothmann, febr. 1589 (VI, 172) nämner Tycho ett annat brev från Benedictus (s. 256–257 i nyssnämnda upplaga) vari behandlas bl.a. månens ljus, Benedictus menar sålunda, att det sekundära ljuset förorsakas av planeten Venus – en åsikt som Tycho trodde sig ha bekräftat genom sina egna observationer.

LostCrec-e-norlind-brasch-varadino
Status

Acquisition
1600; sent by the author; the first copy was lost in transit, a second was sent in September 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, 337; VIII, 380) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 337; VIII, 380
Note
Brasch sent the manuscript poem, which celebrates Melchior von Roedern’s defence of Grosswardein (Várad) in 1598, to Tycho twice: in August 1600, when it was lost in transit (Opera omnia VIII, 337), and as a replacement in September 1600 that ‘probably reached’ him (Opera omnia VIII, 380; Norlind p. 340); von Roedern died on 20 September 1600. No surviving manuscript codex has been located in any catalogue. Martin Brasch the Younger also published a printed Varadini Hungariae propugnaculi... anni 1598 (1598) on the same subject — plausibly the same matter in print beside an authorial manuscript redaction of 1600, though no source collates the two. The first copy never arrived, the replacement only ‘probably’ did, no codex survives, and no ownership mark that could be looked for attaches to the item; the entry therefore rests on the correspondence alone. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique manuscript sent and probably received, not a mass-survival text — the class retired as unlocatable does not fit it.
Norlind 1970, p. 340
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Brasch besjunger här Melchior Rhederus' (von Rödern) segerrika försvar av Grosswardein (Nagy-Várad) mot turkarna. Han skickade dikten till Tycho i aug. 1600 (VIII, 337), men försändelsen kom aldrig fram. Ett nytt exemplar skickade Brasch i sept. s.å. (VIII, 380), vilket förmodligen nådde adressaten.

upper board blind-stamped at the head TY ✿ BRAD, a rosette between the words (the library's photographs, October 2026; the year 1563 that Prandtl, Norlind and Mortensen read with the name is not legible in them — in raking light, 13 October 2026, the band beneath the panel shows only the remains of stamped forms on an abraded surface, a looped figure at its right end that may be the 6 — but is plain to the eye with the book in hand: the library's Rare Books Librarian, asked, read 1563 on the band without doubt, 14 October 2026; the LIBRIS note gives ‘TY BRAD 1563’); light tanned leather over boards, blind-tooled with a portrait-medallion roll of the Reformers type (one medallion lettered IOANNES HVS), a foliate roll and rules, an Annunciation panel on the upper board (legend VIRGO · MARIA · DEI · MATER · SANCTISSIMA · SALVATORVM) and a Baptism-of-Christ panel on the lower (HIC EST FILIVS MEVS DILECTVS IN QVO MIHI COMPLACITVM EST); two brass clasps, the catches on the upper board, the straps lost; five raised bands; edges plain. The numerals ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ on the three titles are the later librarian's, matching the contents note on the front flyleaf
Links: catalogue record · the binding, pastedowns, endleaves and edges photographed by the library (Alvin record 805325) · LIBRIS record of the Camerarius (constituent 1) · LIBRIS record of the Osius (constituent 2) · the scanned card of the old Uppsala catalogue
Bound with: Garcaeus, Johannes, Tractatus brevis et utilis de erigendis figuris coeli (1556); Osius, Hieronymus, Historia excidii Hierosolymorum longe luctuosissimi, cuius exemplum & memoria his temporibus maxime videtur accommodata & necessaria. Item historia Ioseph filii Iacob versibus enarrata (1558)
Road of dispersal
Road 0, Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges. Vedel’s name stands at the head of the title. Walde (1920, p. 329) and Mortensen (1955, p. 27) read the volume as Tycho’s gift to Vedel, the memento of their Leipzig years; Norlind (1970, p. 366) held it more likely that the book was Vedel’s from the start, given to Tycho, who had it bound with the two others — on which reading it did not leave the library in his lifetime and its route to De la Gardie is undocumented.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 58 (‘Xenophon in lateinischer Übersetzung. Wittenberg, 1556’); bound first in Band III. The title page shows the work to be Joachim Camerarius's Hippocomicus with his Latin Xenophon, printed at Leipzig by Valentin Papst in 1556 ([24], 342 pp.), as Norlind 1970, p. 366, already had it under Xenophon; Prandtl's and Mortensen's ‘Wittenberg’ is a slip. Corrected from the facsimile, 12 October 2026.
Norlind 1970, p. 366

Norlind records

Note
Norlind (1970, p. 342), citing Dreyer, states that Tycho ‘skaffade sig under sin Leipzigvistelse’ this edition — acquired it during his Leipzig years — and cites it often in his earliest observation journal (Opera omnia X, 5 ff.). Dreyer’s sentence is narrower: ‘In his observations from 1563–64 he also mentions the Ephemerides of Carellus (Venice, 1557)’ (Tycho Brahe, Edinburgh 1890, p. 18, n. 1); the acquisition at Leipzig is Norlind’s inference. The edition is Venice: Vincenzo Valgrisi, 1557, 4to; its title runs ‘ad annos XIX’, 1557 to 1575, where Norlind prints ‘IX’. Three datings stand side by side: Šolc 2006 (printed p. 190 (scan 4)) places the Carelli ephemerides for 1557 with the Stadius among the tables Tycho ‘procured at once’ after the eclipse of 21 August 1560, unsourced; Norlind's Leipzig purchase is an inference from Dreyer p. 18 n. 1 (the citations in the observations of 1563–64); and the loci record of the Copenhagen years (after Christianson 2020, pp. 19–22) has the Carelli bought with Jens Nilsson in Copenhagen about 1561. Šolc's 1560 is not adopted.
Norlind 1970, p. 342

Clavius, Christoph, Gnomonice (Gnomonices libri octo). Rome, 1581, 2°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-letter-clavius-gnomonice
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Gnomonics/Sundials
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 342 (s.v. Clavius, Christophorus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 15 March 1586 (tekstnet.dk); Norlind 1926
Acquisition
1586; bought for Tycho by Heinrich Brucaeus at Rostock, March 1586, valued at seven Joachimsthaler (Opera omnia VII, 100) (Procured by a correspondent or agent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 100
Note
Brucaeus bought Tycho a copy of Clavius’s Gnomonices at Rostock in March 1586 (his letter of 15 March 1586: ‘emi et tibi Gnomonicen CLAVIJ Bambergensis’, valued at seven Joachimsthaler; Opera omnia VII, 100). The purchase was conditional: the bookseller had deposited the books with Brucaeus at the beginning of the winter and would take them back if Tycho did not want them or already had them (‘Emi autem hac conditione, ut si tibi forte non placerent, aut forte eosdem iam esses nactus, Bibliopola ad se recipiat … Iam enim libros ineunte hyeme apud me deposuit’, VII, 100); whether this copy reached Hven is not recorded (Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3). That Tycho had the work is his own statement to Rantzau of 22 February 1597: Clavius’s writings on Euclid, on Sacrobosco and on gnomonics ‘in promptu habeo, et iamdudum introspexi’ (VII, 381). In December 1584 the Rostock bookseller, back from Frankfurt without the books Tycho had ordered, had sold his one copy, valued at nearly five Joachimsthaler, to Heinrich Rantzau (Opera omnia VII, 88; Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3), so Tycho’s first order went unfilled.
Norlind 1970, p. 342
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
I mars 1586 (VII, 100) skriver Brucæus i Rostock, att han för Tychos räkning köpt ett exemplar för 7 joachimsthaler.

Cort Aslakssøn sent the commentary to Tycho in 1594 (Aslaksson to Tycho, 23 October 1594: ‘CLAVIJ hunc in Sphæram SACROBOSCI Commentarium ad te ablegavi ob tractatulum quendam de Nova Stella’), and Tycho received it. Tycho himself names it among the works of Clavius he has to hand, writing to Rantzau on 22 February 1597 (Opera omnia VII, 381: ‘ea nihilominus quae in Euclidem ingeniose et in Iohannem de Sacrobusco luculenter, et de Gnomonicis copiose conscripsit, in promptu habeo, et iamdudum introspexi’). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified: the one work of Clavius among the Clementinum volumes is the Apologia of 1588, bound after Maestlin’s Alterum examen (Kleinschnitzová 13:2, Sign. 14 G 30), not this commentary. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Norlind 1970, p. 343

Norlind records

Surviving copy

No Tycho mark. The ÖNB description records no former owner (only a 19th-c. half-parchment rebinding). The identification rests on Norlind's attribution and on the volume's Uraniborg-circle content — Longomontanus's 'Responsio ad Capnurianam apologiam' is bound in the same 16th-c. Sammelhandschrift — which is circumstantial, not a mark.
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (ÖNB)
Road of dispersal
Road U, Route out of the library unknown. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
A manuscript of the Commentariolus in the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Vienna, attributed to Tycho’s library by Norlind. Tycho owned the text: Hagecius gave him a copy at Regensburg in 1575, and he printed it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia II, 428). Whether the Vienna manuscript is that copy rests on Norlind’s attribution and on the Uraniborg-circle contents of the same Sammelhandschrift; the volume carries no mark of his, and its catalogue record names no former owner, so both the entry and the identification of the copy are graded C. Walde (1938) showed the Vienna manuscript to have been Longomontanus’s gift to the amanuensis Johannes Eriksen at Benátky on 18 July 1600 and left open whether it passed from Eriksen to Tycho; Eriksen’s books otherwise went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty. The witness therefore belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho’s own shelves. Jardine and Segonds note the copy that came from Hagecius (2008, p. 187 n. 4). The National Library's account of 2026 adds two points to the Regensburg gift: that the original Hájek exemplar is untraced (the same object as Norlind's ‘Tycho's exemplar not located’ if the Regensburg transfer was a gift), and the conjecture that it was Tycho who had Copernicus's name — absent from the anonymous letter as it circulated — set at the head of the transcripts he distributed (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 22 (scan 22); ‘zřejmě’, her conjecture, not a documented fact). The three surviving transcripts she names (Vienna, Stockholm, Aberdeen; p. 20) are those the history essay already records. Status disputed since 20 October 2026: the witness belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho's shelves (Walde 1938 against the transfer), and a located C with the ownership in doubt is the Definitions' disputed, not located.
Norlind 1970, p. 343
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Copernicus' preliminära, endast i manuskript publicerade, förhandsmeddelande om de forskningsresultat han sedermera framlade för offentligheten i »De revolutionibus orbium cœlestium». – I »Prog.» (II, 428) skriver Tycho, att han erhöll ett exemplar av Hagecius vid deras möte i Regensburg 1575 och att han därpå lät göra avskrifter av detsamma, vilka han skickade till andra astronomer i Tyskland. En sådan avskrift var väl det exemplar som Longomontanus vid sin avresa från Benatky d. 18 juli 1600 skänkte Johannes Eriksen, en annan av Tychos lärjungar. Detta exemplar, ett av de få bevarade, finns nu i Wien. Ett annat, tidigare ägt av Hevelius i Danzig, som förmodligen förvärvat det med Keplers kvarlåtenskap, finnes nu i KVA.
Open questions
  • Whether the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek’s Commentariolus manuscript, Longomontanus’s gift to Johannes Eriksen in July 1600 (Walde 1938), ever passed from Eriksen to Tycho or reached Vienna by another route; a mark of Tycho’s in the volume or a record of its arrival in Vienna would decide.

Ex Bibliotheca et Recognitione Tichoniana’ on the title (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 11)
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Google Books)
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
From Tycho’s library: Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 14, his Einzelband X (‘reichverzierter weißer Lederband’). Prandtl (1932) attributed the marginalia to Tycho; Gingerich and Westman showed them to be Paul Wittich’s. The acquisition is documented in the correspondence. After Wittich’s death (1586) Tycho was given procuration of Wittich’s books and papers (Hagecius, 22 March 1589) and pursued the purchase of Wittich’s whole library from the surviving sister for six years, 1589–1595 (Tycho’s letters of 1 November 1589, 10 May 1590 and 12 August 1595: ‘omnem eius supellectilem librariam... iusto pretio nanciscar’; ‘de libris VITICHIANIS... a sorore superstite... obtinere queam’). According to Mosley (2007, pp. 175–179; the despatch at p. 179, following Gingerich and Westman 1988) Jacob Monau eventually succeeded: he despatched three of Wittich’s four annotated De revolutionibus volumes to Prague, the fourth remaining in Wrocław — Gingerich’s Wrocław 9 (Biblioteka Uniwersytecka 437777), the copy Valentin von Sebisch transcribed c. 1604. Gingerich’s Annotated Census traces two of Wittich’s copies to Tycho through Monaw’s delivery of October 1600 — Prague 3, 14 B 16 (p. 23: ‘likely one brought to him in Prague from Wittich’s heirs in Wrocław by Jacob Monaw … in October of 1600’) and Vatican 1, Ottoboniana 1902 (p. 105: ‘presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’) — and gives the Liège copy, Res MS 69C, the provenance of an annotator from Reinhold’s circle, Wittich and the Université de Liège, with no Prague station (p. 8); in his essay of the same year Gingerich writes that ‘another of the Wittich/Tychonic copies was perhaps acquired by a Belgian Jesuit working in Prague, for today it is found in the University Library in Liège’ (Tycho Brahe and Prague, p. 325). Whether the Liège copy was among the books Monaw brought to Prague is thus left open between Gingerich’s two accounts and Mosley’s count of three. The pursuit was bound up with Tycho’s dispute with Ursus over plagiarism. This is the channel by which the Wittich-annotated De revolutionibus entered the Tychoniana. The count of Wittich’s annotated copies that reached Tycho stands at two values: Mosley has three despatched to Prague, Gingerich and Westman two of the four, as Jardine and Segonds cite them (2008, p. 3 n. 1); both stand until the Liège question below is settled.
Norlind 1970, p. 343
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Detta är andra upplagan av Copernicus' berömda verk, i vilken upplaga också ingår Rheticus' första preliminära rapport (»Narratio prima») om världssystemet. – Pr. nr 14. Kl. nr 11. – Prag, UB.
Open questions
  • Whether the Liège De revolutionibus (Université de Liège, Res MS 69C; Nuremberg 1543, annotated by an early reader of Reinhold’s circle and by Wittich) passed through Tycho’s hands: Mosley counts three Wittich volumes despatched to Prague, Gingerich’s Census gives the Liège copy no Prague station, and Gingerich’s essay of 2002 supposes it acquired in Prague by a Belgian Jesuit; evidence of a Prague station in the Liège volume itself would decide.
  • Lead, unadopted: the National Library's account names Andreas Dudith, with Hájek, Monau and Longomontanus, among those Tycho asked to secure Wittich's books (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 33 (scan 33), without a source). Dudith died in February 1589 at Breslau, where the Wittich estate lay, and Tycho was in correspondence with him (the Epistolarium's Dudith letters of 17 August 1588 and 10 May 1589; TBOO VII); the claim is plausible and would add a fourth agent to the three attempts Christianson counts, but it is not adopted until the letter is found — Gingerich & Westman 1988, pp. 17–22 (Desiderata row 4f) or the Dudith correspondence are the places to look.

The dense annotations are Paul Wittich's, not Tycho's -- Gingerich (Census, pp. 105-108) retracts the earlier Tycho-annotation belief, noting the flyleaf longitude list cites Vratislavia (Wittich's Wrocław) but neither Hven nor Copenhagen. Tycho ownership rests on Gingerich's documented acquisition history (one of the copies Monau brought to Prague for Tycho in Oct 1600 -- Gingerich, Census, pp. 105-108; Mosley p. 179 puts the number despatched at three), not on a Tycho mark.
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Vatican Library)
Road of dispersal
Road III, The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague). Tycho (presumably acquired Oct 1600 via Monau) → Rudolf II → 1648 Swedish loot → Queen Christina → Rome 1655 → Ottoboni 1690 → BAV Ott. lat. 1902. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Scholarship argues that Tycho owned or used more than one De revolutionibus. This copy is the Nuremberg edition of 1543 now Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Ott. lat. 1902 (Gingerich: Ottoboniana 1902), described by Gingerich, Annotated Census (2002), pp. 105–108 (I.98, ‘Vatican 1’). The copy is annotated by Wittich; Tycho ‘eagerly sought’ it ‘and presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’. Gingerich conjectures its later route: from Rudolf II to the Swedish booty of 1648, to Christina, to Rome in 1655, to the Ottoboni library and so to the Vatican. The annotations are Wittich’s, not Tycho’s: Gingerich retracts the older belief, the flyleaf longitudes citing Vratislavia rather than Hven or Copenhagen. Tycho’s ownership therefore rests on the documented acquisition through Monau, not on any mark of his. The copy is distinct from the Wittich copy in the Clementinum (Sign. 14 B 16, the Basel edition of 1566).
Open questions
  • Whether a third of Wittich’s annotated copies, the Liège De revolutionibus of 1543 (ResMS 69C), also reached Tycho: Mosley (2007, p. 179, after Gingerich and Westman 1988) has Monau despatch three of the four to Prague, whereas Gingerich’s Census (2002) counts two as reaching Tycho, this copy and 14 B 16, and places the Liège copy outside his hands.

Note
Quercetanus (Joseph Du Chesne), Ad Iacobi Auberti … brevis responsio (Lyon 1575, 8vo): a Paracelsian book Tycho owned only briefly. Its preface is dated 1 April 1575, and he gave the copy to Thaddaeus Hagecius at their meeting in Regensburg in the autumn of that year; in August 1585 he asked Hagecius for another copy, unable to recall author or title (Tycho to Hagecius, August 1585, Opera omnia VII, 95). The work is identified from Hagecius’s marginal note ‘Libellus est Josephi Quercetani’ on Tycho’s letter (autograph in Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek), not from the book; Norlind gives the title as ‘med största sannolikhet’ (Norlind 1970, p. 359). The copy passed into Hagecius’s library; a copy recovered from it would carry his marks, not Tycho’s. Status attested, passed on, since 20 October 2026: the copy left the library in his lifetime as a gift to Hagecius (road 0), which is why no copy is sought — not a mass-survival text retired as unlocatable.
Norlind 1970, p. 359
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
[Preamble printed before the headword, leading into it:] I aug. 1585 (VII, 95) skriver Tycho till Hagecius, att denne vid deras sammanträffande i Regensburg hösten 1575 erhöll en bok, vars författare Tycho dock icke kan erinra sig. Boken handlade om beredning av »kemiska läkemedel» (»de Chymicis medicamentis præparandis»), titeln kan Tycho icke med bestämdhet uppge, men han minns, att formatet var oktav. Fastän han sökt efter den hos bokhandlare i Tyskland, har han inte lyckats komma över den, eftersom han inte kunnat uppge vare sig förf.-namnet eller titeln. Han ber nu Hagecius skicka ett exemplar, så vida ett sådant står att få köpa, eller också ge besked om författarens namn. Vi veta inte, om Hagecius lyckades tillmötesgå Tychos önskan, men i margen till Tychos brev (original i Wien) har han antecknat »Libellus est Josephi Quercetani». (»Quartani» i noten, VII, 407, är en felläsning av utg.) Den bok som här avses och som Tycho alltså en gång ägt är med största sannolikhet: [Here follows the entry line; text after the entry line:] Förf., vars franska namn var Joseph Du Chesne (1546–1609), ansågs som en framstående läkare och var sedan 1593 livmedikus hos Henrik IV. I sina talrika skrifter framträder han dock som en charlatan inom yrket. Att Tycho varit så intresserad av denna skrift, sammanhänger väl med den läkarverksamhet han bedrev på Hven. Quercetanus var en ivrig anhängare av Paracelsus, för vilken Tycho också hyste en viss böjelse. Bokens förord är daterat d. 1 april 1575, den var således alldeles nyutkommen, då Tycho skänkte den till Hagecius.

B.’ on the manuscript-supplied title leaf of the Imago mundi and his glosses (e.g. fol. dd1r), read as his hand by Boldan & Kazanskii 2023; the year 1576 stamped into the front pasteboard (leather stripped, board later papered); ‘Collegii Societatis Jesu Commotovien. catalogo inscriptus 1645’ on fol. <2>2r; a blacked-out note of the Kulm brethren on the Euclid's a1r, recovered under the VSC 8000 (fig. 5)
Links: catalogue record
Bound with: Ailly, Pierre d’, Imago mundi, with his astronomical treatises (the first edition) (Louvain: Johannes de Westfalia, c. 1477–1483 (GW M31954))
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. With the Imago mundi: Chomutov college (catalogued 1645), then the Clementinum after 1773.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
The second piece of the Sammelband 44 F 38: Ratdolt's Euclid of 1482, the first printed edition, with its woodcut diagrams in the outer margins. On the blank recto of its first leaf a blacked-out ownership note, perhaps still of the late fifteenth century, read under the comparator as ‘Hic liber pertinet domui fratrum in Culmen’: the house of the Brethren of the Common Life at Kulm (Chełmno) in Royal Prussia, founded from Zwolle in 1473, with a school Copernicus probably attended before 1491 and, in the years about 1473 to 1478, one of the first presses of east-central Europe; its library was dispersed when the house ended in the 1530s or 1540s, and eleven volumes with twenty-six incunables are known from it (Boldan and Kazanskii 2023, p. 28, citing Szandorowska 1968 and 1973). How the Euclid came from Kulm to Tycho — bought, like his other student books, or through the Prussian connections of his circle — is not recorded; it was in his hands by 1576, when the binding was made. Boldan and Kazanskii call it the first scientific title recovered from the Kulm brethren's library.
Open questions
  • The route from the Brethren of the Common Life at Kulm to Tycho before 1576.

Road II, The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601). No 1642 inscription. The title carries Gabriel Crusius’s mark; the next recorded owner is Jan Josef Klauser (‘Clauser’ in the Tritius record), the Prague printer and gubernial archivist, whose library Strahov bought in 1775 (Neškudla 2021, p. 229). The book left Tycho’s library by a private route and bypassed the transfer of 1642: Crusius gave two other Tycho volumes (5 G 92, 5 J 103) to the Chomutov Jesuits on 5 August 1654, and Klauser died on 31 July 1771, so the book was on the private Prague market before the suppression of 1773.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Found by Hedvika Kuchařová and published by Pařez in 2009. Not the Clavius Euclid that Norlind inferred (one of the editions of 1574–91, of which no copy has been located): this is the Zamberti–Campanus Elements of 1558, a working mathematician's Euclid a generation earlier. The 1567 date places the binding in the Rostock student years, nine years before the earliest dated T.B.O. cohort; Norlind (pp. 344, 363) already knew a ‘T. B.’ initials mark of 1567, so the year is not anomalous — the two-line full name is. Whether this is one of the eight books Mainx found in 1943 is tested by the mark: it is not the gilt portrait plaque Mortensen describes for all eight. The graphite ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ on the title is Gabriel Crusius's (identified 19 September 2026 by the match of formula and ductus with the digitised title leaf of 5 G 92): the Euclid is the third or fourth known book of a named private collector of Tychoniana in mid-seventeenth-century Bohemia, whose holding scattered by more than one route. Munzar and Pařez already counted five books from Tycho's library at Strahov in 2002 (p. 369); whether that count includes this Euclid, found by Kuchařová between 1996 and 2009, or the Mechanica, is not stated.
Open questions
  • Whether the marginal notes — at Book I, prop. 4 and in the Campanus section — are in Tycho’s hand: Pařez (2009) gives them to him (‘přípisky psané jeho rukou in margine’); they have not been compared with his securely attributed specimens.
  • The effaced inscription beneath Crusius's mark on the title — ultraviolet or raking light may recover the earlier owner's name.
  • Klauser's printed ex-libris, which would confirm the 1775 route, has not been looked for on the endleaves; nor Strnad's name or stamp.
  • The trailing ‹K› glyph after Crusius's name on all three Prague instances — a second initial, a locative abbreviation, or a personal mark — is unresolved; if Gabriel Crusius was a Kraus z Krausenbergu the glyph has a candidate expansion.
  • Whether the ‘five books from Tycho's library’ Munzar and Pařez counted at Strahov in 2002 include this Euclid (Pařez 2009 credits its discovery to Kuchařová and calls it new) or the Mechanica.

Fincke, Thomas, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel 1583). Basileæ, 1583, 4°

DisputedCrec-e-mort-kb-fincke
Status
Disputed · entry confidence C
Subject
Mathematics/Geometry
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Fincke, Thomas)
Ownership marks
Inscription: No Tycho mark on either KB copy (both examined on their surrogates). The Geometria rotundi is dedicated to King Frederik II; in the dedication Fincke praises 'in Mathematis excellentissimum virum Dn. Tychonem Brahe' (printed text, present in every copy) — this is Norlind's whole basis, not a copy-level Tycho mark.
Surviving copies
LN 599 4° (eks. 1), Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark. Title-page autograph 'Horrebow'; royal crowned cipher + BIBLIOTHECA REGIA HAFNIENSIS stamp; 18th-c marbled-board binding.
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Hielmst. 1661a 4°, Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark. Contemporary limp-vellum sammelband (gothic-MS pastedown). Flyleaf: 'Severinus Pauli[?]... Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]' + mottoes 'Superna curato, Humana contemnito' / 'Mens generosa ultra polos'. Title page: 'Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620' + motto 'Ex uno omnia'. Hielmstierne bookplate No.1661 + BRH stamp.
Links: digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Note
Thomas Fincke, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel: S. Henricpetri, 1583), dedicated to Frederik II. Both copies in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, have been examined in digital reproduction, and neither bears any mark of Tycho’s ownership. The first copy (LN 599 4, ex. 1) carries the autograph ‘Horrebow’ (the eighteenth-century family of Danish Royal Astronomers) on the title page and royal-cipher and BRH stamps, in an eighteenth-century marbled-board binding. The second (Hielmst. 1661a 4, ex. 2) is a contemporary Sammelband (Fincke 1583 with Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum, Strasbourg 1588) in limp vellum, inscribed ‘Severinus Pauli[?] … Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]’ (mottoes ‘Superna curato, Humana contemnito’ and ‘Mens generosa ultra polos’) and ‘Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620’ (motto ‘Ex uno omnia’), later Hielmstierne’s. Norlind nonetheless placed the book in Tycho’s library — ‘fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg’ (Bilaga I, p. 346) — but his whole basis is Fincke’s printed praise of Tycho in the preface, a compliment present in every copy rather than a mark in any copy. No inventory, inscription or ownership mark attests Tycho’s ownership, and neither surviving Copenhagen copy is his.
Norlind 1970, p. 345
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Fincke bedrev studier vid olika utländska universitet, bl.a. i Basel 1583, blev vid 30 års ålder professor i matematik i Köpenhamn 1591, i retorik 1602 och i medicin 1603. Erhöll 1597 uppdraget att jämte professor Iver Stub resa över till Hven för att undersöka om någon åverkan gjorts på Tychos instrument, vilket misstänkliggjorde dem i Tychos ögon. – Boken är tillägnad konung Fredrik II, men i förordet till läsaren, fol. 3r, talar Fincke mycket vänligt om Tycho och ber honom inte dölja, om det finns något lovvärt i den och icke spara kritik, om så behövs. Boken, som tillkommit under Finckes studievistelse i Basel, fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg.
Open questions
  • Who the two early owners of the second copy were — ‘Severinus Pauli[?]’, Leipzig c. 1583, and Christiern Jensen of Copenhagen, 1620 — is unknown beyond their inscriptions, and neither is Tycho; a full reading of the inscriptions and the university matriculation registers would identify them.

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-mort-kb-flemlose
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Astronomy (eclipse)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 346 (s.v. Flemlöse, Peder Jacobsen)
Ownership marks
Inscription: No Tycho ownership mark. Full 32-image EEB scan of KB Hielmst. 1226 4 read: only the Hielmstierne armorial bookplate (engr. C.M. Tuscher, datable 1743-51), the Bibliotheca Regia Hafniensis stamp, and plain 18th-c paper boards.
Surviving copy
Hielmst. 1226 4°, Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark: the only marks are eighteenth-century Hielmstierne -- the Tuscher bookplate (1743-51) and the Bibliotheca Regia Hafniensis stamp. It is nonetheless the sole surviving copy of the edition (unicum, L. Nielsen).
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Note
That Tycho owned the work is well founded: the Aegloga is dedicated to him (17 October 1574), and Flemløse came to Hven early in 1578 as one of his very first pupils (Norlind 1970, p. 346). This copy, however, is not demonstrably Tycho’s. The only surviving copy known (a unicum, according to L. Nielsen as cited by Norlind 1970, p. 346) is KB Hielmst. 1226 4, an eighteenth-century Hielmstierne Danica acquisition carrying no mark of Tycho’s. No Prague or Clementinum copy is known: the work appears in none of Kleinschnitzová, Prandtl or Šolc, and the Czech National Library’s index of former owners records no copy of Brahe’s. Norlind uses no verb of ownership: he infers only that a copy was ‘högst troligt’ on Hven, from the dedication, not that the Copenhagen copy is Tycho’s. The copy is therefore rejected as Tycho’s, while ownership of the work is retained at grade C. Status attested, B, since 20 October 2026: the work-level ownership is sound on the dedication; the Royal Library's copy, judged in its own volume record, is not shown to be his.
Norlind 1970, p. 346
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Flemlöse blev en högt betrodd assistent hos Tycho, kom till Hven i början av 1578 såsom en av hans allra första lärjungar. Redan dessförinnan hade han emellertid stått i förbindelse med den omkr. 8 år äldre Tycho, såsom framgår av, att han tillägnat denne sin bok. Den utgör en episk herdedikt, behandlande den stundande solförmörkelsen i nov. 1574, vilken enligt Flemlöse bebådar Kristi snara återkomst. Förordet är dat. Köpenhamn i mitten av okt. 1574. Han har alltså avslutat boken vid den tid, då Tycho höll sina föreläsningar vid universitetet där. På dessa föreläsningar syftar Flemlöse fol. A3r; förmodligen har han varit en av åhörarna. Det får anses som högst troligt, att ett exemplar av boken fanns i biblioteket på Hven. – Enligt Lauritz Nielsen är endast ett exemplar numera känt (i Det kgl. Bibliotek i Köpenhamn).

Inferred from Tycho's use (Norlind's principle), retired as unlocatableCrec-e-norlind-gemma-frisius-astrolabo
Status

Subject

Attested by

Norlind records
Opera omnia: III, 74
Note
Norlind 1970, p. 347: listed among the books of the library because Tycho discusses the tract in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 74); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). Norlind shows by textual comparison which edition Tycho used: the sentence ‘Quicquid alii de ea scribant’ stands in the edition of 1556, published after the author’s death by his son Cornelius Gemma, and in Tycho’s text, but not in Everaert’s compendium of 1583 (Ortroy, nos. 129–130). Use is shown; ownership is the inference. If Tycho’s copy survives, it would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.
Norlind 1970, p. 347
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Efter denna upplaga, som utgavs efter förf:s död av sonen Cornelius Gemma, citerar Tycho i »Prog.» (III, 74) och icke efter det av Martinus Everhardus publicerade kompendiet, som trycktes i Antverpen 1583 (Ortroy, a.a. nr 130). Detta framgår av en jämförelse mellan de båda upplagorna och Tychos text. Såväl i uppl. 1556 som hos Tycho står så t.ex. satsen »Quicquid alii de ea scribant», som emellertid saknas i uppl. 1583.

Road of dispersal
Road II, The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601). The copy carries a scored (cancelled) former ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647, both unread, unidentified later annotations on the front endleaf, and an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001): the traces of its route between Tycho's heirs and Felix Mainx's purchase in Prague in 1938. Gingerich 2002 (p. 326) places the book ‘around 1955’ in Harald Mortensen's own collection: a misreading of Mortensen's paper, which reports Mainx's acquisition; Martayan Lan's provenance line (‘the private collection of a professor in Prague’) has it right.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Tycho’s heavily annotated working copy of Gemma’s book on the new star of 1572, printed by Christopher Plantin at Antwerp in 1575. The notes on Muñoz’s observations are the passage he quotes in the Progymnasmata, and Grafton’s report for the dealer found a genetic relation between the marginalia and the printed work (Prague 1602). The copy was recorded as Tycho’s by Mortensen (1955, p. 30) on Felix Mainx’s report that he had acquired it in Prague in 1938, listed by Norlind (1970, p. 347) from Mortensen, and identified as annotated in Tycho’s hand only when Martayan Lan offered it in 2001 (Catalogue 28, item 55, US$ 300,000, with a colour plate of Book II, pp. 124–125); the hand was confirmed by Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and is reproduced as fig. 1 of Gingerich 2002, p. 326, which records the sale to a private American collector. The binding is Tycho’s portrait-and-arms supralibros on flexible vellum. Mortensen’s own sentence says that Professor Felix Mainx acquired the Gemma in Prague in 1938 and told Mortensen of it; the book was never in Mortensen’s collection, and Gingerich’s ‘the same collector’ (2002, p. 326) misreads him.
Norlind 1970, p. 347
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Innehåller i 2:a tomen, s. 111 ff. bl.a. om den nya stjärnan; Gemmas observationer av denna diskuteras i »Prog.» (III, 67–80). Om ett exemplar som tillhört Tycho meddelar H. Mortensen, s. 30.
Open questions
  • Who now owns the book: the private American buyer of 2001 (from Martayan Lan) is unidentified; the dealer’s records or a later sale would name him.
  • In which library the book sat before Mainx bought it in Prague in 1938 — possibly the monastery in which he found the eight further Tycho volumes in 1943; the scored former ownership inscription, the later inscription dated 1647 and the old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001) would name it once read.
  • What the annotations contain in full: Martayan Lan’s list of the annotated locations with partial transcription and Anthony Grafton’s report of 2001 are unpublished, and their publication or an examination of the volume would settle it.

Open questions
  • The number 2781 that Studnička read on the spine in 1901: the spine now shows no number, label or lettering, in direct or in raking light (the Ransom Center’s photographs of 7 October 2026). Whether the number was inked on the parchment and has faded, stood on a paper label since lost, or was never where Studnička placed it cannot be settled from photographs; ultraviolet light on the spine would show faded ink, and the hand that Studnička attributed to Tycho can no longer be examined at all.
  • The pencil note ‘Aus Tycho Brahes Bibliothek!’ on the front flyleaf and the number 760 on the front pastedown: whose hands — Laube's, the Leipzig bookseller's or Prandtl's — is not known; a comparison with Laube's or Prandtl's known hand would settle the note.
  • When and from whom Prandtl bought the volume (after Laube's death in 1923?), and when the University of Texas acquired the Prandtl collection: the catalogue record gives no accession date, and the bookplate none.

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-gessner-thierbuch
Status

Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Gesner, Conradus)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VI, 231; VI, 240; VI, 244
Note
Norlind: ‘Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch’ — Tycho, who also had Gessner’s Thierbuch. The book is attested only by Tycho’s own letter to Landgrave Wilhelm of September 1591, which places the Oryx description on fol. 68 (Opera omnia VI, 244). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Whether his copy was the 1563 or the 1583 edition is unrecorded; Norlind holds it immaterial, the two editions being in his words identical: Zurich, Christoph Froschauer, 1563 (VD16 G 1728), reissued 1583 (VD16 G 1729), folio. It is a different book from the surviving Gessner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zurich 1565; Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 46; now at the University of Texas at Austin). The only Thierbuch physically traced in Tycho’s orbit is Landgrave Wilhelm’s own Kassel copy, not Tycho’s, destroyed in an air raid in September 1941.
Norlind 1970, p. 348
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Lantgreve Wilhelm ägde upplagan 1563, efter vad han skriver till Tycho maj 1591 (VI, 231). Han uppger, att »in dem Deutschen Exemplari Gesneri de Animalibus Quadrupedibus» skulle på fol. 85 stå en beskrivning med bild av ett djur, kallat Rix eller Oryx (till Tycho aug. s.å.; VI, 240). Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch (om uppl. 1563 eller 1583 få vi ej veta, men det är betydelselöst, då båda upplagorna äro identiska), finner fol. 68 en beskrivning dock utan bild av det märkliga djuret (till lantgreven sept. 1591; VI, 244). Han menar därför, att lantgreven måste ha en annan upplaga. Lantgrevens uppgift är emellertid oriktig, ty i de båda upplagorna står fol. 68ᵛ en beskrivning utan bild under rubriken »Von der wilden Geyss Oryx genannt». Fol. 85ʳ finnes däremot bild och beskrivning av en älg (»Von dem Pferdthirtz»). – Lantgrevens exemplar (i Kassel) gick förlorat vid ett bombangrepp i sept. 1941.

Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek), Apodixis physica et mathematica de cometis. Görlitz, 1581, 4°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-hagecius-apodixis
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Astronomy (comet)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2979 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933
Acquisition
1581; a copy sent by Bartholomaeus Scultetus from Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581; Opera omnia VII, 64) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 64; IV, 293-295
Note
A copy was sent to Tycho by Scultetus in Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581, Opera omnia VII, 64). Tycho discusses the work in his book on the comet (Opera omnia IV, 293–295). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified, and the work belongs to the Hagecius gap: Tycho owned at least four works of Hagecius, each documented by a letter, and not one survives in the Clementinum. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78) remarked on the absence: among the Clementinum Tychoniana there is not a single work of Hagecius, though his long friendship with Tycho and Norlind’s list make it likely that Tycho had many if not all of his works, and none of the Clementinum’s Hagecius copies carries a provenance note pointing to him. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 80) names the mechanism by which such a copy could lose its provenance: composite volumes from Tycho’s library were broken up and rebound with pieces of other provenance (5 G 42, 14 J 164, 19 G 20, XII A 12), and Richard Kukula, director of the university library 1897–1918, had old Sammelbände dissolved as a matter of principle, among them, to judge by its modern binding, the Scultetus of 14 F 284. Whether Tycho’s Hagecius copies were lost or survive unrecognised remains an open question. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds three copies of the Görlitz 1581 edition — in a Luther convolute, in a convolute from the Jesuit college at Litoměřice, and as the host volume (record 000030653) of the Hagecius composite owned by the Jesuit college at Chomutov — and none bears a Tycho mark.
Norlind 1970, p. 348

Tycho’s copy, which would carry Hájek’s autograph corrections, has not been identified. The National Library of the Czech Republic’s two copies of the Frankfurt 1574 edition — one inscribed for the Chomutov Jesuit college in 1671 (‘Collegij Soctis IESV Commotonij Ao. 1671’, record 000154680), one stamped ‘REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN.’ (record 000014579) — have no earlier owner in the library’s records.

Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile
Road of dispersal
Road VI, Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik. Chomutov college (catalogued 1671) → by a route not yet established → Biblioteka Kórnicka. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Heidenstein’s history of Stephen Báthory’s Muscovite war in the Basel edition of 1588 (Waldkirch, 184 pp., 4°), in a white parchment binding with Tycho’s gilt portrait medallion on the upper cover and the arms medallion on the lower, each ringed by his distich — the livery he gave presentation copies and books he valued (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 81) — and with the Chomutov college’s catalogue inscription of 1671 on the title. The volume never reached the Clementinum: it is at the Biblioteka Kórnicka (Cim.Qu.2812), whose record notes the supralibros and the arms plate and whose digitisation shows the volume. The one Prague copy of the Cracow edition of 1584 (Sign. 22 B 201) carries no mark of his. How the book went from Chomutov to Kórnik is not established.
Open questions
  • How the volume passed from the Chomutov college, which catalogued it in 1671, to Kórnik: the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’ on the pastedown and ‘hh: 310.’ on the flyleaf, and the red stamp ‘Z HANKOWYCH’ at the foot of the title, have not been identified, and the Kórnik record names no former owner. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 81) supposed that the Chomutov stock reached the Clementinum only in part; this is the first located volume that took another road.

Hipparchus (ed. Petrus Victorius), the copy annotated by Joseph Justus Scaliger, In Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III (the Greek editio princeps, with Scaliger’s annotations). Florence (Giunta), 1567, 2°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-corr-scaliger-books
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Astronomy
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hipparchus Bithynus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 17 April 1599 (tekstnet.dk); Kepler, GW XIX (1975)
Acquisition
1599; lent or given by Scaliger — ‘pro utroque libro mihi tam benigne concesso’ (Tycho to Scaliger, 17 April 1599) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 102; VIII, 151
Note
Hipparchus’s commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus in the Greek editio princeps of Petrus Victorius (Florence 1567), Scaliger’s own copy, annotated in his hand. Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, formerly in Tycho’s service on Hven, met Scaliger in Holland and reported that he owned the Greek text. Tycho asked in August 1598 for the book or for transcripts of the passages he needed (Opera omnia VIII, 102); Scaliger sent excerpts, acknowledged in March 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 151); and in April 1599 Tycho thanked him for two books granted him (‘pro utroque autem libro mihi tam benigne concesso’), of which the Hipparchus is the one identified. Norlind (1970, p. 362) considers that the other may be the Cyclometrica elementa duo of 1594 with Scaliger’s dedication, now Sign. 14 A 59 (Prandtl A 42). That Tycho had the annotated book itself Kepler states to Herwart von Hohenburg in January 1603: Scaliger had once sent Tycho his Hipparchus with his own notes, and it was still in the possession of the heirs (Norlind 1970, p. 350, citing the letter as Caspar nr. 242, p. 354). On 16 November 1624 Kepler asked Tycho’s son Georg Brahe for ‘Hipparchum de fixis graecè, ist ein klains folium, vnd vil drinnen manu Scaligerj’ (KGW XIX, no. 7, pp. 202–203), so the annotated book was still with the heirs two years after Tengnagel’s death. Whether Kepler obtained it is not recorded, and no copy has been traced since.
Norlind 1970, p. 349
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ed. princeps, utg. av Petrus Victorius, av det enda originalverk vi äga av antikens store astronom. – Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, tidigare i Tychos tjänst på Hven, hade under en resa i Holland träffat Scaliger. Ripensis meddelade Tycho, att Scaliger ägde en bok på grekiska om Hipparchus' observationer, tryckt »för några år sedan» i Italien. Att härmed avses ovanstående verk är otvivelaktigt. Tycho ber Scaliger (aug. 1598; VIII, 102), att antingen skicka boken eller ock en avskrift av vissa partier. Varför Tycho var så intresserad av Hipparchus' skrift, beror på att de häri meddelade noggranna uppgifterna om den heliakiska uppgången resp. nedgången för vissa stjärnor samt observationerna av deras läge på himmelssfären, jämförda med sådana uppgifter från följande århundraden, voro viktiga för hans undersökningar av precessionen. Scaliger måste ha tillmötesgått det ena alternativet i Tychos anhållan, eftersom denne i mars 1599 (VIII, 151) tackar honom bl.a. för hans besvär med excerpering av vissa ställen hos såväl Hipparchus som Ptolemeus. Härav framgår alltså icke, att Tycho erhållit boken utan endast Scaligers excerpter ur densamma. Men från annat håll veta vi, att Tycho verkligen ägt ett exemplar av boken med Scaligers egenhändiga anteckningar. I jan. 1603 (Caspar nr 242, s. 354) skriver nämligen Kepler till Herwart, att Scaliger en gång skickade till Tycho Hipparchus' skrift med sina egenhändiga anteckningar och att den ännu befinner sig i Tychos arvingars ägo. Kepler har tydligen varit mycket intresserad av att förvärva exemplaret, ty så sent som i nov. 1624 (Caspar till nr 242, s. 499) skriver han till Tychos son Jörgen Brahe: »Sonderlich hett ich gern Hipparchum de fixis græce, ist ein klains folium, und vil drinnen manu Scaligeri.»
Open questions
  • Where the Victorius Hipparchus of 1567 with Scaliger’s annotations went after November 1624, when it was last recorded with Tycho’s heirs; it has not been found.

Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Manuscriptorium)
Note
A Prague imprint of 1606, five years after Tycho’s death, carrying ‘Ex Biblioth. Tijchoniana’, the Clementinum inscription of 1642 and the Tychonian shelf-mark ‘T.B. 27’; bound with it is Kepler’s De Jesu Christi servatoris nostri vero anno natalitio (Frankfurt 1606). Kukula, who published the volume in 1906–07 (no. VII), took the two tracts as proof that the family and Kepler kept the library together and added to it after 1601 and 1604; Prandtl (1932, p. 16) read it the same way — the heirs had apparently left the working library to Kepler, who carried it on for some years. The volume belongs to the Tychoniana as the Jesuits marked them, not to Tycho’s own library. Šolc 2006 (printed p. 192 (scan 6)) names the heirs' additions ‘for example’ as De Stella Nova in pede Serpentarii and De stella tertii honoris in Cygno (both Prague 1606) and the Frankfurt ‘pars altera’ of 1606 — the two Prague titles one book, the Frankfurt piece the De Jesu Christi … vero anno natalitio bound with it here, the identification being the house's — and has them given to the Clementinum Jesuits together with the harder-to-sell, predominantly astronomical part of the library.

Note
Kepler to Tycho, Graz, 13 December 1597 (Opera omnia VIII, 14–15), sent no copy of the Mysterium cosmographicum (Tübingen 1596), supposing that Tycho already had one: ‘Exemplaria non dubito, quin antea habeas: quare facile patior, ut difficultas transmittendi per tantum intervallum a mittendo me avocet’. Tycho to Kepler, Wandsbek, 1 April 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, 44), replied that he had seen and read the book before: ‘Librum tuum, quem Prodromum vocas Dissertationum Cosmographicarum, iam ante videram et … perlegeram’. So already Norlind 1970, p. 350. How and when his copy reached him is not recorded; no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.

Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Keplers berömda ungdomsverk. – Egendomligt är, att Tycho åtminstone icke till att börja med fick något dedikationsexemplar. Kepler skriver nämligen i sitt första brev till Tycho (dec. 1597; VIII, 14), att han förmodar, att Tycho redan förut äger boken; därför skickar han icke något exemplar. Tycho svarar från Wandsbek i april 1598 (VIII, 44), att han fick brevet från Helmstedt. Boken hade han förut och han hade tagit del av densamma. Tychos brev innehåller många lovord över boken. Jfr s. 199 ff.
Open questions

Krabbe, Johannes, Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae. 1600, Manuskript

LocatedACopenhagen, Royal Libraryrec-e-norlind-krabbe-observations
Status
Located · entry confidence A
Type
Manuscript
Subject
Astronomy (observations)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 351 (s.v. Krabbe, Johannes); TBOO
Acquisition
after 30 June 1600; procured through Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg at Tycho's request of April 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, p. 295) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
inscriptions: Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunæ per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factæ; copy located by Norlind at: Gl. kgl. S. 2° 318, fol. 159r (a leaf among Tycho's own observations; Norlind prints only the shelfmark, i.e. Köpenhamn, KB, Gammel kongelig Samling); Opera omnia: VIII, 295
Surviving copy
GKS 318 2°, Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) · identification A
sewn among Tycho's own observation books, in the codex of his observations of 1600–1601; Tycho's autograph marginal notes on the leaf
Links: catalogue record
Road of dispersal
Road VIII, With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604). The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Observation codex
The leaf is sewn into one of Tycho’s own observation volumes, the codex GKS 318 2°.
Note
Not a book: a single manuscript leaf of another astronomer’s eclipse observations, obtained by Tycho, annotated in his hand and kept among his own observation books. In April 1600 Tycho asked Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg to procure the eclipse observations that Johannes Krabbe, since 1585 mathematician to Duke Heinrich Julius of Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, was said to have made, together with the method by which the times had been taken, so that a comparison with his own observations would give the difference in meridian between the observing places (Tycho to Rollenhagen, April 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 295). The leaf arrived. Headed ‘Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae’, it records seven lunar and six solar eclipses of 1581–1600 observed at Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel and Gröningen near Halberstadt, the times as a rule derived from star altitudes; the solar eclipse of September 1595 could not be observed. The last observation is dated 30 June 1600, so the leaf reached Tycho after that date. In the margin Tycho wrote the mean times for Krabbe’s observations and for his own. Dreyer did not print the leaf in the Opera omnia; his commentary records it as sewn among Tycho’s observations of 1600–1601 in the Royal Library’s codex GKS 318 2°, which his edition numbers codex I, with Tycho’s annotations (Opera omnia VIII, 438, note to p. 295 line 2), and Norlind describes it from the codex (Norlind 1970, p. 351). It is entered because Norlind’s list of Tycho’s books includes the manuscripts he is known to have possessed, and because the leaf is a text by another author that Tycho acquired, owned and annotated; the observation codices themselves, being Tycho’s own writing, are not entries.
Norlind 1970, p. 351
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
I april 1600 (VIII, 295) skriver Tycho till Rollenhagen i Magdeburg, att han fått veta, att Krabbe (som sedan 1585 var astronom hos hertigen av Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel) anställt noggranna observationer av sol- och månförmörkelser. Tycho ber Rollenhagen skaffa honom detta observationsmaterial. Det räcker emellertid inte endast med vederbörliga observationsresultat utan han måste också få veta på vad sätt dessa resultat erhållits (om genom stjärnhöjder eller på annat sätt). Anledningen till att Tycho önskade alla dessa uppgifter var, att han ur en jämförelse mellan Krabbes och sina egna observationer ville bestämma meridianskillnaden mellan de båda observationsorterna. Rollenhagen har tydligen lyckats skaffa materialet, eftersom det nu befinner sig på ett blad bland Tychos egna observationer (Gl. kgl. S. 2° 318, fol. 159r). Det är icke utg. av Dreyer. Under rubriken »Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunæ per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factæ» upptagas 7 månförmörkelser och 6 solförmörkelser (den ena i sept. 1595 kunde dock icke iakttagas) för tiden 1581–1600. Tycho har gjort egenhändiga anteckningar i manuskriptet. Den sista observerade förmörkelsen är för d. 30 juni 1600; någon gång efter detta datum har Tycho således mottagit materialet. Observationsorten är icke en och densamma, utan olika (Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel och Gröningen, vid Halberstadt). Tiderna ha i regel bestämts ur stjärnhöjder. I margen har vidare Tycho antecknat medierna dels för Krabbes tider dels för sina egna.
Open questions
  • On which folio of GKS 318 2° the leaf is sewn: Dreyer’s commentary gives fol. 157, Norlind fol. 159; the codex itself would decide.

Note
Norlind 1970, p. 351 (Zinner 2632), lists the tract among the books of the library because Tycho discusses it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 218–225); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). The edition Tycho discusses is the Lauingen edition, not the reprint De nova stella iudicia … Leovitii et Gemmae (s. l. 1573, Zinner 2633). As an unbound tract, Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised, and none has been identified.

Note
Tycho reprinted Maestlin’s tract in full in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 58–67) and praised it (‘liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande’). Reprinting the tract in full implies that the Frischlin volume containing it was in Tycho’s hands, but Norlind frames the passage as discussion rather than ownership, and the attestation is accordingly graded C. There is no documented receipt, no inventory entry, and no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
Norlind 1970, p. 352
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ingår på s. 27–32 i: Frischlin, Nicodemus: Consideratio novæ stellæ ... Tubingæ 1573.4°. Z. 2622. Tycho har avtryckt den lilla skriften helt i »Prog.» (III, 58–67), där han också diskuterar den; den är, skriver han, liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande och gedigen än de flesta större avhandlingar i ämnet. Dock nämner han ej, att den ingår i Frischlins verk.
Norlind 1970, p. 347
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Se: Mæstlinus, M., Demonstratio ...
Open questions
  • Whether the Swedish words ‘liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande’, given as Tycho’s praise of the tract, are Norlind’s own wording or his rendering of a passage of Tycho’s; Norlind’s page and the Progymnasmata passage (Opera omnia III, 58–67) would decide.

1600; commissioned copy (Manuscript copying and transmission)
Note
Herwart had the Revelatio ascribed to Methodius transcribed for Tycho because the volume that contained it was too bulky to send, and despatched the copy from Munich with the Alphonsine tables (Herwart to Tycho, 10 December 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 393: ‘METHODIJ uti fertur Revelationem, quam describi curavi, cum liber, cui inserta fuerat, ob molem transferri nequeat’). The transcript is not among the Clementinum volumes and has not been identified at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, or the Austrian National Library; the text survives in many copies, and a transcript without Tycho’s own mark cannot be told from them. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique transcript made for Tycho and sent, not a mass-survival text.

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-offusius-divina
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
