Astronomy/Astrology/Mathematics
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 355 (s.v. Offusius, Iofrancus)
Acquisition
1575; received from Hagecius at their meeting at Regensburg in November 1575 (Opera omnia VII, 184; II, 421) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 184; II, 421; VII, 121; VII, 147
Note
Norlind 1970, p. 355: Tycho received a copy of the printed book from Hagecius at their meeting at Regensburg in November 1575 (Opera omnia VII, 184; II, 421) and was particularly taken with its section on the planets’ influence at their varying distances from the earth; in May 1588 he wrote to Hagecius that he could no longer find the book in his library and asked him to procure another copy (VII, 121; Hagecius’s answers of November 1588 and May 1589, VII, 147 and 184). A book that left the library, or was mislaid in it, in Tycho’s own lifetime. Norlind adds that a copy stood in Queen Christina’s library which he could not find among the Reginenses in the Vatican — a lead he did not pursue, and one worth the question, since books from Prague reached her library in 1648.
Norlind 1970, p. 355
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Förordet är dat. d. 8 jan. 1556, men verket trycktes först 14 år senare. I Turin fanns före branden 1904 två manuskriptexemplar av verket (Thorndike, 6, s. 109²⁰). Ett exemplar fanns i drottning Kristinas bibliotek men kunde ej återfinnas av mig bland Reginenses i Vatikanbiblioteket. – Tycho erhöll ett exemplar av den tryckta boken genom Hagecius vid deras sammanträffande i Regensburg nov. 1575 (VII, 184, II, 421). Han var särskilt intresserad av det avsnitt som behandlade planeternas inverkan på jorden på olika avstånd från denna. Härom skriver han till Hagecius i maj 1588 (VII, 121). Han säger vidare, att han nu inte längre kan finna boken i sitt bibliotek och han ber Hagecius skaffa ett annat exemplar. Denne synes först inte ha vetat vad det gällde för bok (brev nov. s.å.; VII, 147); hans efterforskningar efter denna i biblioteken i Prag hade ej lett till något resultat. I ett senare brev maj 1589 (VII, 184) skriver han emellertid, att han nu minns, vilken bok det varit.
Open questions
  • Whether Hagecius sent the second copy Tycho asked for in 1588; and whether the Offusius Norlind records in Queen Christina’s library, unfound among the Reginenses, is a copy from Prague (Norlind 1970, p. 355).

Norlind (1970, p. 356): ‘Ett exemplar har Tycho säkerligen ägt’ — of either the Ferrara edition of 1591 or the Venice edition of 1593, perhaps the later. His basis is a note in Tycho’s hand in the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences copy of the Progymnasmata (p. 165), naming Patritius among the authors whose writings reached him only after the chapters they belonged to were printed. Tycho complained to Kepler that Patrizi misrepresented his world-system (Tycho to Kepler, December 1599, Opera omnia VIII, 206). The only surviving evidence of Tycho’s ownership is that annotation in his own Progymnasmata, not a mark in a copy of Patrizi; the work is common, and no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
Norlind 1970, p. 356
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ett exemplar har Tycho säkerligen ägt av endera upplagan Ferrara 1591 eller Venedig 1593 (kanske den senare att döma av en hans anteckning i KVA:s exemplar av »Prog.», se ovan s. 165). Till Kepler skriver han i dec. 1599 (VIII, 206), att Patritius i sin bok lämnat en helt vilseledande framställning av Tychos världssystem. Tycho menar väl vad Patritius skriver fol. 91ʳ (=Pancosmia, liber XII), att enligt Tychos världssystem skulle Merkurius' och Venus' banor skära solbanan i två punkter. Enligt Tychos framställning i kometboken var det dock endast Mars-banan som skar solbanan.
Open questions
  • Which edition Tycho owned, the Ferrara folio of 1591 or the Venice issue of 1593: Norlind (1970, p. 356) inclines to the later on the strength of Tycho’s note in the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences copy of the Progymnasmata (p. 165), which names Patritius among the authors whose writings reached him only after the chapters they belonged to were printed.

Sächsische Landesbibliothek Dresden
Note
A book by another author that Tycho owned (Paulus Alexandrinus, edited from Heinrich Rantzau’s library, Wittenberg 1588), in its original Tychonic binding. Reported by Isak Collijn to Flora Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78 n. 1) as a Tychonianum in the Landesbibliothek Dresden, the companion to the Waldstein (Mnichovo Hradiště) copy of Tycho’s own De nova stella, which, as a copy of one of Tycho’s own works, lies outside this library. The volume is lost: Norlind (1970, p. 356) records the Dresden library’s own communication that the copy ‘gått förlorat under senaste världskrig’ — was lost in the Second World War. Šolc still lists the volume in Dresden — ‘befand sich … in der Sächsischen Landesbibliothek Dresden’ (1999, § 2.533, printed p. 150) and, in the present tense, ‘se nachází v Zemské knihovně v Drážďanech’ (2006, p. 192) — and nowhere mentions the loss Norlind reports from the library itself; neither text cites a sighting. The entry keeps ‘lost’ on Norlind's report; a question to the SLUB (its war-loss records, and whether a Paulus Alexandrinus, Wittenberg 1588, in a Tychonic binding has since been acquired) would close it.
Norlind 1970, p. 356

Praetorius, Johannes, De cometis qui antea visi sunt et de eo qui ... Novembri apparuit, narratio. Nürnberg, 1578, 4°

Attested, not locatedCrec-e-norlind-praetorius-decometis
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence C
Subject
Astronomy (comet)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 357 (s.v. Prætorius, Johannes); Zinner no. 2845 (after Norlind)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: IV, 356–358; III, 153–157; VII, 120; VII, 147; VII, 212
Note
Tycho treats the work at length in the comet book (Opera omnia IV, 356–358; cf. Progymnasmata, Opera omnia III, 153–157). Thorndike (History of Magic and Experimental Science VI, p. 84) held that neither Tycho nor Hagecius owned a copy. Norlind shows that Thorndike misread the three passages of the correspondence on which he relied (Opera omnia VII, 120, 147 and 212), which concern Apianus and Pena and not this book, and so defends Tycho’s ownership against Thorndike’s denial. The Czech National Library holds the work as the fourth tract of a Hagecius composite volume from the Jesuit college at Chomutov; its record notes no mark of Tycho’s.
Norlind 1970, p. 357
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Behandlas utförligt i kometboken (IV, 356–358; jfr »Prog.»; III, 153–157) – Thorndike, 6, s. 84 menar, att varken Tycho eller Hagecius ägt något exemplar. Thorndike har dock missförstått de tre ställen i Tychos korrespondens, där enligt honom detta skulle bekräftas. Samtliga ställen (VII, 120, 147, 212) avse Apianus och Pena.

Ptolemaeus, Claudius, Almagest (old Venetian edition, c. 1515). Venetiis, 1515, 2°

Attested, not locatedArec-e-letter-ptolemy-almagest-venice
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence A
Subject
Astronomy
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 358 (s.v. Ptolemæus, Claudius); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 20 January 1587 (tekstnet.dk); Fund og Forskning 1965
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VI, 95
Note
Tycho states that he owns an old Venetian Almagest, some seventy years old in 1587 (letter of 20 January 1587: ‘vetus quoddam exemplar Almagesti, ante annos proxime 70. Venetijs editum’), that is, the Latin Almagest printed at Venice by Petrus Liechtenstein in about 1515. It is distinct from the Ptolemy volumes among the Clementinum copies — the Opera (Basel), the Geographia (Cologne 1597) and the De analemmate (Rome 1562). Norlind identified the edition in print (Fund og Forskning XII, 1965, p. 156, ‘Efterslæt’): the Latin Almagest printed at Venice in 1515 (Petrus Liechtenstein; Gerard of Cremona’s version), whose prefatory life of Ptolemy — ‘indledningen til en oversættelse af Almagesten, trykt i Venedig 1515, som Tycho Brahe har ejet og nævner i et brev’ — is the source of the royal descent and the physical description of Ptolemy in Tycho’s elegy In effigiem Cl. Ptolemaei (Epistolae astronomicae, 1596, p. 239). No copy of the Venice Almagest with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Norlind 1970, p. 358
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Detta är den första tryckta latinska översättningen. Den återgår på Gerards från Cremona översättning från arabiskan. – Tycho ägde säkerligen själv detta verk (till Rothmann jan. 1587; VI, 95: »adhibui ... vetus quoddam exemplar Almagesti, ante annos proxime 70. Venetiis editum ...»).
Open questions
  • Whether a copy of the Venice Almagest of 1515 with Tycho’s marks survives; such a copy coming to light would decide.

Surviving copy

brown stamped leather with the blind initials ‘I. P. 1561’ (Johannes Pratensis); the purchase note ‘Emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris’ (hand disputed: Tycho — Dreyer, Studnička 1901; Pratensis — Boldan & Vackářová 2024); marginalia Kleinschnitzová gives to Tycho; on the title ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A°. 1642’, ‘NB. Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe’ and, in another hand, ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 4)
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Manuscriptorium)
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 31; Kleinschnitzová no. 4; National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum), shelfmark 5 B 70, bound as Band I. Friis (1868–69, p. 267) and Dreyer (1890, p. 14) read the title-page note «emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris» (bought at Copenhagen for two Joachimsthaler on the last day of November 1560) as Tycho’s own hand, and Dreyer made this the first book of the library, procured after the predicted eclipse of 21 August 1560. The same title page carries the name of Johannes Pratensis (1543–1576) and the binding his stamped initials «I P 1561»: Studnička (1901, p. 39) took Pratensis for the seller; Boldan & Vackářová (2024, pp. 143–144) take him for the first owner and suppose the book passed to Tycho from his estate. The hand of the note has not been examined. Norlind (1970, p. 358) took the ‘Ptolemaeum Tychonis’ that Benjamin Ursinus asked Kepler to request from the Rožmberk librarian (March 1614; Caspar no. 681, p. 105) to be this copy, and found the work entered in Václav Březan’s catalogue of Peter Vok of Rožmberk’s library at Třeboň, drawn up 1602–08 and now in the Royal Library, Stockholm. The copy survives, is digitised, and carries an early note beside the 1642 inscription that the marginalia are Tycho’s. Šolc (2006, printed p. 190 (scan 4)), explaining how the Ptolemy came from Pratensis ‘by 1576 at the latest, after the friend's death’, has Tycho visit him often and observe at his house ‘for example on 3 December 1573’ the lunar eclipse whose beginning and course he had computed from the Prutenic tables to within 20 minutes. Tycho's own observation note places that eclipse on 8 December 1573 at Knutstorp (‘Hanc ego Eclipsin in curia mea Knusdorpiana observavi’, TBOO X, 38–39), with the new gilt-brass quadrant and his sister Sophie's help (the loci record of the Knutstorp years); Šolc's date and place are not adopted, and the visit is not evidence for when the book passed to Tycho.
Norlind 1970, p. 358
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Det är väl på detta verk som Benjamin Ursinus syftar i ett brev till Kepler mars 1614 (Caspar nr 681, s. 105); exemplaret synes ha hamnat i Peter Vok Ursini Rosenbergs bibliotek: »Posce per me et literas a Bibliothecario Rosenbergiaco Ptolemæum Tychonis serio: spondeo te habiturum. Posce saltem. Egi iam cum eodem, ille tuas literas videre vult.» Det finns upptaget i den väldiga fyra folioband starka katalogen över det rosenbergska biblioteket på Třebon, uppgjord åren 1602–08 av Peter Vok Ursini Rosenbergs bibliotekarie Václav Březan och nu förvarad i KB., Sthm.

Ramus, Petrus (Pierre de la Ramée), Arithmeticae libri duo, geometriae septem et viginti. Basel (Episcopius), 1580, 1580

LocatedAPrague, Strahov Libraryrec-e-strahov-ramus-1580
Status
Located · entry confidence A
Subject
Mathematics (arithmetic, geometry)
Attested by
Pařez 2009; Strahov Katalog Tritius; Kleinschnitzová 1933
Ownership marks
Inscription: No Jesuit inscription. Title leaf: in ink beside the printer's device, ‘G: Crusio ‹K› / inservio.’ — the ownership formula of Gabriel Crusius, as on the National Library's 5 G 92 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 89) — and the two round Strahov stamps (read on the volume, 18 September 2026). Annotations: One reader's note seen: p. 7, cap. V De divisione, ‘Divisio igitur’ underlined and ‘Analogia divisionis & multiplicationis’ in the margin; hand not assessed. Binding: gilt portrait supralibros on the front board (bust in cloak and ruff, the Order of the Elephant on a long chain; legend HIC PATET EXTERIOR TYCHONIS FORMA BRAHEI PVLCHRIVS ENITEAT QVAE LATET INTERIOR) and the arms supralibros on the back (ARMA GENVS FVNDI PEREVNT DVRABILE VIRTVS ET DOCTRINAE DECVS NOBILITATIS HABENT), each 76 × 59 mm, on a binding of gilt-tooled brown calf over boards — not the parchment Pařez 2009 (with photographs) reports — Katalog Tritius: ‘vazba se zlacenou podobou Tychona de Brahe’
Surviving copy
AG XIV 7, Strahov Library (Strahovská knihovna, Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově) · identification A · Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
gilt portrait supralibros (front) and arms (back), 76 × 59 mm (Pařez 2009), on a gilt-tooled brown leather binding — not parchment (autopsy 18 September 2026)
Links: catalogue record · Gabriel Crusius’s inscriptions on the title of NK ČR 5 G 92, as the National Library’s record transcribes them (Manuscriptorium)
Road of dispersal
Road II, The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601). Route to Strahov undocumented beyond the Crusius layer: no Jesuit inscription, no Klauser ex-libris photographed, no later owner named in the catalogue. The same collector's other volumes went to the Chomutov Jesuits (1654) and, in the Euclid's case, to Klauser.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
One of the two Strahov volumes with the full-size portrait/arms supralibros (Pařez 2009); the other, the Opus palatinum Σ V 5/a, is bound in parchment, this one in gilt-tooled brown calf. Books carrying this plaque were printed 1584–1598 (Norlind) — this 1580 imprint sits at the lower edge, and Pařez leaves open whether the plaques were applied as the books came or in one campaign after 1598. The title inscription ‘G: Crusio ‹K› / inservio.’ is Gabriel Crusius's — the same hand and formula as on 5 G 92 (compared 19 September 2026 on the digitised leaf) — which ties this volume to the Euclid AV II 2 and to the two Chomutov gifts of 1654.
Open questions
  • The endleaves and spine for a Klauser ex-libris, Strnad's name or a Mathematical-Museum spine — the volume's last step into Strahov.

Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 33; Prandtl Einzelband XXII (National Library of the Czech Republic, Clementinum, shelfmark 1 H 56; Kleinschnitzová no. 3). The volume carries Rantzau’s autograph dedication of 1584 to Henrik Ramel, who probably passed it to Tycho (Norlind 1970, p. 359). Šolc 2002 (p. 330) lists ‘Astrologicae quaedam praedictiones; adiectus est tractatus De annis climactericis’ as a second item of the volume; it is the continuation of this print’s title. Three further works are bound with it (Kleinschnitzová 3:2–4). Heinrich Rantzau’s own library of more than six thousand volumes reached the same National Library by another road: taken from Breitenburg by Wallenstein in 1627 (1626 in Walde), given to the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana, partly confiscated by the Swedes on 2 September 1648, and in the Clementinum since the suppression of 1773 (Veselá 2025, pp. 9–10, 180–183; Lohmeier 2000, pp. 103–104). This copy came by the road of 1642 from Tycho’s heirs; the two are not to be conflated. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Norlind 1970, p. 359
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
I ett saml.-bd. På försättsbladet egenhändig dedikation 1584 av Rantzau till sedermera riksrådet Henrik Ramel, som förmodligen har skänkt exemplaret till Tycho. Av en dikt, som Tycho skrev till Rantzau och som trycktes på Uraniborg 1585, daterad d. 1 mars d.å. (IX, 187–190), framgår, att Tycho blivit smått På försättsbladet egenhändig dedikation 1584 av Rantzau till sedermera riksrådet Henrik Ramel, som förmodligen har skänkt exemplaret till Tycho. Av en dikt, som Tycho skrev till Rantzau och som trycktes på Uraniborg 1585, daterad d. 1 mars d.å. (IX, 187–190), framgår, att Tycho blivit smått förargad över, att Rantzau i en bok kallat Uraniborg för »specula», varav det är uppenbart, menar Tycho, att Rantzau icke haft klart för sig, hur byggnaden såg ut: »Cuius fama tuas siquidem pervenit ad aures, Intuitu vero forte minora refert: Quippe vocas speculam, quas Divæ struximus Ædes, Vnde liquet, formam te latuisse domus.» Den bok av Rantzau som Tycho här åsyftar, är just hans »Catalogus». Första upplagan trycktes i Antwerpen 1580 och såväl här som i alla de senare upplagorna står om Uraniborg följande: »Tygonique Braden (cuius vix similem in disciplinis Mathematicis hic Septentrionalis tractus habet) rex insulam nomine Vueen cum omnibus reditibus inter Zelandiam et Schaniam ad tempus vitæ concessit, ingentemque speculam erigi curavit» etc. Detta står som sagt i alla upplagorna. Vi kunna således inte med säkerhet avgöra i vilken Tycho läste det, men det kan ha varit i upplagan 1584 (s. 75–76), vars förord är daterat d. 1 febr. 1584. Exemplaret i Prag fick han dock säkerligen först senare.

Note
Norlind records the book as received from the author (‘Erhöll Tycho av förf.’), on the evidence of Tycho to Rantzau, April 1590 (Opera omnia VII, 243). Rantzau’s own copy, into which a transcript of Tycho’s elegy to Denmark was bound and which King Christian leafed through on a visit to Rantzau (Opera omnia VIII, 63), is a different book. Two copies of the 1590 edition in the Royal Library, Hielmst. 547 2° and Hielmst. 146 2°, examined in facsimile, descend from Henrik Hielmstierne and bear neither a mark of Tycho’s nor the bound-in transcript. No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
Copies of the edition examined
  • Det Kongelige Bibliotek (Royal Library), Copenhagen, Hielmst. 547 2° [19,-167] — Hamburg: Jacob Wolf, 1590 (Zinner 3399; USTC 689799). Henrik Hielmstierne (1715–1780); his library to the Royal Library. Earlier: contemporary presentation inscription on the title-page foot, “Reverendo et Doctiss[imo] viro Johanni Fab[…]” — a gift to a clergyman named Johann, not Tycho. Title-page presentation inscription (16th/17th-c., to “Johann Fab[…]”); 18th-c. octagonal armorial ex-libris (harpy supporters) = Hielmstierne; interior printed calendar tables clean of annotation.
  • Det Kongelige Bibliotek (Royal Library), Copenhagen, Hielmst. 146 2° [19,-167] — Hamburg: Jacob Wolf, 1590 (Zinner 3399; USTC 689799). Henrik Hielmstierne (1715–1780); his library to the Royal Library. None of note: no inscription, no ex-libris, blank flyleaves.

Status
Located · entry confidence A
Subject
Astronomy (ephemerides)
Attested by
GW M37507 (+ M37488); ISTC ir00108500 (+ ir00105000 gatherings a4 a10); Straka 1913; Boldan 2025; Strahov Katalog Tritius; Munzar & Pařez 2002; Munzar 2001; Hyklová 2017; Voit 2015
Ownership marks
Inscription: fol. a2r: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (Straka 1913; Boldan 2025; Katalog Tritius 1064031). Later hands: ‘Ex libris Johannis Nachlovsky’ (fol. a1v) and ‘Nachlovsky’ (a2r) — later than Tycho per Boldan 2025; ‘Joannes Josephus Worell’ and ‘Anna’, with a drawn basket, on the second leaf (Straka 1913) Annotations: A 34-line Latin note on the winter of 1495/96 on the verso of the leaf carrying December 1495 (‘fol. 75.b’ in the old foliation, Straka; ‘e4v’, Boldan 2025; ‘e14b (75v) druhého přívazku’ — of the second constituent, the 1492 almanac — Katalog Tritius). Munzar and Pařez's transcription (2002, p. 372): ‘Haec hiems tanta frigoris in Bruma asperitate referta erat tantaeq(ue) nivium moles passim conglomoratae, ut agrestium casarum culmina superantes desup(er) homines in redis iter expeditissime facerent at sequuta est in sequente aestate maxima lues wulgo gallica scabies dicta Germanis & Danis ante ea tempora non solum incognita sed pro(r)sus inaudita q(uod) multa hominum milia infecit. Ratio e(st) quod omnes planete sint in frigidis & humidis signis praesertim introeunte ☉ in initia solstitii hiberni. Ex quibus certissimum inditium frigoris & copiosae nivis sumi poterat. Rarum exemplum.’ — then a table of the seven planets' signs. Attributed to Tycho's own hand by Straka in 1913 on an undocumented comparison by eye; compared letter by letter, again by eye, with the DG IV 25 motto and the AG XI 56 dedication by Munzar & Pařez (2002, pp. 372–373), who find the hand ‘with a high probability’ Tycho's and at the least that of his immediate circle, who read the note as a retrospective astrometeorological reconstruction from historical reports rather than a weather record, and who date the winter to 1495/96 from independent climate records and a reconstruction of the planetary positions; called ‘vlastnoruční’ by Boldan (2025) — and called hypothetical by Pařez himself (2026). Their fig. 5 (p. 371) reproduces the note. Never examined graphonomically. Other hands in the volume: the reference-meridian note above the Tabula regionum (‘Nota hec Ephemerides sunt supputate ad longitudinem …’) and three front flyleaves of mathematical calculations running onto fol. 1a1a, signed ‘Josephus Worel’ above a drawn basket (Katalog Tritius dates the hand c. 1766; Straka read ‘Joannes Josephus Worell’ and ‘Anna’), which also foliated the volume. Binding: Contemporary binding: wooden boards 230 × 150 mm covered in leather for a third of their width only, the leather nailed to the boards with small brass nails and blind-tooled in a frame composition now almost worn away; the spine damaged at the head, undecorated; a faint ‘ALMANACH’ on the front board; the central clasp removed; yellow edges (Katalog Tritius 1064031; Straka 1913: bare boards with a glued and nailed leather spine; Boldan 2025: a contemporary tanned-leather binding with the blind-tooling worn).
Surviving copy
DR VII 19/1–2, Strahov Library (Strahovská knihovna, Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově) · identification A · contemporary bare-board binding, not Tycho's bindery
fol. a2r: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (the Jesuit accession inscription; Straka 1913, Boldan 2025, Tritius); the 34-line weather note attributed to his hand (Straka 1913) — attribution open
Links: catalogue record
Road of dispersal
Road VI, Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik. Carries the 1642 inscription yet stands at Strahov. Straka 1913: Clementinum → the astronomer Antonín Strnad (d. 1799) → Strahov, whose purchase of Strnad's library is documented (Munzar 2001); Strahov's present cataloguer objects that the volume is in neither published catalogue of Strnad's library (Seydl 1939; Kouklová 1989) and suspects Straka confused it with Stoeffler–Pflaum's Almanach nova (Venice 1507), which did come from Strnad and bears AG VII 87. Boldan 2025 leaves it open whether Tycho acquired the volume before or after coming to Bohemia. The library's own record agrees with Straka on the first step and doubts the second: ‘then the volume became part of the so-called Mathematical Museum in the Clementinum, from which it passed to Strahov (original shelfmark AG VII 84)’ — but Seydl and Kouklová do not list it in Strnad's library, and Straka may have confused it with the Stoeffler–Pflaum almanac AG VII 87. Munzar and Pařez (2002, p. 369) supposed the Strahov purchase ‘probably not before the abolition of the Jesuit Order in 1773’. The calculations signed by Worel, which the catalogue dates c. 1766, would then have been written while the volume was still in the Clementinum.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Not a second copy of Kleinschnitzová 14. Boldan 2025 (33.b, 33.c, 36.a): the National Library's Venice 1481 Ephemerides (his shelfmark 40 F 39; our Kleinschnitzová no. 14 records 14 H 188) LACKS its first gatherings a4 a10, and the Strahov volume CONTAINS exactly those gatherings, bound before the Augsburg 1492 Ephemerides 1492–1506 — the two are halves of one Tycho book, both inscribed by the Jesuits in 1642. Straka's ‘first incunable, Ephemerides c. 1476–82, a fragment lacking eight leaves and its end’ is the 1481 prefatory gatherings; his second, ‘Almanach … ad annos XV … 1492’, lacking seven leaves in the text and eighteen at the end, is the almanac that carries the note. The weather note is the case Pařez calls hypothetical; its attribution rests on Straka's eye and on content — the ‘Germanis et Danis’ of the plague sentence is the strongest internal pointer — and the note stands as attributed, not as autograph. The 1481 part is 358 leaves short: only gathering 1a4 (Ratdolt's and Regiomontanus's prefaces) and fol. a5–6 of gathering 2a (Mariensüss's Expositio) survive, their printed initials uncoloured and the rubrics unfilled (Katalog Tritius).
Open questions
  • The National Library twin (Kleinschnitzová no. 14, now 40 F 39 according to Boldan 2025) is reported by Boldan to lack gatherings a4 and a10; the two copies have not been compared.
  • The published halftone of the note (Munzar & Pařez 2002, fig. 5, p. 371) allows a first comparison with the securely attributed specimens of Tycho’s hand; a photograph of fol. e4v at specimen scale would allow a full one.
  • Who Josef Worel was, and whether a hand dated c. 1766 inside a volume the Jesuits held until 1773 belongs to a Clementinum student or shows the volume outside the college earlier than supposed.

Inferred from Tycho's use (Norlind's principle), retired as unlocatableCrec-e-norlind-reinhold-practica-1574
Status
Inferred from Tycho's use (Norlind's principle), retired as unlocatable · entry confidence C
Subject
Astronomy (nova 1572)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 361 (s.v. Reinholdus, Erasmus); Zinner no. 2681 (after Norlind)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: III, 212–216
Note
Norlind 1970, p. 361 (Zinner 2681): listed among the books of the library because Tycho discusses the tract in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 212–216); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). The Practica is the work of the astronomer’s son, the physician Erasmus Reinhold the younger, whom Norlind’s headword does not distinguish from the author of the Prutenic tables. An unbound tract of this kind, if Tycho’s copy survives, would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.
Norlind 1970, p. 361
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)

Det framgår av flera yttranden av Tycho, hur viktigt detta arbete var för honom. Till Herwart skriver han sålunda i nov. 1599 (VIII, 200), att han för 20 år sedan hade börjat syssla med detta verk. Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 388
Surviving copy
Σ V 5/a, Strahov Library (Strahovská knihovna, Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově) · identification A · Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
gilt portrait supralibros (front) and arms (back), 76 × 59 mm (Pařez 2009; measured c. 76 × 58 mm on the front board, 18 September 2026), on a parchment binding of the Knihvazač rudolfínského okruhu II, 1599–1601 (Pařez 2009; Voit 2020, pp. 250–252; NUSK 33); Jesuit inscription of 1642
Links: catalogue record
Road of dispersal
Road VI, Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik. Carries the 1642 inscription yet stands at Strahov: a volume that left the Clementinum core — the documented route is Ungar's post-1773 duplicate screening and Strnad's purchase of the surplus, whose library Strahov bought after 1799; not yet documented for this volume.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Norlind: ‘kanske detta stora verk som Tycho erhöll som gåva av lantgreve Moritz’ — perhaps the ‘Opus illud Palatinum’ Tycho received as a gift from Landgrave Moritz and thanked him for in November 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, 388; the relevant lines are struck in the draft). The copy at the Strahov Library, Σ V 5/a, carries Tycho’s portrait and arms supralibros on a parchment binding of the Rudolfine circle and the Jesuit inscription of 1642 (Pařez 2009; Voit 2020, pp. 250–252; Katalog Tritius 1046995). Whether it is the ‘Opus illud Palatinum’ of the November 1600 letter is an open question. The binder is no guide to the route: Voit (2021, p. 117) counts about seventy volumes of the Rudolfine-circle binder II at Strahov, arrived by several hands — Pontanus’s gifts of 1595, Troilo von Lessoth’s books, Pistorius z Lucka. The library’s record cites, beside Voit 2020, his Boj o volnou plochu (2023), pp. 209 and 560, and lists the copy in the NUSK binding database (exemplar 5089). The Czech National Library holds two copies of the Neustadt (Harnisch) edition of 1596, 14 A 12, complete, and a second, defective copy; neither record names a former owner.
Norlind 1970, p. 361
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Det var kanske detta stora verk som Tycho erhöll som gåva av lantgreve Moritz och för vilket han tackar i ett brev till denne (nov. 1600; VIII, 388: »Opus illud Palatinum»; några rader i brevet, inkl. detta ställe äro emellertid strukna i konceptet).
Open questions
  • Whether this is the ‘Opus illud Palatinum’ for which Tycho thanked Landgrave Moritz in November 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, 388): neither Pařez 2009 nor the Tritius record reports a gift inscription, and the wording of the Jesuit inscription of 1642 is unpublished; a reading of the inscriptions in the volume would decide.
  • By what route the volume passed from the Clementinum to Strahov, which is undocumented for this copy; a Mathematical Museum spine signature or Strnad’s name-stamp would settle it.

Open questions
  • Whose hand the main text is in: Prandtl (1932, Verzeichnis A no. 41) records the manuscript as Tycho’s own copy (‘eigenhändige Abschrift Tycho’s’), but the Truhlář catalogue, followed by Manuscriptorium, dates the codex 1539–1550, before Tycho’s birth; whether the hand is Tycho’s, the codex a later copy of a work of 1539, or the writer another scribe with Tycho only as owner, a comparison with his securely attributed specimens would decide.
  • Whose account the cost note on f. 1r is — it is headed ‘Andreas Schöner’ and reckons in pfennigs — and whether the monogram beside it, read as T B, is Tycho’s: Studnička (1901) took both for Tycho’s; a comparison of hands, none of which has been published, would decide.

Scaliger, Joseph Justus, De emendatione temporum (revised ed.; Leiden, Plantin 1598). Lugduni Batav., 1598, 2°

LostArec-e-letter-scaliger-emendatione
Status
Lost · entry confidence A
Subject
Chronology
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 362 (s.v. Scaliger, Joseph Justus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 14 March 1598 (tekstnet.dk); Walde 1938; Norlind 1926; Mortensen 1955
Acquisition
1598; purchase or gift (disputed: the author’s gift according to Norlind 1926, an ordinary purchase according to Walde 1938) (Procured by a correspondent or agent)
Norlind records
copy located by Norlind at: Braunsberg, Bibliothek der Staatlichen Akademie; Opera omnia: VII, 373; VIII, 32; II, 15; VIII, 20
Dispersal
seen by Walde in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg in 1937; the library burned in January 1945; not traced since
Note
Sought in 1584 through Johannes Maior, Tycho’s agent at the Frankfurt fairs; the first edition of 1583 then reached Tycho twice in June 1584, from Maior at Augsburg on 8 June (Maior to Tycho, 8 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 83: ‘Inprimis autem mihi curae fuit SCALIGERI de emendatione temporum’) and from Heinrich Brucaeus at Rostock on 12 June (Brucaeus to Tycho, 12 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 86: ‘Mitto IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM de emendatione temporum’). One of the two copies survives: Prague, National Library, Sign. 19 A 46, initialled ‘T. B.’ on the title-page; Kleinschnitzová (no. 41, p. 92) could not say which: ‘Dürfte das von Brucaeus oder Major an Brahe gesandte Exemplar sein.’ The entry concerns the revised edition of 1598, which Tycho acknowledged to Scaliger from Wandsbeck on 14 March 1598 (Tycho to Scaliger, 14 March 1598: ‘redintegratum de Temporum Emendatione... primum accepi’); Norlind (1926, no. 28) read the copy as the author’s gift, Walde (1938, p. 14 n. 2) as an ordinarily procured copy, the letter containing no thanks. A copy of this edition from Tycho’s library was found by Walde in the summer of 1937 in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg: white parchment with Tycho’s portrait on the upper and his arms on the lower board, both blind-stamped, and the decor usual on his bindings; not bound on Hven, which he left in 1597, perhaps at Wandsbeck in 1598; many marginalia in several hands, photographs of which Hans Ræder judged not to be Tycho’s; no dedication; the only later note ‘M. Braunhardt i Gotha 1761 … Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’, which Walde could not explain (a person named Oppel, or the town of Oppeln near Neisse, where Tycho’s great globe was found in 1632). Mortensen cited the find in 1955 without the title; nothing later is recorded of the volume, and Norlind’s catalogue of 1970 does not include it. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Norlind 1970, p. 362
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Originalbd med porträtt och vapen. I sept. 1595 (VII, 373) skriver Tycho till Pontanus, som då befann sig i Holland, att han önskade, att denne skulle sända Scaligers »de Emendatione Temporum præstans illud opus recognitum, ubi illud consummatum fuerit» – varmed tydligen menas föreliggande upplaga, som då ännu icke förelåg färdigtryckt. Måhända var det Pontanus, som sedan skickade det exemplar som nu finns i Braunsberg. Tycho måste ha fått verket kort efter dess publicering. Förordet är nämligen dat. d. 11 jan. 1598 (g.st.) och i mars s.å. (VIII, 32) tackar han Scaliger för dennes omnämnande av honom i boken, som han fått »just i dagarna». Tycho syftar på den tabell över sina observationer av ekvinoktierna som Scaliger på ett smickrande sätt meddelat på s. 728–729: »Tabella æquinoctii utriusque in Dania observati ab eximio artifice nobiliss. Tychone Brahe.» Denna tabell är den som Tycho tryckte i »Prog.» (II, 15) och som han måste ha skickat Scaliger tidigare, väl genom samme Pontanus, som i ett odaterat brev, sannolikt från slutet av 1597 eller början av 1598 (VIII, 20), omtalar, att Scaliger satt in Tychos observationer i verket och att Tycho snart skall få se dem. Dreyer menar i en not (»Tycho Brahe», s. 270,¹ efter Kästner, »Geschichte der Mathematik», 2, Gött. 1797, s. 409), att Scaliger som tack för några böcker Tycho skickat honom sänt honom ett exemplar av sina »Conjecturæ et notæ in Varronem», vilket exemplar Tycho skänkte eller lånade professor Taubmann i Wittenberg. Denna notis grundar sig på en fullständig missuppfattning av ett ställe i Taubmanns kommentar till Plautus »Pœnulus», vers 34 ff. (M. Acci Plauti »Comœdiæ XX. superstites ...». Wittebergæ 1612, s. 309). Taubmann hänvisar här dels till Scaligers »Conject. Varron.», dels till sammes »in Appendice operis, De emendatione temporum». Längre ned refereras till Scaliger »in Emendata quidem prædicti Operis editione». Detta syftar givetvis icke på hans »Conject. Varron.» – som Kästner och efter honom Dreyer trott – utan på den strax förut nämnda »De emendatione temporum». Vi kunna också fastställa, att upplagan 1598 avses. Endast i denna och ej i någon annan upplaga står det av Taubmann citerade stället i ett appendix, »In Fragmentum Berosi Babylonii», s. XXV. Vidare berättar Taubmann i sin Plautus-kommentar, att Scaliger skickat Tycho boken, som just lämnat pressen. Tycho var då i Wittenberg, skriver Taubmann. Det var vid ung. samma tid som han skänkte Taubmann ett exemplar av sin »Mech.» (Berlin-exemplaret) och Taubmann å sin sida sjöng hans lov i ett alkaiskt ode till kejsar Rudolf (dat. d. 21 okt. 1598; avskrift bl.a. i slutet på ett exemplar av Resen, »Inscriptiones Haffnienses», Det kgl. Bibliotek, Köpenhamn). Dreyer har varit tveksam om Tycho skänkte eller lånade Taubmann sitt exemplar (det står concessit hos Taubmann). Att det varit fråga om ett lån, framgår dock av vad Taubmann själv skriver om detta exemplar i ett brev till Scaliger, sannolikt från våren 1599 (i: P. Burmannus' »Sylloge epistolarum a viris illustribus scriptarum», T. 2, Leidæ 1727, s. 339): »quem hisce diebus ab amicissimo et pœne mihi domestico, Tychone Brahe utendum habui». Taubmanns uppgift i Plautus-kommentaren är emellertid icke fullt klar. Ty det exemplar av verket varom Tycho talar i brevet till Scaliger i mars 1598 var säkerligen icke något gåvoexemplar från denne. Hade så varit fallet, skulle Tycho omtalat det som en gåva och framfört sitt tack därför, vilket han icke gör – utan han tackar Scaliger för dennes omnämnande av hans observationer. Och vidare befann sig Tycho då på Wandsbek, icke i Wittenberg. Inget tyder på, att detta exemplar varit en skänk från Scaliger. Däremot synes Tycho, om vi få tro Taubmann, ha erhållit ett dedikationsexemplar från Scaliger under vistelsen i Wittenberg, vilket exemplar dock icke var så färskt som Taubmann skriver. Scaliger skickat Tycho boken, som just lämnat pressen. Tycho var då i Wittenberg, skriver Taubmann. Det var vid ung. samma tid som han skänkte Taubmann ett exemplar av sin »Mech.» (Berlin-exemplaret) och Taubmann å sin sida sjöng hans lov i ett alkaiskt ode till kejsar Rudolf (dat. d. 21 okt. 1598; avskrift bl.a. i slutet på ett exemplar av Resen, »Inscriptiones Haffnienses», Det kgl. Bibliotek, Köpenhamn). Dreyer har varit tveksam om Tycho skänkte eller lånade Taubmann sitt exemplar (det står concessit hos Taubmann). Att det varit fråga om ett lån, framgår dock av vad Taubmann själv skriver om detta exemplar i ett brev till Scaliger, sannolikt från våren 1599 (i: P. Open questions
  • Whether the Braunsberg copy survived the Second World War. The Hosianum library's wartime losses and the post-war route of its rescued early prints — to Moscow, back to Poland and to the seminary library at Olsztyn, with East Prussian library material also gathered at Toruń — are not documented in anything held here and are not asserted; a Scaliger, De emendatione temporum, Leiden 1598, in white parchment with the blind-stamped portrait and arms plaques and the note of M. Braunhardt, Gotha 1761, ‘Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’, in one of the successor collections would decide.

Steinmetz, Valentin, Von dem Cometen, welcher im November des 1577. Jars erstlich erschienen. , 4°

Inferred from Tycho's use (Norlind's principle), retired as unlocatableCrec-e-norlind-steinmetz-cometen-1577
Status
Inferred from Tycho's use (Norlind's principle), retired as unlocatable · entry confidence C
Subject
Astronomy (comet)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 364 (s.v. Steinmetz, Valentinus); Zinner no. 2794–96; 2860 (after Norlind)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: IV, 363–364
Note
Norlind 1970, p. 364 (Zinner 2794–96, 2860; Hellman 102, 103, 103a), lists the tract among the books of the library because Tycho discusses it in the comet book (Opera omnia IV, 363–364); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). The tract exists in several nearly identical editions (Augsburg, Leipzig, Magdeburg; Zinner 2794–96, 2860; Hellman 102, 103, 103a); which of them Tycho had is not known. As an unbound tract, Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised, and none has been identified.
Norlind 1970, p. 364

Flera upplagor tryckta resp. Augsburg, Leipzig och Magdeburg, nästan helt identiska. – Diskuteras i kometboken (IV, 363–364).

Ursus, Nicolaus Reimers (Bär), De astronomicis hypothesibus, seu de systemate mundano. Prague, 1597, 4°

Attested, not locatedArec-e-norlind-ursus-hypothesibus
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence A
Subject
Astronomy (world-system polemic)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 365 (s.v. Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus); Zinner no. 3739 (after Norlind); Jardine et al. 2005; Jardine & Segonds 2008; Švédská knižní kořist (database)
Acquisition
1598; several copies in 1598: one received at Wandsbek with Kepler’s first letter (Tycho to Kepler, April 1598; Opera omnia VIII, 46), one from Rollenhagen (VIII, 51), one from Hagecius by way of Denmark and Helmstedt (VIII, 56) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 46; VIII, 51; VIII, 56; VIII, 126
Note
Norlind records that Tycho received the book (‘erhöll boken’). It was printed ‘Absque omni privilegio’; in it Ursus denies having stolen the system, dedicates the work to Landgrave Moritz, prints a laudatory letter from Kepler (Graz, 15 November 1595), and violently attacks Tycho and Rothmann. Tycho lent his copy, with the offending passages marked, to Holger Rosenkrantz in 1598 and complained that it was not returned (Opera omnia VIII, 126). Jardine, Launert, Segonds, Mosley and Tybjerg (2005, pp. 98–103) found the Royal Library’s copy from the Rosenkrantz sale of 1695 unmarked; the copy now in the Danish National Library of Science and Medicine, 4° Astr. 8050, perhaps transferred from the Royal Library between 1918 and 1926, is inscribed ‘Donum Autoris’ on the title and carries sixteen clear marginal marks, all against passages insulting to Tycho and all but two of them in the dedication to Landgrave Moritz or in the invective poem that follows it. They argue that this is the copy prepared for Lange and lent to Rosenkrantz. The identification rests on the pattern of the marks, not on a mark of ownership; the hand of the marks has not been compared with Tycho’s or with those of his assistants. A book lent out of the library in 1598 and never returned is a survivor of the library’s lifetime, not of its dispersal. The Czech National Library holds a copy of the Prague 1597 edition, 14 J 81/adl.2, bound second in a re-bound convolute after della Faille’s Theoremata (Antwerp 1632); its record, recatalogued under Kukula, carries no provenance. Jardine and Segonds restate the identification in 2008: the copy is the one Caspar Lehmann obtained from Ursus himself and sent through Rollenhagen in the spring of 1598; Tycho had the marks made for Erik Lange’s testimony and lent the volume to Holger Rosenkrantz, who did not return it despite the demands of 9 September 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, p. 112) and 5 December 1598 (pp. 125–126); their ‘about a dozen’ marked passages answers to the twelve puncta Lange attested, the article of 2005 counting sixteen clear marks and two doubtful (2008, pp. 175, 195–196, 243 n. 3). Three copies of the book reached Tycho in the spring of 1598 — from a student of Helmstedt, from Lehmann through Rollenhagen, and from Hagecius (pp. 157 n. 3, 191–192). A second surviving copy of the book Jardine and Segonds call rare: Västerås Stadsbibliotek, from the Olomouc Jesuit college (‘Collegij Olomu. Soctis JESV Catalogo inscriptus an: 1604’), through the Stockholm royal library of 1650–51, in a parchment binding cut from a coloured Hebrew manuscript (the Swedish-booty database, record SJ 203; Gawryś, Slavica Arosiensia III, no. 213). Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Norlind 1970, p. 365
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
I denna skrift, tryckt »Absque omni privilegio» såsom det står på titelbladet, förnekar Ursus, att han tagit idén till sitt i »Fundamentum» framställda världssystem från Tycho vid besöket på Uraniborg. Skriften är tillägnad lantgreve Moritz, son till lantgreve Wilhelm. I början är (fol. D) avtryckt ett mycket berömmande brev från Kepler, dat. Graz d. 15 nov. 1595. Bokens innehåll utgöres till en del av våldsamma personliga angrepp på såväl Tycho som på Rothmann. Tycho erhöll boken på Wandsbek samtidigt med Keplers första brev (Tycho till Kepler april 1598; VIII, 46). Från flera andra håll fick han emellertid exemplar, så från Rollenhagen (april 1598; VIII, 51) och Hagecius, som hade skickat boken till Danmark, varifrån den eftersändes över Helmstedt till Tycho på Wandsbek (VIII, 56). Ett lånade han till Rosenkrantz, vilket han var angelägen att återfå på grund av de däri (förmodligen av honom själv) införda marginalanteckningarna (brev till Rosenkrantz dec. 1598; VIII, 126).
Open questions
  • Whether the marginal marks in 4° Astr. 8050 (Royal Danish Library, formerly the Danish National Library of Science and Medicine) are in Tycho’s hand or in that of an assistant, and by what route the volume left the Royal Library; the ink and hand of the marks set against the Uraniborg hands, the binding and any earlier shelfmark would test the identification argued by Jardine et al. 2005.

Ursus, Nicolaus Reimers (Bär), Fundamentum astronomicum, id est nova doctrina sinuum et triangulorum. Strasbourg, 1588, 4°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-ursus-fundamentum
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Astronomy (world-system)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 365 (s.v. Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus); Zinner no. 3316 (after Norlind); Jardine & Segonds 2008; Balsem 2020
Acquisition
1588; several copies: one from Rantzau (Tycho to Rantzau, December 1588; Opera omnia VII, 387), one from Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg, one probably through Christian Ripensis (Tycho to Rothmann, February 1589; VI, 179) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 387; VI, 179
Note
Ursus set out in this book a world-system that, in Norlind’s words, differs only slightly from Tycho’s. Tycho held that Ursus had taken it from a sketch seen during his stay at Uraniborg in the autumn of 1584, in Erik Lange’s company, and pressed the charge of plagiarism in the correspondence with the Landgrave and Rothmann printed in 1596; Norlind, with Dreyer, holds the charge probably unwarranted. Tycho received several copies: one sent by Rantzau (Tycho to Rantzau, December 1588; Opera omnia VII, 387), a second probably from Christian Ripensis, which may be the other copy Tycho mentions in that letter, and one from Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg (Tycho to Rothmann, February 1589; Opera omnia VI, 179). Rollenhagen sent a copy to Rantzau on 16 October 1588 (Landesarchiv Schleswig-Holstein, Breitenburg-Archiv Abt. 127.21, Hss. 293, p. 552); Tycho already had one from elsewhere, ‘aliunde’ (to Rantzau, 21 December 1588, Opera omnia VII, p. 387) (Jardine & Segonds 2008, pp. 120–121). A copy with a Prague provenance of 1595 — ‘Daniel Muller à Mollenberg, '95 Prag’ on the title, ‘Raymari’ on the fore-edge, interleaved and annotated in a hand the Kepler-Kommission declared in 1964 not to be Kepler's — is at Leiden, 538 E 2, from Isaac Vossius's library; Balsem declines to call it Swedish booty for want of any trace of Christina's shelfmark on its ruined spine (2020, p. 37 and Cat. Math. 730). Not Tycho's copy, but a Prague copy of the year of the quarrel.
Norlind 1970, p. 365
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
I denna skrift framlägger Ursus bl.a. ett eget världssystem, som endast obetydligt avviker från Tychos. Denne misstänkte därför, att Ursus plagierat en skiss av detta under besöket på Uraniborg. I sin korrespondens, särskilt i den 1596 tryckta brevväxlingen med lantgreven och Rothmann framför Tycho mot Ursus kraftiga beskyllningar för plagiat. Ursus svarade med nedanstående skrift. Tycho erhöll flera exemplar. Ett skickade Rantzau (Tycho till denne dec. 1588; VII, 387), ett annat kom förmodligen från Ripensis och kan vara det andra exemplar, varom Tycho talar i brevet. Från Rollenhagen i Magdeburg fick han ett, efter vad han skriver till Rothmann i febr. 1589 (VI, 179). Se vidare s. 113 ff.

Viète, François (Vieta), Two tracts newly published in 1600 (‘libelli duo’), one of them probably the Apollonius Gallus. 1600

Attested, not locatedArec-e-letter-viete-tracts
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence A
Subject
Mathematics
Attested by
Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 26 April 1600 (tekstnet.dk)
Acquisition
1600; gift/exchange (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Note
Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho from Munich two booklets Viète had just published, without naming them (Herwart to Tycho, 26 April 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 305: ‘libelli duo, quos … FRANCISCUS VIETA, nuper in lucem prodire voluit … his iunctos ad te mitto’); Tycho acknowledged receipt in his letter to Herwart of 28 August 1600. Norlind (1970, p. 208) identifies one of them from Kepler’s letter to Herwart of July 1600 (Caspar no. 168), which reports that Kepler had seen at Tycho’s Viète’s ‘Opus de aequationibus’: not the De aequationum recognitione, printed only in 1615, but the Apollonius Gallus of 1600, whose second appendix (problems I and IV) determines a planet’s apogee and eccentricity from three observations. On 8 November 1600 Herwart described Viète’s Canon mathematicus under the title ‘Francisci Vietaei opera Mathematica’ and offered to procure it if Tycho wished (Herwart to Tycho, 8 November 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 386: ‘Quod si eum desideres, curabo omnino, ut habeas’) — an offer, not a sending, and not the Opera of 1646. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Open questions
  • Which was the second of the two tracts of 1600: Norlind identifies only the Apollonius Gallus, and the De numerosa potestatum resolutione, printed at Paris the same year, is the other candidate; a letter naming it, or a copy with Tycho’s marks, would decide.

It is the only Witelo–Dürer Sammelband in the library, and distinct from Dürer’s star charts, which Tycho is attested to have owned but of which no copy has been identified. Wooden boards, the spine in brown leather lettered ‘Vitellio Mathematicus, Albertus Durerus’. Šolc (p. 332) prints the shelfmark as XIV B 38 and the imprints as Nuremberg 1585 and Paris 1582, ‘Geometriae lib. III’; the library’s records give 1535, 1532 and four books, and the entry follows them. The library’s provenance note names the Jesuit college (‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESU Pragae Anno 1636’) and the Mathematical Museum and records no Tycho note, so the identification rests on Šolc’s reading of the initials on the front cover and of the verse annotations. The volume has been digitised by the library with Google Books. Šolc 2006 (p. 192) has the volume reach the Jesuits ‘probably by sale’ in 1636 — six years before the transfer of 1642 and by a different act; his chapter of 1999 (§ 2.532) says the same with ‘presumably’. Dürer's Institutiones geometricae, bound before it, have their own entry since 20 October 2026 (the unit rule).

Note
Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 7; NK Clementinum Sign. 7 B 27. Kleinschnitzová prints the title as ‘de naturalia librum secundum’; it is normalised here to ‘de naturali historia librum secundum’, the reading of the book itself (Ziegler’s commentary on Book II of Pliny’s Natural History, Basel 1531). The inscription on the title records the purchase: Magnus Bartholin bought the book in Tycho’s name from Johannes Aurifaber, one of the assistants on Hven, for a barrel of Rostock beer (‘Hunc librum Magnus Bartolinus emit ab J. A. nomine Tychonis Brahe una Tonna Cerevisiae Rostochiensis. n: Haec plus sapit palato, quam cerebro liber’); Norlind (1970, p. 366) takes Aurifaber to be Hans Crol, who died on Hven in 1591. The last leaf carries notes in Tycho’s hand (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 7). Jardine and Segonds connect the annotated Martianus Capella passage with the formal refutation of Ursus’s Demonstratio that Johannes Müller drew up on 23 August 1600, the transcriptions of Martianus being authenticated the same day by Tycho’s advocate Johannes Fritsch; they hold it likely that Müller used Tycho’s notes and possible that Tycho annotated the commentary in direct response to the Demonstratio, in 1599–1600 — their inference, so marked (2008, pp. 188–189 and n. 4). Whether these are the notes on the last leaf that Kleinschnitzová records is not settled by either source.
Norlind 1970, p. 366

LocatedAGöteborg, Röhsska Museumrec-e-prandtlA-57
Status
Located · entry confidence A
Subject

Attested by

Ownership marks
Binding: Gilt superexlibris: Tycho’s portrait on the upper board and his arms on the lower, each in an oval medallion ringed by a distich, ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat quae latet interior’ and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt, durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’. Brown leather over wooden boards, blind-tooled in three frames, the inner one with fourteen portrait medallions of scholars, four gilt rosettes, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands (Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X, 1906–07, pp. 42–43). Mortensen (1955, pp. 28–30) takes it for a Renaissance trade binding that Tycho probably acquired bound (‘vistnok har erhvervet i indbunden Stand’) and then had stamped with the superexlibris, which he calls especially finely struck and well preserved; the 1906 notice supposed the binding made at Basel for Tycho, Bargum (1906–07) held it Danish work under Tycho’s direction, and Prandtl (1932) lists the volume among the Prachtbände. The superexlibris was imitated in press gilding on the cover of Lauritz Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri (1946) (Mortensen, p. 30).
Norlind records
copy located by Norlind at: Göteborg, Röhsska konstslöjdsmuseet
Surviving copy
Zwinger, Theodor, Röhsska Museum · identification A · Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
Tycho's gilt portrait+arms superexlibris — the finely struck, well-preserved exemplar figured in the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X (1906/07). On a Renaissance binding: the 1906 notice took it for Basel work made for Tycho, Bargum for Danish work made under his direction, Mortensen (1955, p. 28) for a binding Tycho acquired bound and then stamped. The 1906 description: brown leather over wooden boards, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames (the inner one with fourteen scholar-portrait medallions), four gilt rosettes, the two gilt medallions with the distichs.
No online catalogue record traced.
Road of dispersal
Road U, Route out of the library unknown. The route out of the library and to Sweden is undocumented. In 1906 with the Munich bookseller Ludwig Rosenthal; with Baron Per Hierta (1864–1924) of Främmestad, Västergötland, so Prandtl 1932 (Band XXV); by 1955 in the Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseum, Göteborg (Mortensen 1955, pp. 28–30). Whether it came to the museum with Hjalmar Wijk’s donation of Hierta’s books in 1915 or from the sale of Hierta’s library after his death (Björck & Börjesson, Stockholm, October–November 1932, catalogue 272) is not established.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 57, his Einzelband XXV, then with Per Hierta at Främmestad. Mortensen (1955, pp. 28–30) places the same volume in the Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseum, Göteborg, and Norlind (1970, p. 366) describes it as the last tome of the Theatrum, volumina XVIII–XXIX, 33 books (pp. 3251–4373 with the index). The volume was first published in 1906, when the Munich bookseller Ludwig Rosenthal sent it to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde (the plaques reproduced, Heft 1, pp. 42–43); Bargum replied in the same volume (Beiblatt, pp. 124–126) that the binding was Danish work made under Tycho’s direction, that Gellius Sascerides may have procured the book at Basel or at the Frankfurt fair after the summer of 1588, and that Tycho may have taken from Zwinger’s title the name of his projected Theatrum astronomicum.
Norlind 1970, p. 366

Pr. nr 57. — Göteborg, Röhsska konstslöjdsmuseet (tidigare ägare: frih. P. Hierta). Endast den sista delen, omfattande 33 böcker (s. 3251-4373, index) av denna gigantiska universal-encyklopedi. Praktbd med Tychos porträtt och vapen (se: H. Mortensen, s. 28-29).
Open questions
  • How the volume came to the Röhsska museum — with Hjalmar Wijk’s donation of Hierta’s books in 1915, or from the sale of Hierta’s library after his death (Björck & Börjesson, 1932, catalogue 272) — is not established; the museum’s accession record would decide.

Note
Felix Mainx reported to Mortensen that in 1943 he had found, in a Prague monastery library, eight further books, not further specified, bearing Tycho’s superexlibris and many autograph marginalia; he intended to describe the find in a later paper (Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘otte andre ikke nærmere angivne Bøger, som foruden Tycho Brahes Superexlibris havde mange egenhændige Marginalnoter’). The books have not been traced since.
Open questions
  • Which Prague monastery held the eight Tycho books Mainx saw in 1943, and whether he published them; the monastery's catalogue or Mainx's papers would settle it.
  • Strahov is excluded: its only Tycho volume with autograph-attributed marginalia and a mark on the binding is the Euclid AV II 2, and its mark is a blind-stamped name and date of 1567 (Pařez 2009), not the gilt portrait plaque Mortensen ascribes to all eight; the Regiomontanus DR VII 19 has the 1642 inscription and no supralibros. Strahov's Tychoniana were surveyed by its own librarian in 1996 and 2009 and its bindings by Straka (1919, 1920), Hamanová–Nuska (1966) and Voit (2020). On Mortensen's description Strahov is not Mainx's monastery; the question stays open for Emauzy, Břevnov and the others. Mainx's own notice on Strahov of 1940 (S_MAINX1940) names no supralibros volume and predates the find: it neither names nor excludes Strahov, the exclusion resting on Mortensen's description; the leaves of the three plaque volumes — Σ V 5/a and Σ VI 3 unexamined, AG XIV 7 with one reader's note recorded — are the residual test.

5Surviving volumes

The 72 physical volumes identified as Tycho’s own (three of them under an identification now disputed), holding 131 of the catalogued works, by holding institution: the National Library of the Czech Republic first, the other holders after it; the table at the head sorts them by shelfmark, holder, binding, grade, road and first custodian, and each volume has a page of its own. Each record gives the shelfmark as the holder catalogues it, the earlier catalogue numbers, the marks that secure the identification and their grade, the contents, the holder’s own provenance note where one is published, the chain of custody, and the catalogue record and the facsimile where the holder publishes them. The one volume marked Tychoniana but not his and the three copies examined and ruled out follow in sections of their own.

For the Prague volumes the National Library’s own catalogue record, as published in Manuscriptorium, is quoted beneath the constituents: the binding and physical description, the former owners with the dates the catalogue attaches, provenance notes not already given, the library’s notes on each tract, the literature the record cites, and the digital copy where one exists — in the library’s Czech, verbatim. Where the entry of the printed manuscript catalogue has been converted into a database record, it is quoted too.

A key to the terms that recur in the library’s Czech notes: titulní list, titulní strana = title page; přídeští = pastedown; předsádka = flyleaf; rukou, rukopisný, rkp. = in manuscript; přípisek = inscription; razítko = stamp; exlibris; iniciály = initials; starší signatura = earlier shelfmark; supralibros; tužkou = in pencil; modře = in blue; pochází z knihovny = comes from the library of; jezuitská kolej = Jesuit college. In the catalogue’s physical lines s. = pages, l. = leaves, nečíslovaných = unnumbered.

National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum), Prague — 51 volumes

vol. 1

Sign. 1 H 56 — Prague, National Library

Bvol-orphan-band-xxii
Earlier catalogues
Kleinschnitzová no. 3; Prandtl, Verz. B, Band XXII
Identification
B · identified by Prandtl, Die Bibliothek des Tycho Brahe (Verzeichnis B)
Marks securing the identification
plain binding, no mark of Tycho’s (Prandtl 1932, Band XXII, ‘Einband ohne Kennzeichen’; Prusík 1901, group A); on the flyleaf Heinrich Rantzau’s dedication to Henrik Ramel, ‘affini ac amico suo’, dated 1584; on the title ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A°. 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 3)
Binding
unmarked binding
Contents
  1. Rantzau, Heinrich (Ranzovius), Henrici Ranzovii catalogus imperatorum regum ac virorum illustrium qui artem astrologicam amarunt, ornarunt et exercuerunt (1584) (no. 192)
  2. Conradinus, Henning, Epigrammatum historicus liber, continens encomia heroum, imperatorum et ducum … quos in arce sua Bredenberga depingi … curavit Henricus Ranzovius; item De claris et fortibus aliquot viris … familiae Ranzovicae (1581) (no. 60)
  3. Coroneus, Martinus, Vita et res gestae praestantissimi, nobilis et generosi herois, domini Iohannis Rantzovii, equitis aurati et trium Daniae regum … consiliarii (1567) (no. 65)
  4. Epitaphia aliquot in obitum nobilis matronae Annae Walstorpiae, d. Iohannis Rantzovii equitis aurati coniugis, conscripta; item Ecloga de eiusdem matronae obitu (1582) (no. 249)
Provenance note of the holding library (verbatim)
Tisk pochází z knihovny Tychona Brahe.
Na titulní stránce kulaté razítko s dvojhlavým orlem a opisem REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN. a drobné fialové razítko ve tvaru erbu s dvojhlavým orlem a písmeny ZK.
Na rubu přední předsádky rukopisná dedikace autora: Clarissimo Viro, nobilitate generis uirtute ac prudentia praestanti D. Henrico Ramel affini ac amico suo amicitia ergo hunc librum ddt Henricus Ranzouius Anno Domini 1584. Anno aetatis 59.
Na titulní stránce rukopisný přípisek: Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana.
Na titulní stránce rukopisné exlibris: Collegij Caesarei Soc[ieta]tis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague 1642–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Soc[ieta]tis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1623
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970

  3. Jesuit college, Český Krumlov (Krumau) 1654–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis Jesu Crumlovij per commutationem datur A. 1654.’; ‘Congreg. B.M.V. Annunc. Crumlovij.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. The library’s record also lists the Minorite convent of Český Krumlov (‘Klášter minoritů’) among the volume’s former owners, without a date; Kleinschnitzová (p. 93) prints the congregation’s inscription without attributing it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1671–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A[nn]o 1671.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Provenance note of the holding library (verbatim)
Na titulní straně dole rukou: Emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 Vltimo Nouembris.
Na titulní straně dvakrát rukou: Ioannes Pratentis.
Na titulní straně rukou poznámka: NB. Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe. Na přídeští je nalepená cedulka s rukopisným textem upozorňujícím na vlastnictví a rukopisné poznámky Tychona Brahe.
Na titulní straně exlibris pražských jezuitů: Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.
Na titulní straně dodatečně jinou rukou: Bibliothecae Mathematicae.
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). Norlind (1970, p. 358) read Benjamin Ursinus’s letter to Kepler of March 1614 (Caspar no. 681, p. 105), asking him to request ‘Ptolemaeum Tychonis’ from the Rožmberk librarian, as referring to this copy, and found the work in Václav Březan’s catalogue of the Rožmberk library at Třeboň (1602–08; Royal Library, Stockholm). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague — the Mathematical Museum 1642–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it; the later note ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae.’ places the volume in the college’s mathematical library. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

Notes
Prandtl’s Band I, his Einzelband 31, a single volume of 1551: Tycho’s first book, acquired on 30 November 1560. Friis described the volume in 1868: ‘Johannes Pratensis’ twice on the title, the purchase note, which he read as written by Tycho himself, and the Jesuit inscription, which he printed with the year ‘Ao. 1644’ — a transcription slip, since the National Library’s record and the title page read 1642 (Friis 1868–69, p. 267). Prusík listed the volume in 1901 as group A, no. 7, Sign. 5 B 70, with the purchase note read as Tycho’s and the Jesuit note on the title, ‘Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe. 1642’. The hand of the purchase note is disputed.

Studnička described the volume in 1901 among the newly found Tychoniana (Bericht, pp. 46–50), with the two sentences on the title of the De triangulis and the one on that of the dialogue De quadratura circuli; under the colophon of August 1533 he read a further note as Tycho’s: ‘Proportio circumferentiae ad suum diametrum est sicut 88 ad √785’ — a value of 3.1409 for the ratio, which Moritz Cantor, he adds, had found nowhere else (p. 49). The volume is the Archimedes Sammelband of Basel, Herwagen, 1544, Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 5, Sign. 5 C 31. Prusík 1901, group A, no. 8: Sign. 5 C 31, ‘Archimedis Syracusani … Opera. Baseleae. 1548’ (p. 200); his year is a slip for 1544, the Herwagen edition the volume holds (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 5:1; the library’s record).

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague — the Mathematical Museum 1642–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Soctis JESU Pragae Ao 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tychonis’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it; the note ‘Musei Mathem.’ on a title (the library’s Manuscriptorium record) places the volume in the college’s mathematical museum (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 78). — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Manuscriptorium; Kleinschnitzová 1933
  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970

  3. The Marian sodality at Chomutov (Sodalitas B. V. Mariae Assumptae) — a congregation attached to the Jesuit college, possibly the college's own body
    The National Library's record lists the Church of the Assumption at Chomutov among the former owners, from the inscription on a2 ‘Sodalitat[is?] in Co[???] B. V. MARIAE Assumptae’, undated and with its place-word illegible; Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 89) prints only ‘ein unleserlich gemachter Provenienzvermerk’. Whether the sodality held the book before or after Crusius's gift of 1654, and whether it was a body distinct from the college, the record does not say: a station of uncertain order, entered as the record names it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933

    Crusius’s gift of 5 August 1654 — the title carries, after an effaced note, ‘[Commotouij] 5. Augustj A. D. 1654 Nobilis ac Doctissimus Dominus Gabriel Crusius. — G.   5. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970

    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1672
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1672–1773
    The college’s catalogue inscription ‘Collegij Societatis Jesu Commotovii catalogo inscriptus A° 1672’ on the title (the library’s record). — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Provenance note of the holding library (verbatim)
Tisk pochází z knihovny Tychona Brahe.
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1672
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1672–1773
    ‘Coll. Soc. Jesu Commotouij Cat. inscr. A. 1672’ on the title (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 32); the library’s record names Tycho as former owner without transcribing the note. — Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933
