Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague — the Mathematical Museum 1642–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Soc[ieta]tis JESU Pragae A[nn]o 1642.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it; the later note ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae’ places the volume in the college’s mathematical library, the department Kleinschnitzová describes as the college’s ‘mathematisches Museum’ (1933, p. 78). — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

Notes
Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 as no. VI of the seven Tychoniana found since 1902, under the shelfmark XIV A 63: Stoeffler’s Calendarium Romanum magnum (‘Tubingae 1518’ in Kukula; the book was printed at Oppenheim by Jacob Köbel in 1518, as Kleinschnitzová, no. 33, and the library’s record give it), Peurbach’s Tabulae eclipsium (Vienna 1514), Apianus’s Pronunciata (Nuremberg 1541) and an Introductorium astronomicum (Paris 1517), with ‘T. B.’ on the first title; the binding is without special character. The volume is Prandtl’s Band VII of 1932: the library’s owner index lists it under Sign. 14 A 63, Kleinschnitzová’s 1933 shelfmark for the Stoeffler and the Peurbach is 14 A 63, and the Stoeffler, the Peurbach and the Apianus are confirmed as its constituents. The volume is digitised in full view in the National Library’s programme with Google Books, the whole Sammelband under one digitisation id attached to the library’s record and to the four adligata records; the Manuscriptorium record is catalogue-only. The National Library’s provenance survey of 2021 counts 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions and ‘at least four books from Tycho’s estate’ among them, all stamped ‘TBO 1576’; its authors suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under P. Jan Jüngling in the eighteenth century; the dated Chomutov notes of 1645 (44 F 38) and 1654 (Crusius’s gifts) are earlier.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970

  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

digital facsimile (Google Books)
Sources
Šolc 2002; Kleinschnitzová 1933; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Friis 1868–69; Gingerich & Westman 1988; Prusík 1901; Hanslik 1851; Kukula 1906–07; Vackářová 2026; Norlind 1970
Notes
The De revolutionibus mis-attribution copy; entered via the Wittich-library purchase. Friis had already denied the marginalia to Tycho in 1868: the notes ‘næsten paa hver Side’ cannot be attributed to him ‘som man hidtil har antaget’, though the book ‘kan hidrøre fra hans Samling’ (Friis 1868–69, pp. 266–267, citing Hanslik 1851, p. 274, and Hanuš, Zusätze, Prague 1863, p. 9); the hand was identified as Paul Wittich's by Gingerich and Westman in 1988. The library's own catalogue of 1851 (Hanslik, pp. 274–275) had given the glosses to Tycho; Prusík 1901 (group A, no. 6) and Kukula 1906–07 repeated the attribution, Kukula calling for a specialist's study of the glossed Copernicus; Prusík noted the quantity of blank paper bound in with the book. Binding, as the National Library describes and photographs it in 2026: pale leather over boards, blind-tooled with ornament rolls and a pictorial centre panel on each board — Christ on the cross under an arch, figures at the foot and a lettered plaque below, on the front board; the risen Christ with banner and soldiers beneath on the back — a binding that in its execution stands apart from the rest of Tycho's volumes (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 9 (scan 9), Obr. 5–6; the front board, a graphite frottage of the whole board made to bring out the blind stamp, and the two centre panels are reproduced). The description supports what the provenance already implies: the volume was bound before it reached Tycho, for Wittich or an earlier owner, and carries none of Tycho's marks. Exhibited: in the Copernicus year 1973 the volume was the principal exhibit of the Prague quincentenary exhibition, shown as Tycho's annotated copy and prized as from his estate — the showing that the reattribution of 1981–88 overtook (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 8 (scan 8); she names neither venue nor organiser). Facsimile: Horský's edition (Nicolai Copernici De revolutionibus … cum commentariis manu scriptis Tychonis Brahe, Cimelia Bohemica 16, Pragae 1971), printed for the Copernicus year 1973, is held by the National Library as BMMS Facs F 158: smooth leather boards with the gilt initials NC and TB in a line device, the spine lettered COPERNICUS · BRAHE · DE REVOLUTIONIBUS (Vackářová 2026, printed pp. 9–10 (scans 9–10), Obr. 7); its title perpetuates the attribution to Tycho that the Debunked Claims Register records as overturned. The first-person note on fol. 82 in which the annotator writes of a discovery he himself made — the note John Craig copied into the Edinburgh copy as made by ‘M. Witt’, the clue of 1977/78 — does not stand in this copy: the National Library's curator states expressly that the Clementinum volume lacks it (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 32 (scan 32)), consistent with Gingerich's placing of that note, on the mean motion of precession, in the Liège copy at ff. 81–83v.

Handwriting survey

Sources
Kleinschnitzová 1933; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Friis 1868–69; Šíma & Valeška 2002; Prusík 1901; Hanslik 1851; Norlind 1970; Šolc 2002
Notes
Friis described the volume in 1868, brought forward for him by the custos Dambeck: the Rheticus of 1551 with the Jesuit inscription, and ‘en Snees Blade’ (a score of leaves) of manuscript appended — the Praxis, dated at the Calends of January 1591 and ‘A. C. 1595, 13 Cal. Xbris’ — in a hand ‘som man hidtil, men vistnok med Urette, har anseet for den berømte Astronom’; a photograph of the volume had been sent to Copenhagen in 1862 by Dr Joseph Böhm (Berlingske Tidende, 9 March 1863), and Hanslik's history of the library (1851, p. 612) had noticed it (Friis 1868–69, p. 266). Šíma and Valeška (2002) established the hand as a professional copyist's. Prusík listed the Praxis first among the four manuscripts in 1901: a paper manuscript of twenty quarto leaves bound as the first appendix to the printed work at 14 C 20, the binding of the earliest period without special character, ‘Tycho Brahe Calend. Jannuar. 1591’ and the distich dated ‘A. C. 1595. 13 Cal. Xbris’ under the title; its authenticity, doubted by Dreyer, he held proved by Studnička. Hanslik's catalogue of 1851 (pp. 612–613) already printed the appended manuscript as Tycho's autograph, ‘Dogmata geometrica’, found by the custos Dambeck in the mathematical section of the library.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry.     The inscription ‘Collegij Soc[ieta]tis IESV Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A[nn]o 1671.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933

Notes
Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 (no. V of the seven found since 1902, Sign. XIV F 8): the Arithmetica communis with Peurbach’s and Gmunden’s algorithms (defective), Strabo’s Hortulus (Nuremberg 1512), the Liber diversarum rerum ascribed to Ptolemy (Venice 1509) and Faber’s Meteorologia Aristotelis (Nuremberg 1512), ‘T. B.’ on the first title; the binding without special character. The National Library’s owner index lists the volume under Sign. 14 F 8 with the Strabo, the Ptolemy and the Faber among its constituents. The National Library’s provenance survey of 2021 counts 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions and ‘at least four books from Tycho’s estate’ among them, all stamped ‘TBO 1576’; its authors suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under P. Jan Jüngling in the eighteenth century; the dated Chomutov notes of 1645 (44 F 38) and 1654 (Crusius’s gifts) are earlier. There is no digital facsimile of the volume; the library’s record offers five photographs (title page, front pastedown, boards, spine).

  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970

Handwriting survey
536 images examined; 199 images with handwriting flagged, 19 uncertain (an automated survey of the facsimile; no hand attributed). Kinds: other marks (images 303, 304, 409, 535); marginal notes (images 9, 303, 406, 409); diagrams and tables (images 303, 304, 535).
Sources
Prandtl 1932; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Studnička 1901 (Bericht); Prusík 1901; Kukula 1906–07; Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
Notes
Bound volume IV, in Studnička’s reconstruction of its original make-up four constituents, nos. 41, 20, 1 and 11: the Sacrobosco manuscript, the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus. The manuscript was separated from Sign. 14 F 16 before 1901, at an earlier revision of the manuscripts (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21; Kukula 1906–07, p. 22). Studnička described the volume in 1901 as Tycho’s astrological study-book, brought to his notice by the custos Josef Truhlář: a manuscript compendium of Sacrobosco’s Sphaera first (now Sign. VII E 29), then the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus (Bericht, pp. 17–18, 30). He reports ‘constat 5 lb 15 d.’ on the inside of the front board — the sum of the cost note on the first leaf of the manuscript, which lists a Glareanus, the Gauricus with Montulmo, the Albubater, the Cardanus and the binder’s fee (pp. 20–21; the boards are not in the facsimile) — and reproduces as Tycho’s own work eight pages from the leaves bound at the end of the Albubater (pp. 22–29) and a horoscope from the Cardanus with a line of manuscript above it (p. 30). The first page he reproduces is the nativity of Andreas Schöner, cast for Nuremberg (‘Anno M.D.XXX die XXI Junij … natus Andreas Schönerus. Dies Martis’; 21 June 1530 fell on a Tuesday), and the cost note is headed with the same name. Which of the annotations in the volume are Tycho’s has not been established by a comparison of hands. Prusík 1901, group A, no. 3: Sign. 14 F 16, ‘ein Sammelband ohne besonderen Wert’, to which the Sacrobosco manuscript (now MS VII E XXIX) originally belonged; Kukula told in 1906–07 how the custos Truhlář, finding the price list on the manuscript’s flyleaf, recovered the Sammelband it had been taken from, its upper board marked ‘constat 5 15’, the sum of the list. The National Library’s digital facsimile of Sign. 14 F 16 shows the volume as it now stands: the three Petreius imprints — the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus — and nothing else; the Sacrobosco manuscript is at Sign. VII E 29.

Provenance note of the holding library (verbatim)
Podle supralibros pochází tento tisk z osobní knihovny astronoma Tychona Brahe.
Na přídeští modře rukou starší signatura: T.B. 8.
Na titulní straně přípisek: Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana.
Na titulním listě rukopisné exlibris pražské jezuitské klementinské koleje: Collegij Caesarei Soc[ieta]tis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.
Na titulním listě jinou rukou pozdější přípisek: Musei Mathemat.
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague — the Mathematical Museum 1642–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Soc[ieta]tis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it; the later note ‘Musei Mathemat.’ places the volume in the college’s mathematical library. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

Provenance note of the holding library (verbatim)
Tisk pochází z knihovny Tychona Brahe. Dalšími držiteli byli chomutovští jezuité.
Na přídeští rukou modře: T.B. 13. Na předsádce rukou černě iniciály: T. B.
Na titulní straně rukou: Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij Cataogo inscriptus A[nn]o 1671.
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1671–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij Cataogo inscriptus A[nn]o 1671.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague 1642–1773

  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

Prusík (1901, group A, no. 4) already saw the composite with its post-Tycho host in place. The Christmann carries Tycho’s note ‘emi Pragae mense Majo’ (Kleinschnitzová; the year 1601 is Prandtl’s inference); the third piece, an Apianus Cosmographia of 1540, she leaves open.

Sources
Prandtl 1932; Kleinschnitzová 1933; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Studnička 1901 (Bericht); TBOO; Prusík 1901; Kukula 1906–07; Vackářová 2026; Norlind 1970; Šolc 2002
Notes
Prandtl’s Band XXIX, Einzelband 40: Reinhold’s Prutenicae tabulae of 1551, the presentation copy to the Counts of Mansfeld, which Prandtl locates in the Prague University Library. Studnička described the volume in 1901 (Bericht, pp. 41–45) and reproduced Reinhold’s dedication and the two manuscript pieces on the flyleaf: a passage headed ‘Plato’ (‘Unum est naturae vinculum, doctrina numerorum, figurarum et motuum coelestium …’), and the draft of the epigram ‘Quamvis mortalis vescor mortalibus auris’, a first version corrected and struck through and a second written under ‘Aliter’. Dreyer and Ræder printed the epigram from this leaf (Opera omnia IX, p. 215; the cancelled version p. 316). Studnička supposed that Tycho had kept both pieces from an earlier time and inserted them here, and took the binding as proof that the stamps were Tycho’s own and had come with him to Prague (pp. 41, 45). Prusík 1901, group C (Prachtbände), white leather, no. 1, lists Sign. 14 J 176 as the Prutenicae with Reinhold’s dedication to the Counts of Mansfeld, Tycho’s note ‘Est manus Reinholdi. Emi Pragae anno 1601 mense Junio’, and a leaf of verses in his hand at the front; Kukula in 1906–07 described the two drafts of the distich with their deletions. Reproduced: the front board with the gilt portrait medallion — a faded red inscription above it — and the arms stamp of the back board, photographed by Zdeněk Rerych for the National Library's volume of 2026, which presents the binding as the ‘second variant’ of Tycho's bindings beside the ‘typical’ T·B·O leather of 14 J 190 (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 8 (scan 8), Obr. 4; she does not say there were only two). The photograph places the portrait die on the front board and the arms die on the back, as the Iconographia's supralibros records assume.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1671–1773
    The inscription ‘Na titulním listu rukou "Collegij Soc[ieta]tis IESV Commotovij Catalogo inscriptus A[nn]o 1671".’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

  2. route unknown until 1675
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry.     Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

74 images examined; 38 images with handwriting flagged, 2 uncertain (an automated survey of the facsimile; no hand attributed). Sources
Kleinschnitzová 1933; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Studnička 1901 (Bericht); Walde 1938; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021; Norlind 1970
Notes
A cost note on the first leaf of the Sacrobosco manuscript Sign. VII E 29, which was once bound before the Gauricus of Sign. 14 F 16, is headed ‘Andreas Schöner’ and lists ‘Henricus Glareanus constat 21 ₰’, then the Gauricus and Montulmo, the Albubater, the Cardanus and the binder’s fee (reproduced by Studnička 1901, Bericht, p. 20); the binder's instruction on the last leaf of this volume names the Gauricus with Montulmo and the Albubater. Walde suggested in 1938 that the Glareanus, bought by Vedel in August 1564, may have come to Tycho in exchange for the Sammelband of 1563 now at Uppsala. The library’s records of the three adligata (docs 000082484–000082486, read 20 October 2026): Apianus, Cosmographia, ed. Gemma Frisius, Antwerp: Gregorius Bontius, 1545, inscribed on the title ‘Cubiculi Mathematici Pragae ad S. Clementem A[nn]o 1719’, with Joannes Walthrinus as an earlier owner; Theodosius, De sphaericis, ed. Vögelin, Vienna: Singriener, 1529, with the Charles College ex-libris ‘Col. Caroli IV Mathema. n° 30’; Stöffler, Cosmographicae aliquot descriptiones, ed. Dryander, Marburg: Cervicornus, 1537, inscribed ‘Dom[us] Professae Soc. Jesv ad S. Nicol. Pragae. Catalogo inscriptus 1733’. Each adligatum thus carries a later Prague provenance of its own, which indicates that the composite was assembled in the Clementinum after 1733 (an inference from the inscriptions; the records themselves say only that the three are bound with the Glareanus).

    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1645
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1645–1773
    ‘Collegii Societatis Jesu Commotovien. catalogo inscriptus 1645’ on fol. <2>2r (Boldan & Kazanskii 2023, p. 28 and fig. 5). — Boldan & Kazanskii 2023
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970

Sources

Notes
Kleinschnitzová no. 2. Manuscript: six folio leaves, the third item of a volume of manuscripts which, according to Studnička, was made up when the Jesuit library was put in order in 1642, the lower and right margins folded in to fit the boards; headed in red ‘Cap. IIII. Quare his disciplinis prae ceteris prima et indubitata sit concludendi ratio’, with sections De puncto, De linea recta, De angulo and De figuris. Found by the custos Josef Truhlář and published by Studnička as Tycho’s autograph, the first page in facsimile in 1901 (Bericht, pp. 51–53) and the whole in 1903 as Brevissimum planimetriae compendium; Kleinschnitzová listed it as an autograph in 1933. Dreyer rejected the hand and the ownership alike — ‘manus non est Tychonis … neque ullum adest indicium, quod in hujus potestate libellum umquam fuisse ostendat’ — and reported from J. L. Heiberg that the text is taken from Proclus’s commentary on the first book of Euclid (Basel 1533) (Opera omnia I, p. 317). Šíma and Valeška (2002) assign the hand to a professional writer. Prusík listed the fragment in 1901 as the third manuscript, ‘eine mathematische Schrift ohne besonderen Titel’, beginning ‘Cap. IIII’, the binding without special character, under the shelfmark MS XII A XII (p. 198), the composite from which Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 83) reports it taken out and bound alone. The manuscript has not been digitised.

Notes
Kleinschnitzová no.1; Manuscript. A parchment manuscript in its original binding with the initials T. B. O. and the year 1582 (Norlind 1970, p. 340); Studnička counts it, in brown leather with the initials, to the second period of the bindings (Bericht, 1901, p. 7). He published the tables as Tycho's autograph and held them copied from Regiomontanus's sine tables of 1541 in the Archimedes volume, Sign. 5 C 31 (Bericht, p. 47); Norlind describes them as a copy and reworking of Copernicus's ‘Canon semissium subtensarum rectarum linearum in circulo’. Šíma and Valeška (2002) assign the tables to a professional writer; of the short inscriptions on the end leaves they conclude that they can neither prove them Tycho's nor exclude him. Prusík described the manuscript in 1901 as MS VI E IX: eighteen strong parchment leaves, the brown binding of the middle period full of ornament with ‘T. B. O.’ at the top of the upper board, the title ‘Tabulae sinuum 1582’, no distich on the title but at the lower right, added later in Tycho's hand, the words ‘οἰστέον καὶ ἐλπιστέον’; written for his own use and much worn; Kukula added Studnička's conjecture that the words were set down at the parting from the library on leaving Denmark.

Provenance, as catalogued
Na f. Ir jméno dřívějšího majitele, norimberského astronoma Andrease Schönera a zapsané ceny původních částí konvolutu a cena za svázání s celkovým součtem (vzhledem k datům vydání tištěných částí konvolutu a Schönerovu roku narození 1528 je jeho vlastnický záznam snad mladší). Na f. Ir a 1r (zde dvakrát) iniciály pozdějšího majitele Tychona Brahe T B. Na f. 31v signatura O VII 44 (upravovaná vyškrabáváním a přepisováním). Na f. Ir dále tužkou údaj o starším umístění v konvolutu Antea praeligatum tractatui Lucae Gaurici Norimbergae a. 1540 edito, sign. 14.F.16., Truhlářův katalog uvádí další obsah konvolutu Albubatris Genethliacus, Norimbergae 1540, Hieronymi Cardani libelli duo, Norimbergae 1543.
Ve spodní části hřbetu štítek s částí současné signatury (29). Na přední desce štítek s dřívější pomocnou signaturou Tres. M 24, která se opakuje i na předním přídeští. Tam také přírůstkové číslo (?) A. B. 5/1900, údaj T B. 6 (číslo 6 přepsáno na 24) a současná signatura MS VII E 29.

Notes
This Sacrobosco-commentary manuscript was separated from Sign. 14 F 16 before 1901, at an earlier revision of the manuscripts (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21; Kukula 1906–07, p. 22), and shelved as VII E 29, while the three printed constituents (Gauricus A 20, Albubater A 1, Cardano A 11) remain in 14 F 16; Prandtl’s four-part Band IV is Studnička’s reconstruction of the volume’s original make-up. The first leaf (f. 1r) carries a cost note headed ‘Andreas Schöner’: ‘Henricus Glareanus constat 21 d. / L. Gauricus & Jo: De monte ulmo constat 24 d. / Albubater 42 d. / Cardanus 42 d. / 36 d. Ligatori’, summed to 165 pfennigs, that is 5 lb 15 d. at thirty pfennigs to the pound; beside it a large monogram in ink, read as T B, with an astronomical diagram and pen trials of the planetary signs below; at the foot, in a later library hand, ‘Antea praeligatum Tractatui Lucae Gaurici Norimbergae a. 1540 edito, sign. 14. F. 16.’ On the verso: ‘Nota. Tribus rebus res comprobantur. I Ratione. II Autoritate. III Experientia’, and under it, in a larger hand, the conclusion drawn for astrology (‘Ergo etiam astrologia vera erit …’). Studnička reproduced the cost note and the upper note of the verso in 1901 as Tycho’s (Bericht, p. 20): the custos Josef Truhlář had concluded from the cost note that the works it lists must be in the library and found them in the Sammelband Sign. 14 F 16, where the removal of the manuscript had left a gap (p. 21). The hands have not been compared with Tycho’s or with Schöner’s. Prusík listed the manuscript in 1901 as the fourth, ‘Sphaera Johannis de Sacrobusto in compendium digesta, Anno salutis nostrae MDXXXIX’, formerly bound in the printed volume 14 F 16 and newly bound as MS VII E XXIX.

Notes
Walde showed in 1938 that the manuscript belonged to Johannes Eriksen of Hamburg, tutor to Tycho’s sons at Wittenberg in February 1598 and Tycho’s amanuensis at Prague in 1601: it carries the inscription, as Curtze transcribed it, ‘Dominus M. Christiernus Severinus Longomontanus reliquit amico suo Iohanni Ericksen [a Greek word] Benachia Bohemorum 18. Julii discedens A° 1600’ — Longomontanus’s parting gift at Benátky. Walde left open the assumption that it then passed to Tycho and with his papers to Vienna, observing that Eriksen’s other books and manuscripts went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty (a Pitiscus of 1600 bought at Prague on 14 August 1601, now at Hanover; two chemical manuscripts at Leiden from Vossius’s share; a Lull of 1593 at Västerås with the Christina shelfmark), and supposed that his literary property came into Rudolf II’s hands. The manuscript is a sixteenth-century Latin Sammelhandschrift of 45 leaves containing the Commentariolus of Copernicus and the Responsio ad Capnurianam apologiam of Longomontanus, Tycho’s chief assistant. The Austrian National Library’s description records a nineteenth-century half-parchment rebinding and no former owner, and does not mention Brahe; Norlind’s attribution of the manuscript to Tycho’s library is not corroborated by the catalogue, and the link to Tycho rests on the Longomontanus text and the circle of Uraniborg. The library has published a full digitisation of the manuscript.

Notes
The 1543 Nuremberg first edition, distinct from the Clementinum Wittich copy (Sign. 14 B 16, the 1566 Basel edition). Gingerich traces its passage (Census, pp. 105–108): from Wittich to his sister, and to Tycho, who ‘presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’; thence, by conjecture, to Rudolf II; taken in the Swedish plunder of the west bank of Prague under Königsmarck in July 1648; to Queen Christina, and with her to Rome in 1655; to Pope Alexander VIII (Pietro Ottoboni) in 1690; and so to the Vatican Library, the spine bearing the papal arms of Pius IX. Richly annotated by Wittich on four preliminary pages and on thirty pages after f. 196; the observation notes include a conjunction of Venus and Regulus on 16 September 1574 and of Jupiter and Fomalhaut on 8 November 1572, and ff. 197v–211v carry the proto-Tychonic geo-heliocentric diagrams dated 27 January to 17 February 1578 (Gingerich, ‘Vatican 1’). Digitised in full on the Vatican Library’s digital site as Ott. lat. 1902, with Wittich’s manuscript notes bound in at the end.

Cui negat esse DEVM cœlos et sidera spectet Esse etenum monfrat Stella vel vna DEVM. Tycho Brahe scripsj Anno 1599 Junij die 14, quo Vitebergà discessj Pragam a CÆSARE vocatus.

Links
digital facsimile (ThULB Jena) · Tycho's inscription leaf, image 123 of the facsimile
Sources
Prandtl 1932; Rauch 1914; Norlind 1970; Gingerich 1971; Christianson 2000; Forschungsbibliothek Gotha, copy record (K10plus)
Notes
What the volume shows. The only trace of Tycho is one inscription, on the recto of the blank leaf that follows the pasted-in leaf of Apianus’s later arms (image 123 of the Jena facsimile): Psalm 19:1 (‘Coeli enarrant gloriam Dei et opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum’), a distich whose hexameter Tycho had used in his Copenhagen oration of 1574 (‘Cui negat esse Deum, coelos et sidera spectet’, here with the pentameter ‘Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum’), and the subscription ‘Tycho Brahe scripsi Anno 1599 Junij die 14, quo Vitebergâ discessi Pragam a Caesare vocatus’ — written on the day he left Wittenberg for Prague. The hand is that of his Wittenberg album entries of 1598–99, and a separate album leaf of the same day carries the same departure formula. The title page bears no owner’s name, the text no annotation, and the binding is a Gotha rebinding of 1967, made after the volume had been taken apart for the Edition Leipzig facsimile; the restoration report pasted inside the lower board records that the original leather was plain. The copy also carries, in a sixteenth-century hand close to the Apian family, captions on the old and the new arms and red crossings through the old shield on the title — the apparatus of a copy completed after Apianus’s ennoblement of 1541. What it proves, and what it does not. The inscription proves that Tycho held the book on 14 June 1599 and wrote in it. It is a dated motto entry of the album-amicorum kind (‘scripsi’, not ‘emi’ or ‘possidet’), not an ownership mark, and nothing else in the volume connects it to his library. Prandtl listed the volume among Tycho’s books on the strength of the entry alone. Norlind thought it more likely the book of someone else, perhaps of Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxe-Weimar, Administrator of Electoral Saxony and Tycho’s patron at Dresden in November 1598, in whose book Tycho would have written as in an album. The Gotha library records the volume as Tycho’s gift to the duke and the duke as its recipient; the duke’s other Tychoniana — the Mechanica Memb. I 110 and the star catalogue Chart. A 984, both with dedications to him — are in the same library, and the library of his line at Altenburg came to Gotha in 1672. On either reading the volume is a book that passed through Tycho’s hands, not one shown to have stood on his shelves; hence grade B. Rauch, who first published the entry in 1914 on information from the Gotha librarian Rudolf Ehwald, wrote that the book had come to Gotha from Munich; nothing later explains the remark. Gingerich, who examined the copy for the facsimile, reports the entry as ‘written in what is now the Gotha copy’. Catalogued by the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha at Math gr2° 00038/02; the copy record transcribes the inscription and names the duke as recipient. Digitised by the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha; the page-by-page facsimile is served in the ThULB Jena viewer (URN urn:nbn:de:urmel-ufb-191132).

front board: TVCHO BRADE, rear board: ANNO 1561 (stamped, originally gilt); fly-title: ‘tico brade ven:’ (struck through), ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions (leaf half torn, repaired); fly-title verso: ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ (struck through), ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’, beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost; a note in ink on the front pastedown; fol. 53r–v of the Apianus: four places with their positions in Tycho's hand; on the spine the remnant of a label with a library shelfmark 204; Latin plant names at the head of a run of recto pages in a hand other than Tycho's, and small plant remains between leaves (Magasin 1987, p. 31; Björklund 1992, p. 26 — unexamined); at the head of the front pastedown the pencil figure ‘+125’, Maggs's price of 1933, and a second figure (the museum's photograph); Thykier (1985 inspection; report of 13 January 2003) reads the forperm's front as the autograph ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through and ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through (‘en lidt barnlig skrift’), and in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part; on its back, under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed, the price ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’; short astronomical notes in Tycho's hand inside the binding and on the forperm's back, and one in the margin of the preface's tenth (unpaginated) page; Latin plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand other than Tycho's, plant remains in the gutter of 26 of them (microscoped by Jette Baagøe, re-housed in annotated envelopes of acid-free silk paper), further remains between pages without names, one plant name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner and Baagøe)

  2. Regiomontanus, Johannes, Joannis de Monte Regio tabulae directionum profectionumque; ejusdem Regiomontani tabula sinuum (1550) (no. 198)
Chain of custody
  1. route unknown
    The route out of Tycho's hands is undocumented. The two struck ownership lines on the forperm (the museum: ‘tico brade ven:’ and ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’; Thykier 2003: ‘Tyge Brahe’ and ‘tico brahe ven’) may mark a transfer in his lifetime or a later owner's cancellation; a third inscription in another hand reads ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part of the leaf (Thykier 2003) — the only name of a later owner the volume yields. The book was used as a herbarium by a hand other than Tycho's, one of whose plant names is unattested before c. 1623 (Thykier 2003, after Wagner and Baagøe), so it was in a plant-collector's hands after Tycho's death. It stands in no Prague catalogue and its first title carries none of the Jesuit, Chomutov or Crusius marks of the Bohemian roads; the remnant of a label on the spine with the shelfmark 204 records a library between Tycho and the Munich trade that no source names (Thykier: ‘formodentlig katalognummeret i Tychos eller et senere bibliotek’; the dossier of 20 October 2026). — Thykier 2003; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart)

The pencil ‘+125’ at the head of the front pastedown is this price. The firm's archive (British Library Add MS 89311) would name the seller. — Maggs 582 (1933); Maggs 600 (1934); Maggs 666 (c. 1938); New York Times Book Review, 28 May 1933

(købt for 1 thaler og 4 groschen); han studerede der 1559-62, og var 15 år, da han købte bogen.
Holding
M/S Museet for Søfart, Deponeringer div, 1957:0030
Links in the record
photograph 1 in the record · photograph 2 in the record
Sources
Prandtl 1932; Norlind 1970; Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart); Björklund 1992; Grinder-Hansen 2006; Gingerich 2002; Bogvennen 1966; Magasin 1987; Museet for Søfart 2026; Maggs 582 (1933); Maggs 600 (1934); Maggs 666 (c. 1938); Reichner, Catalogue 1 ([1939]); Royal Library, Håndskriftafdelingen, Aktuelt (November 2001); Kraks Blå Bog 1937; New York Times Book Review, 28 May 1933; Christianson 1967; Mortensen 1955; Thykier 2003
Notes
Prandtl’s Band II, the student binding of 1561. Prandtl recorded it in 1932 at Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich, and as sold to America; Gingerich (2002) still placed it at an undisclosed location. It had in fact returned to Denmark within a generation: the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg reported it among the acquisitions of 1956–57 as the gift of Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman, and Norlind placed it there in 1970 (pp. 338 and 361). The museum’s record (Museernes Samlinger, inventory 1957:0030, priref 400004307, revised 16 June 2026) describes the volume leaf by leaf. Regiomontanus’s Tabulae directionum (Tübingen, Ulrich Morhart, 1550), first in the volume: title, [43] pp. text, [268] pp. tables, a few notes in the head margin. Apianus’s Cosmographia in Gemma Frisius’s recension (Paris, Vivant Gaultherot, 1553; the colophon dated 1551): title woodcut, fol. 1–74 with the volvelles, the cordiform world map inserted between fol. 34 and 35, the tables of positions from fol. 37; on fol. 53r–v Tycho has added four places with their figures, which the museum reads ‘Elzingborgum 35 46. 57 0 / Lunda Lundt 36 30 57 23 / Vesby Gotlandiæ 47 5. 59 50 / Rumefalche [?] 46 35 60 15’ — Helsingborg, Lund, Visby, and a fourth place the museum could not read. Quarto; stained, water-stained and wormed. Brown calf, blind-ruled mirror panels on both boards with originally gilt floral stamps, TVCHO BRADE stamped on the front board and ANNO 1561 on the rear, three raised bands, and on the spine the remnant of a label with the library shelfmark 204 — an owner between Tycho and the Munich trade whom no source names. The inscriptions: a note in ink on the front pastedown; on the fly-title, struck through, ‘tico brade ven:’, then ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions, the leaf half torn and repaired; on its verso ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’, struck through, the purchase note ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’, and beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost. Prandtl’s ‘Vorsatzblatt’ with the note and the name three times is thus placed: the purchase note is on the verso of the fly-title, not on the pastedown. Kept in a cloth-covered box; restored in 1957 by Birgitte Dall, Copenhagen. The record’s two photographs show the front board, and the volume open in its box at the Regiomontanus title with the fly-title raised, its verso with the purchase note and the astronomical note towards the camera. The record is filed in the museum’s case ‘Deponeringer div:’ (deposits), which agrees with the Royal Library deposit of 1987. Björklund (1992) reported the volume deposited at the Royal Library’s manuscript department, and the Nationalmuseet catalogue of 2006 reproduced it from a Royal Library photograph. The Danish record of the volume, in order: Klem’s museum report for 1956–57 (Årbog 1957, p. 8) lists it among the year’s acquisitions as ‘en gave fra fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle, civilingeniør Oscar Ekman’, bought by Tycho ‘i 1561’ for ‘1 Thaler, 4 Groschen’. Bogvennen (1966, p. 205), reviewing the Ekman sale (Bruun Rasmussen auction 186, 1–4 November 1965), names among the show-pieces withdrawn as bequests ‘en bog fra Tycho Brahes bibliotek (til Kronborg — Rundetaarn bød samtidig meget højt, men forgæves på en lignende hos Sotheby)’: the volume was still the museum’s in 1965. The Kronik of Magasin fra Det Kongelige Bibliotek (2:1, 1987, p. 31) records its deposit in the Royal Library’s Håndskriftafdeling, the contact arranged by museumsleder Claus Thykier of Ole Rømers Museum, the museum on Kronborg remaining the owner — an earlier witness to the deposit than Björklund 1992. The Kronik prints the front-board stamp as ‘Tycho Brahe’, a normalisation of the museum’s reading TVCHO BRADE; it reports ‘adskillige notater med flere hænder, deriblandt Tycho Brahes’, and gives the herbarium use as a suggestion that had not been examined (‘foreslået … endnu ikke kunnet undersøges’, p. 33), which Björklund 1992 then states as fact. The deposit has ended: the museum’s curator, Thorbjørn Thaarup, confirmed in writing on 13 October 2026 that the volume is part of the museum’s collection and is kept at the museum (‘en del af vores samling og opbevares hos os’); when it returned from the Royal Library is not stated. The twentieth-century route, established on 20 October 2026: Prandtl's ‘sold from Munich to America’ was wrong about the first step. Maggs Bros. of London offered the volume in Catalogue 582 (1933), item 155, at £125 — the entry collates both works, gives the stamps, transcribes ‘Sum Tychonis Brade / Epts thaliro & 4 Gross’, notes the half-torn fly-leaf and the Helsingborg note, and cites Prandtl for ‘our volume’ — again in Catalogue 600 (1934), item 260, and still in Catalogue 666 (c. 1938), always at £125, the figure pencilled on the front pastedown; the New York Times reviewed the 1933 catalogue on 28 May 1933. It reached New York only with Herbert Reichner's first catalogue ([1939], item 72, probably $850) and is in none of his later ones. Between about 1940 and 1956 nothing is known. The Kronik's argument of 1987 that the price in thaler and groschen is Saxon coin and that the Leipzig matriculation register enters Tycho under 16 October 1561 does not hold: the Copenhagen Ptolemy of 1560 is itself priced in Joachimsthaler, and 16 October is the winter-semester heading, the rector entering the term's students at its end (Norlind 1970, p. 16; Strömgren 1928); the binding's ‘Anno 1561’ and every other witness put the purchase in Copenhagen. The Helsingborg and Lund figures on fol. 53r are the book's own printed values from the Scania table on fol. 41v, transcribed beside the Zealand–Scania island entry; Visby and the fourth place stand beside the printed Gotland entry on fol. 53v. Christianson 1967 (Isis 58, p. 201), citing Prandtl, puts the ‘Anno 1561’ stamp on the spine — a slip; it is on the rear board. Dossier: the deep-research dossier of 20 October 2026 on the volume's provenance. Claus Thykier's report of 13 January 2003 (Ole Rømer Museet; absorbed 20 October 2026) is the examiner's own account: he inspected the volume at the museum's library in 1985, arranged its deposit at the Royal Library in 1986 (acc. 1986/116), and records the gift as January 1957 from civilingeniør Oskar Ekman with further provenance unknown. He reads the forperm's front as ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through and ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through, and in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part — the only later owner's name the volume yields; the price, under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed, as ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’ in Saxon coin, which led him to leave open a journey abroad in 1561 or a book sent by courier (both answered by the semester convention: Norlind 1970, p. 16). He describes the herbarium: plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand not Tycho's, remains in the gutter of 26 of them identified under the microscope by Jette Baagøe and re-housed in envelopes with the modern names, one name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner), so that the user ‘formentlig ikke har haft kontakt med Tycho’; and an astronomical note in Tycho's hand in the margin of the preface's tenth page. The book is to be kept horizontal in its capsule so that the plant remains do not fall out.

    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970

Notes
A Tycho Sammelband, a Prachtband containing Calvin’s Epistolae et responsa (Hanau 1597) and the Theocritus of 1596, repatriated from the USA through the ship-broker (skibsmægler) Hjalmar Bruhn, the Royal Library’s benefactor (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘Det kongelige Biblioteks altid redebonne Velgører Skibsmægler Hjalmar Bruhn’); the first book from Tycho’s own library to enter the Royal Library, which until then had owned none apart from the autograph observations (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘har det hidtil ikke ejet en Bog fra hans egen Bogsamling (bortset fra de haandskrevne Observationer)’). Given by Tycho to his cousin Hans Lindenov after the Calvin edition of 1597 had appeared — probably before 1599, Mortensen supposes, unless the book was sent to Lindenov later (pp. 26–27). The dedication stands on the verso of the free endpaper facing the title; the supralibros is small. Mortensen describes the binding (1955, pp. 25–26): ‘et slidt Pergamentbind med Spor af grønne Bindebaand’, the portrait and arms plaques on the two boards, ‘derudenom en ret bred rektangulær Ramme trykt med Rullestempel, og inden i Rammens Hjørner Rosetter. Den udekorerede Ryg har haandskreven Titel fra senere Tid.’ His expansion of the dedication’s abbreviation is corrected by the corrigenda in Fund og Forskning X (1963), p. 155: ‘bør forkortelsen ddt opløses til dono dedit eller dedicavit’. The Royal Library’s catalogue lists two copies of the Hanau 1597 edition (VD16 C 304): 88, 201 01800, in the ordinary stacks, with the provenance of L. M. Schavenius, and 88, 201 01801, kept in the library’s store of rarities and lent only to the reading room, with no provenance or item note. The library’s copy of the Theocritus (Commelinus, 1596) at 168, 370 02401 is a separate copy; a constituent of the Sammelband would be shelved under the Calvin call number. The library has not confirmed that 88, 201 01801 is the volume acquired through Bruhn in 1954.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1604
    The heirs ceded Tycho’s instruments and manuscripts to Rudolf II by contract; the library stayed with them, while the instruments ‘cum libris observationum’ were ordered to Vienna in 1604 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 75). Kepler received the observations, originals and copies, under a contract with Tengnagel in 1604 (Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 370). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970; Dreyer 1890
  2. Johannes Kepler, with the observation books 1604–1630
    Kepler received Tycho’s observations, originals and copies, under a contract with Tengnagel of 1604 and never returned them (Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 370); the leaf is sewn into the codex of the observations of 1600–1601. — Dreyer 1890
  3. Ludwig Kepler, as a pledge against the court’s bond of 1633 1630–1655
    Mortensen 1955, pp. 31–32; Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 373 (by the beginning of 1662 at the latest). — Mortensen 1955; Dreyer 1890
  4. Frederik III of Denmark; the Royal Library, Copenhagen, GKS 318 2° from 1655

Catalogue record of the holding library
catalogue record of the codex — Royal Danish Library, catalogue record of the codex GKS 318 2°; the record as of 31 August 2026
As catalogued

Names in the record

For mikrofilm, se: Ms. micro 555.
Mention in Ilsøe, Støbeskeen (1999)

Sources
Norlind 1970; TBOO; Mortensen 1955; Ilsøe 1999; Kleinschnitzová 1933; Dreyer 1890
Notes
One manuscript leaf, not a book. Its heading reads ‘Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae’; it records seven lunar and six solar eclipses of 1581–1600 observed at Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel and Gröningen, the times as a rule from star altitudes, and it carries in Tycho’s hand the mean times for Krabbe’s observations and for his own. Tycho had asked Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg in April 1600 to procure these observations and their method, in order to fix the meridian difference between Krabbe’s observing places and his own (Opera omnia VIII, 295); the last entry on the leaf is 30 June 1600. The leaf is sewn into the codex of Tycho’s observations of 1600–1601 and passed with the observation books from his heirs to Kepler, to Ludwig Kepler, and by sale to Frederik III in 1655 (Mortensen 1955, p. 31). The library’s record is that of the codex: it names Tycho’s Benátky and Prague observations and the observations Kepler sent from Styria, not the Krabbe leaf. The leaf is not printed in the Opera omnia; Dreyer’s commentary places it at fol. 157, Norlind at fol. 159. No digital facsimile of the codex exists: the library’s record for GKS 311–318 is a physical-only record, and of the observation codices only GKS 316 is digitised; the library’s microfilm is Ms. micro 555.

Tycho's gilt portrait+arms superexlibris — the finely struck, well-preserved exemplar figured in the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X (1906/07). On a Renaissance binding: the 1906 notice took it for Basel work made for Tycho, Bargum for Danish work made under his direction, Mortensen (1955, p. 28) for a binding Tycho acquired bound and then stamped. Chain of custody
  1. route unknown from 1601
    The route out of the library and to Sweden is undocumented (possibly the Swedish sack of Prague in 1648, but no evidence places the volume on that road).
  2. Ludwig Rosenthal, antiquarian bookseller, Munich until 1906
    Rosenthal sent the volume to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde, which reproduced its plaques in 1906. — ZfB 1906–07 (binding note)
  3. Per Hierta (1864–1924), Främmestad, Västergötland
    Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band XXV (p. 14: ‘Per Hjerta, Frammestad, Schweden’); Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘tilhørte tidligere Per Hierta, Främmestad, Sverige’. — Prandtl 1932; Mortensen 1955
  4. Röhsska museum, Göteborg
    There by 1955 (Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘findes nu i Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseet, Göteborg’; p. 28: one of the Nordic volumes ‘har skiftet Ejer siden Prandtls Liste udkom’); the museum’s accession is not documented. — Mortensen 1955
Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Sources

Notes
Theatri humanae vitae vol. XVIII (Basel 1587). Mortensen 1955 (pp. 28–30) identifies the volume Prandtl catalogued as no. 57, ex Per Hierta, with the one now at the Röhsska museum, Göteborg. The modern inventory number and the museum’s accession are not recorded. The volume was first published in 1906, when Ludwig Rosenthal of Munich sent it to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde: wooden boards covered in brown leather, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames, the innermost with fourteen portrait medallions of scholars, four gilt rosettes, and the gilt portrait and arms medallions with their distichs; a manuscript note inside the board called it a ‘Schweizer Ledereinband mit Blinddruck und Goldmedaillons’, and the writer supposed the binding made at Basel for Tycho. Bargum answered from Copenhagen in the same volume that the binding was Danish work made under Tycho’s direction — though he could not match the fourteen medallions on any other Tycho binding — that Tycho was not at Basel in 1587, that Gellius Sascerides may have procured the book at Basel or at the Frankfurt fair after the summer of 1588, and that Tycho may have taken from Zwinger’s title the name of his projected Theatrum astronomicum. Mortensen in 1955 took the volume for a Renaissance binding that Tycho acquired bound and then stamped, the reading followed here. Neither notice names the volume’s owner between Rosenthal and Hierta.

Petrus Ramus, Arithmeticae libri duo, geometriae septem et viginti, Basel: Episcopius 1580 (the title leaf reads ‘P. Rami Arithmeticae libri duo, Geometriae septem et viginti’). The route by which the volume reached Strahov is not documented. The binding is not parchment, as Pařez’s ‘pergamenových vazbách’ for both mathematical works would have it, but brown leather (calf) over boards, with a wide gilt border roll of putti and foliage, a gilt lozenge frame of the same palmette roll as on the Opus palatinum, blind-tooled corner rosettes with a star, and remnants of green silk ties; Pařez’s description holds for Σ V 5/a only. The large portrait plaque stands in the lozenge on the front board and the arms plaque on the back (76 × 59 mm, Pařez 2009), with the shelf label at the foot of the back board. The title leaf carries the two Strahov stamps and, in ink beside the device, ‘G: Crusio ‹K› / inservio.’ (Gabriel Crusius). One reader’s note is recorded: p. 7, cap. V De divisione, ‘Divisio igitur’ underlined and ‘Analogia divisionis & multiplicationis’ in the margin; the hand has not been assessed.

Crusio ‹K›’ of Gabriel Crusius, mid-seventeenth century. Examination of the volume found one annotated opening: Book I, prop. 4 (Theon’s exposition, ‘Si duo triangula …’), with marginal and head-of-page notes and a lettered triangle, together with a short jotting in the Campanus section — the ‘few notes’ of Pařez, who attributes them to Tycho’s hand. The hand has not been established as Tycho’s. The volume was found by Hedvika Kuchařová and published by Pařez (2009); the Katalog Tritius provenance note reads ‘Brahe, Tycho; Clauser, Jan Josef’ (record 993601).

Číslo jednotky: __AG VII 84 = DR VII 19
Jedno z vydání kumulovaných hvězdářských tabulek, které započaly vycházet v autorově tiskárně už roku 1474.
Premonstráti (Strahov) |AG VII 84 = DR VII 19
Na fol. 1a1b záznam z konce 16. století "Ex libris Johanni Nachlovskij" a na fol. 1a2a "Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana". O Tychonově vlastnictví (1546 - 1601) svědčí autografní zápis meteorologické povahy na fol. e14b (75v) druhého přívazku. Pak se konvolut stal součástí tzv. Matematického muzea v Klementinu, odkud přešel na Strahov (původní signatura AG VII 84). Cyril Straka: Zápis Tychona Brahe v knihovně Strahovské. Časopis Českého muzea 87, 1913, s. 382-384, zvl. 384 uvádí, že konvolut přešel na Strahov počátkem 19. století jakožto součást knihovny astronoma Antonína Strnada (1746 - 1799). To&nbsp;se však nezdá být pravděpodobné, neboť Seydl&nbsp;ani Kouklová&nbsp;v katalogu&nbsp;Strnadovy knihovny tuto položku neuvádějí. Je možné, že u Straky došlo k záměně s&nbsp;efemeridami, které sestavili Johann Stoeffler - Jakob Pflaum: Almanach nova plurimis annis&nbsp;[1499 - 1531] venturis inservientia. Venezia, Peter Liechtenstein 1507 (EDIT 16 CNCE 35579), v nichž se nachází Regiomontanova předmluva. Tyto efemeridy&nbsp;se do Strahovské knihovny&nbsp;dostaly skutečně ze Strnadova majetku a nesou signaturu AG VII 87 (srov. Kouklová, s. 217, č. 459, kde však záznam veden mylně jako prvotisk s odvoláním na H 15085, což je předchozí edice z Ulmu 1499).&nbsp;
Chybí 358 listů. Dochována je&nbsp;jen&nbsp;složka 1a4 s Ratdoltovou a Regiomontanovou předmluvou a ze&nbsp;složky 2a pouze fol. a5-6 Mariensüssova Expositia. ; Natištěné iniciály v červeno-černém tisku nekolorovány, rubriky nedoplněny. Před hlavním dílem předvázány [3] zachovalé předsádkové listy s matematickými výpočty, sahajícími až na nepotištěné fol. 1a1a, kde se jejich autor ca 1766 nad kresbičkou koše podepsal "Josephus Worel". Táž ruka nesoustavně pročíslovala listy celého konvolutu.
Hlavní dílo konvolutu v pozdně gotické vazbě na prkénkových deskách 230 x 150 potažených usní jen do jedné třetiny (přední deska mírně naprasklá). Přídeštní část usně, přibitá k deskám malými hřebíčky, byla zdobena dnes už zcela setřelým slepotiskem s rámovou kompozicí. U horního kapitálu poškozený hřbet nebyl zdoben. Na přední desce se zachoval sotva znatelný nápis "ALMANACH". Středová spona odstraněna. Žlutá ořízka.

References cited by the library
H 13797 = 10770*.; R 1046.; GW(M) 37488.; ISTC ir00105000.; BMC 12, 19.; BSB-Ink R 61.
Holding
Strahovská knihovna, DR VII 19/1
Sources
Straka 1913; Boldan 2025; Strahov Katalog Tritius; Voit 2015; Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970; Munzar 2001
Notes
Regiomontanus, Ephemerides 1492–1506 (Augsburg: Ratdolt 1492), with the prefatory gatherings a4 a10 of the Venice 1481 Ephemerides bound before it — the gatherings missing from the National Library’s copy (Kleinschnitzová 14). The identification as Tycho’s rests on the inscription at fol. a2r, ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (Straka 1913; Boldan 2025, 33.c and 36.a; Tritius), the same basis as the Clementinum volumes; the authorship of the 34-line weather note at fol. e4v, which Straka (1913) attributed to Tycho’s hand, is the open question, and the note has not been subjected to a comparison of hands. Munzar and Pařez (2002, fig. 5) reproduce the weather note. The binding is a contemporary one, not from Tycho’s bindery: bare wooden boards with a strip of leather over the spine nailed to the boards with brass nails, the shelf label DR VII 19 at the foot; a marginal ink ‘156/2/1’ stands beside the Tabula regionum, above which is the reference-meridian note ‘Nota hec Ephemerides sunt supputate ad longitudinem …’. The Katalog Tritius (record 1064031) describes a late-gothic binding on wooden boards, 230 × 150 mm, leather over a third of the boards only, nailed, the blind-tooled frame worn away, ‘ALMANACH’ faintly on the front board, the clasp removed, yellow edges; the 1481 part reduced to gathering 1a4 and fol. a5–6 of 2a; three front flyleaves of mathematical calculations signed ‘Josephus Worel’ above a drawn basket, c. 1766, the same hand foliating the volume; a late-sixteenth-century ‘Ex libris Johanni Nachlovskij’ at fol. 1a1b, the 1642 formula at 1a2a, and Tycho’s ownership attested by an autograph note of meteorological character at fol. e14b (75v). The record states that the volume ‘then became part of the so-called Mathematical Museum in the Clementinum, from which it passed to Strahov’; the Strnad step of Straka (1913) is doubted because neither Seydl nor Kouklová lists it. The old shelfmark was AG VII 84.

Sources
Gingerich 2002; Schaffner catalogue 1977; Chicago, Schaffner exhibit; Newberry, Movable Mayhem; Gingerich & Westman 1988; Mosley 2007; Christianson 2000; TBOO; University of Chicago Library, catalogue record 146807
Notes
The volume carries Tycho’s presentation inscription, which the library’s catalogue record transcribes: ‘D[omi]no Paulo Witichio Wratislauiensj ob amicitam & comune[m] mathemati[cum] amorem d[ono] d[edit] Tÿcho Brahe Huanae anno 1580 29 Octobris.’ — to Master Paul Wittich of Wrocław, for friendship and a shared love of mathematics, Tycho Brahe gave this, at Hven, on 29 October 1580 (a Saturday). The record’s ‘amicitam’ and ‘Huanae’ are its own readings. Gingerich and Westman, who examined the book, place the inscription on the title page. The record further notes former owners’ manuscript annotations in two hands with underscoring, a manuscript pagination 1–46 beginning on page [2], the original silk threads to the volvelles ending in small pearls or coloured glass beads, the volvelle on page [17] lacking its moving parts, a cancel slip over two lines of page [75], some initials hand-coloured by a former owner, a paper tab at the first page of the Meteoroscopion, Louis H. Silver’s book label and Joseph Halle Schaffner’s bookplate. The binding is half leather and marbled paper over boards, with an armorial device pasted to the front cover and the date 1686 tooled on it, and fabric ties, one missing. Tycho’s own words settle the ownership: writing to Hagecius on 1 November 1589 about Wittich’s library, he says that among the books will be found ‘that Astronomicum of Apianus, which I bought for 20 florins and gave to him when he was here; I do not reclaim it after his death unless it can be bought at a fair price’, and that he has another copy to hand. The book was therefore Tycho’s, left his library by his gift on 29 October 1580 — two days after his return from Helsingborg, in the weeks of the comet he and Wittich had observed — and did not come back: what Monaw brought from Wrocław in October 1600 were the annotated copies of Copernicus. It is a documented gift in Tycho’s lifetime, with his autograph, not a survivor of the posthumous dispersal. Whether one of the two annotating hands is Wittich’s, or Tycho’s, is not stated. The record names the owners the inscription does not: Louis H. Silver of Chicago, whose library the Newberry Library bought in 1964 and from which this volume, never accessioned, was sold at Sotheby’s in London on 8–9 November 1965 as lot 4 (‘Silver 4’ in the catalogue of 1977); Joseph Halle Schaffner, who bought at that sale through Warren Howell and whose science library came to the University of Chicago by bequest after his death in August 1972 (exhibited 1977, entry 15). The owners between Wittich’s sister at Wrocław and Silver are not recorded; the binding of 1686 is the one fixed point. Catalogued by the University of Chicago Library at alc ff QB41.A639 1540 (the exhibit label gives alc ff QB41.A63). The volume has not been digitised.

Holding
Harry Ransom Center, Harry Ransom Center Book Collection, QE 362 G391d 1565 (available)
Sources
Prandtl 1932; Gingerich 2002; Norlind 1970; Studnička 1901 (Bericht); Mortensen 1931; Mortensen 1955; Ransom Center 2026; Walde 1938; University of Texas Libraries, catalogue record
Notes
Gesner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zürich 1565, 8vo): the parchment Prachtband that Prandtl owned himself and reproduced, spread open with both boards, as the frontispiece of his catalogue of 1932; his Verzeichnis B lists it as Band XXI, ‘Prachtband, Pergament’, with the previous owner Prof. Dr. G. C. Laube of Prague, who had bought it from a Leipzig antiquarian bookseller. The volume was first noticed in 1901 by Studnička, who saw it in Gustav Laube's possession and read the number 2781 written on the spine as Tycho's own shelf number in his hand, remarking that the binding, unlike those of the Clementinum volumes relabelled in 1642, was intact — the single datum behind every estimate of several thousand volumes for the library (Norlind 1970, p. 335; Gingerich 2002, p. 323, ‘at best speculative’); the hand is Studnička's attribution. Gingerich (2002, p. 325) places the volume at the University of Texas at Austin (Harry Ransom Center), acquired with Prandtl's collection in the 1950s; his ‘private hands in Moravia’ is a conjecture, Prandtl's own account being the Leipzig trade. Catalogued by the University of Texas Libraries at QE 362 G391d 1565, Harry Ransom Center Book Collection, with the local note ‘Wilhelm Prandtl Collection’; the record names neither Tycho nor the binding, and the volume is not digitised. Examined and photographed at the Ransom Center on 7 October 2026 (twenty photographs: both boards with a ruler, the spine straight on and in raking light, the pastedowns and flyleaves, the title page, and the leaves that carry marks). The boards, about 17.5 × 11.5 cm, are as in Prandtl's plate: the portrait oval with the distich Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius enitet quae latet interior on the upper board, the arms with its distich on the lower, each within a lozenge of gilt foliate roll, with corner fleurons and a border roll; the portrait oval measures about 8 × 6 cm against the ruler, which is the larger of Mortensen's two dies (7.6 × 5.8 cm), not the smaller (5.9 × 4.3 cm in Mortensen’s measurement of 1931, 5.8 × 4.3 in that of 1955). The spine, in four panels between gilt-ruled bands with a gilt foliate tool in each, carries no lettering, label or number at all, in direct or in raking light: the 2781 that Studnička read in 1901 is no longer visible, and whether it was inked on the parchment and has faded, or stood on a label since lost, cannot be told from photographs. The title page bears Laube's blue stamp ‘Prof. Dr. G. C. Laube, Prag’ at the foot and no other inscription; the Jesuit inscription of 1642 is absent, as Studnička's remark on the intact spine implied. The front flyleaf carries a pencil note in a modern German hand, ‘Aus Tycho Brahes Bibliothek!’, the front pastedown a pencilled ‘760’ within an oval (a bookseller's or collector's number), the title verso a pencilled ‘HS-67’ and the gutter of leaf a2 the Texas call number in pencil; the rear pastedown has the printed bookplate ‘The University of Texas — The Wilhelm Prandtl Collection — The History of Science Collection’; the rear flyleaf is blank. A leaf-through of the whole volume found one marginal entry, on p. 103 of Gesner's De figuris lapidum: beside the woodcut of the goat-engraved gem that Francesco Calzolari of Verona had sent Gesner, a pen drawing of a goat copying it, and below the paragraph a single word in a German cursive hand, apparently ‘mein’, with a long flourish — a reader's doodle in a German hand, with nothing in it to suggest Tycho, whose marginalia are Latin in a humanist cursive; pp. 16–17 of Cordus's De halosantho show only hair-thin curving lines without ink, a dry pen rather than writing. Prandtl, who noted Tycho's hand systematically in other volumes, recorded none here, and the examination confirms it: the volume carries no annotation attributable to Tycho. Walde noted in 1938 that whether the number 2781 came from Tycho himself or from some cataloguing in his library was undecided, and that if it did the library must have run to several thousand works.

Walde (1920) and Mortensen (1955) read the volume as Tycho’s gift or exchange to Vedel; Norlind (1970, p. 366) read it the other way, as Vedel’s book given to Tycho, who had it bound — in which case it did not leave the library in his lifetime and its road to Sweden is unknown. — Walde 1920; Mortensen 1955; Norlind 1970; Mortensen 1942

    No owner is recorded between Vedel and De la Gardie. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie (1622–1686) until 1669
    His red seal inside the front board (the library’s record, revised 11 September 2026; Alvin record 805325). — Uppsala UB 2026 — catalogue, photographs, EOD facsimile; Uppsala UB, Alvin record 805325
  4. Uppsala University Library, Script. Graeci (Xenophon) from 1669
    De la Gardie’s donation of 1669; the library’s older shelfmarks ‘V. XI. 4.’, ‘238’ and ‘Pp. IX. 2. 398’ (Alvin record 805325; the library’s catalogue). — Uppsala UB, Alvin record 805325; Uppsala UB 2026 — catalogue, photographs, EOD facsimile

Handwriting survey
680 images examined; 31 images with handwriting flagged, 7 uncertain (an automated survey of the facsimile; no hand attributed). Kinds: marginal notes (images 19, 20, 21, 22, 24, 30…); diagrams and tables (images 33, 34, 129, 143, 155); underlining or marks (images 90, 176); corrections (images 124).
Sources
Prandtl 1932; Walde 1920; Walde 1938; Norlind 1970; Mortensen 1955; Thoren 1990; Uppsala UB 2026 — catalogue, photographs, EOD facsimile; Uppsala UB, Alvin record 805325; Mortensen 1942; Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
Notes
Prandtl’s Band III, the Sammelband of 1563: Camerarius’s Hippocomicus with his Latin Xenophon (Leipzig 1556), Osius’s Historia excidii Hierosolymorum (Wittenberg 1558) and Garcaeus’s Tractatus de erigendis figuris coeli (Wittenberg 1556), in that order, the three titles numbered ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ in ink. Light tanned leather over boards with rich blind tooling and traces of clasps, the front board stamped TY BRAD and dated 1563; Vedel’s name ‘Andreas Seuerinus Velleius’ at the head of the first title; Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie’s red seal inside the front board; a handwritten index on the rear endleaf (the library’s catalogue; the LIBRIS note common to the three records: ‘På främre pärmen tryckt: "TY BRAD 1563"; på titelsidan handskrivet: "Andreas Seuerinus Welleius"; Magnus Gabiel De la Gardies röda sigill på främre pärmens insida’). Walde, who came upon the volume at Uppsala, took it for a book Tycho procured on the study journey of 1563 and soon gave or exchanged to Vedel, his companion on that journey — in an exchange Tycho may have received the Glareanus of 1536 that Vedel bought in August 1564, now at Prague (19 G 20); Mortensen followed him; Norlind read it the other way, as Vedel’s book given to Tycho, who had it bound with the two others. The library’s facsimile of October 2026 (the text block only; binding, pastedowns and endleaves not photographed) shows the annotation leaf by leaf. The Camerarius carries a red-brown subject heading at the head of sig. A2 recto, red-brown underlining of the Greek style-terms in the preface (image 24) and of the opening of De nominibus equestribus (p. 97), and pen strokes against a passage on p. 141; the Osius nothing beyond its ‘2.’ and a small numeral ‘7’ at the foot of one page (image 58); the Garcaeus the ‘strödda marginalanteckningar’ of the catalogue — subject headings and section numbers in the calendar chapters (images 19–37 of the Garcaeus), the solar cycle for 1555 worked by long division (33), the dominical-letter table numbered by hand with the years 1488–1501 and a 1–7 counter (34), ‘obliquam’ correcting the misprint ‘aliquam’ (124), figures checking the Elector August’s nativity and part of fortune (129, 143, 155), the rule of the part of fortune written out (136), the revolution of 1556 recomputed from Reinhold’s tables (171: ‘Ego R[…] juxta Reinholdum ☉ in 16 37 ♌’), a note on the meridian of Reinhold’s equinox table (174: Königsberg at longitude 44¼ against 53½, ‘37 circiter min[uta]’), ‘Directionis finis’ with underlining at Propositio XXII (176) and a faint unread note (152). These are two registers of a sixteenth-century hand, in brown and black ink; whether they are Tycho’s student hand of 1563–65 or Vedel’s is not decided. Thoren (1990, p. 17) and Christianson (2020, p. 24) record that Tycho, during his Leipzig studies, bought ‘an astrological work by Johannes Garcaeus’ and began a notebook of horoscopes on its model; Thoren’s note points to this copy. The library’s photographs (Alvin record 805325) show the rest: the upper board with TY ✿ BRAD at the head and the Annunciation panel, the lower board with the Baptism-of-Christ panel, the Reformers roll, the brass catches of the lost clasps, five raised bands, plain edges; on the front pastedown the library’s labels (‘Script. graeci (Xenophon)’, ‘Pp. IX. 2. 398’) and Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie’s red wax seal; on the front flyleaf verso the older shelfmarks ‘V. XI. 4.’ and ‘238’ and a contents note in an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century library hand (‘Accedunt: 2. Hieron. Osius … Witeb. 1558. 3. Joh. Garcaeus Jun. … Witeb. 1556’), whose numbering is the ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ written on the three titles; and on the rear endleaf, in a sixteenth-century cursive, an unfinished index of the Garcaeus — ‘Index monstrans quid quaelibet propositio in hoc libello contineat’, propositions I to V with their signatures (B, C, D …), a pen flourish beneath. The index is in the same hand, and belongs to the same work, as the marginal headings and section numbers of the Garcaeus, and it was written in the bound volume: whoever annotated the Garcaeus did so after the binding of 1563 — the owner of the bound book, Tycho in 1563–65 or Vedel afterwards; the index is the longest specimen of that hand. The year 1563, read on the upper board by Prandtl, Norlind and Mortensen, is not legible in the photographs, nor in the three raking-light photographs the library supplied on 13 October 2026: the band beneath the panel, where a Saxon binder stamps the year under the owner’s name, carries the remains of stamped forms — a looped figure at its right end that may be the 6, the rest on an abraded surface — but no numeral can be read from them. With the book in hand the year is plain: Peter Sjökvist, the library’s Rare Books Librarian, confirmed in October 2026 that 1563 is seen quite clearly with the naked eye and that there is no doubt that is what stands on the binding. The year therefore stands on four readings of the book itself — Prandtl, Mortensen, Norlind and Sjökvist — and on the library’s catalogue note; the photographs fail to reproduce it, they do not contradict it. The Alvin record names De la Gardie, Tycho Brahe and Vedel as former owners. A Sammelband at KB, RAR:142 A, bound with Peucer 1553, is a different volume. The volume is kept in Specialsamlingar; the Osius also carries the older control number Pp:398 (2).
