Gemma, Cornelius — private collection

Avol-s-ging-gemma
Identification
A · identified by Harald Mortensen 1955, p. 30 (from Felix Mainx's report of 1938); Norlind 1970, p. 347; the annotations recognised as Tycho's by Owen Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and Anthony Grafton (report for Martayan Lan, 2001); Gingerich 2002, p. 326
Marks securing the identification
Tycho's autograph annotations throughout, from a word or two to a note filling the margin, incl. the long note written upside down in the lower margin of Book II, pp. 124–125 (the hand confirmed by Owen Gingerich, per litteras 25 May 2001, and studied by Anthony Grafton); Tycho's gilt portrait supralibros with the motto ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ on the front cover and the Brahe arms with ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’ on the back
Binding
Period 4 (gilt supralibros): contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, the portrait-and-arms supralibros (Martayan Lan 2001)
Contents
  1. Gemma, Cornelius, De naturae divinis characterismis; seu raris & admirandis spectaculis, causis, indiciis, proprietatibus rerum in partibus singulis universi, libri II (1575) (no. 102)
Chain of custody
  1. route unknown from 1601
    The route out of the library is undocumented: the library remained with Tycho’s heirs in 1601 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76, 78), but nothing places this volume with them, and the first dated witness on the copy is the inscription of 1647.
  2. An owner not identified: an inscription dated 1647 on the copy from 1647
    A scored earlier ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647, both unread, and an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan, Catalogue 28, 2001, item 55). — Martayan Lan Cat. 28 (2001)
  3. route unknown
    No owner is recorded between 1647 and 1938.
  4. Felix Mainx, Prague from 1938
    Mainx told Mortensen in 1938 that he had acquired Tycho’s copy (Mortensen 1955, p. 30). — Mortensen 1955
  5. ‘A private European collector’ until 2001
    Martayan Lan’s provenance line (Catalogue 28, item 55). — Martayan Lan Cat. 28 (2001)
  6. Martayan Lan, New York, Catalogue 28, item 55 2001
    Offered at US$ 300,000 with Owen Gingerich’s confirmation of the hand and Anthony Grafton’s report. — Martayan Lan Cat. 28 (2001)
  7. A private collector in the United States from 2001
    Gingerich 2002, p. 326 n. 16. — Gingerich 2002
Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Sources
Martayan Lan Cat. 28 (2001); Gingerich 2002; Mortensen 1955; Norlind 1970; Kleinschnitzová 1933
Notes
Martayan Lan’s description (Catalogue 28, item 55, pp. 66–67, headed ‘Tycho Brahe reads & annotates the new star of 1572: unpublished notes on “the greatest cosmological crisis in Western history” – Grafton’): 4to; 229, (1) pp., (5) ff., 284 pp., 18 ff.; three woodcut star charts and several depictions of constellations and related astronomical phenomena in the text. Binding: contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, a gilt medallion portrait of Tycho in the centre of the front cover, worn, with ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ in the surround; the back cover with the Brahe family arms and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’; covers soiled, remnants of ties; an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine. Condition: front endleaf soiled, with unidentified later annotations; waterstain and soiling in the upper right corner of the title and on scattered leaves; a scored former ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647; even toning, occasional light browning; ‘for a working copy, very good’. The price asked was US$ 300,000. The annotations in Tycho’s hand range from a word or two to notes virtually filling the margin; on pp. 124–125 of Book II the lower-margin note was entered with the copy held upside down (the colour plate at the front of the catalogue, captioned ‘Tycho Brahe’s Annotated Copy No. 55’; Gingerich 2002, fig. 1). The dealer supplied a list of the annotated locations with a partial transcription, and Anthony Grafton’s detailed but preliminary report, available on request, which found a genetic relation to the Progymnasmata (Prague 1602); Owen Gingerich confirmed the hand (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and wrote that the book ‘contains source material used directly by Tycho in composing his Progymnasmata … this is a working text that is feeding directly into his published work, and we have nothing else like this’. The dealer called it ‘one of only two known copies of any book owned by the astronomer in private hands’. Provenance as given: ‘a private European collector. In 1955, the Danish librarian H. Mortensen described the present copy as being in the private collection of a professor in Prague’ – that professor is Felix Mainx, who told Mortensen in 1938 that he had acquired Tycho’s copy (Mortensen 1955, p. 30); Gingerich 2002, p. 326, which places the book in Mortensen’s own collection about 1955, misreads Mortensen’s paper. Gingerich 2002, p. 327: Tycho annotated heavily the section on Muñoz’s observations of the new star of 1572 and quoted the passage in the Progymnasmata; n. 16: now in the hands of a private American collector. References cited by the dealer: Norlind 1970, p. 347; Adams G-373; Durling 2042; Warner, The Sky Explored, p. 92; Daston & Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, p. 175; Christianson 2000, p. 139; Prandtl 1932 (cited by the offprint pagination, pp. 1–16).

Avol-s-ging-apianus-tbo
Identification

Binding stamped ‘T.B.O.’ above the date ‘1583’; Tycho's annotations in the comet section near the end of the Astronomicum Caesareum (Gingerich 2002, fig. 2: f. O1 verso, a marginal heading reading, in the reproduction, ‘Motus diurnus Cometae in suo circulo’ beside Apianus's table of the comet's daily motion)
Binding
Period 3 (T.B.O. 1583; the binding is not otherwise described)
Contents
  1. Apianus, Petrus, Astronomicum Caesareum (Ingolstadt, 1540), bound with Johann Schöner's equatorium of 1521 (1540) (no. 13)
  2. Schöner, Johann, Aequatorium astronomicum (Nuremberg, 1521) — bound with Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum of 1540 in the T.B.O. 1583 volume (1521) (no. 255)
Chain of custody
  1. route unknown from 1601
    The route out of the library is undocumented. The star names written in French on the planisphere and a note partly in Dutch, partly in Flemish place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; Gingerich supposed Jesuit hands, a conjecture (Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328).
  2. A monastery library in the Low Countries c. 1960
    Gingerich 2002, p. 328. — Gingerich 2002
  3. A private owner in Belgium null–c. 2000
    Who wrote to Gingerich about the binding stamp about 2000 (Gingerich 2002, p. 327). — Gingerich 2002
  4. A private collector in the United States from c. 2001
    Gingerich 2002, p. 328. — Gingerich 2002
Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Sources
Gingerich 2002
Notes
Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328: about two years before he wrote (so about 2000) an e-mail enquiry came from Belgium about a copy of Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum bound with an even rarer equatorium, an earlier one by Johann Schöner: why, the owner asked, would books printed in 1521 and 1540 be in a binding stamped 1583, with the initials TBO above the date? Gingerich recognised Tycho's mark at once. Further enquiries showed several annotations by Tycho, all in the comet section near the end; fig. 2 (‘courtesy of another private collector’) is a detail of f. O1 verso with Tycho's marginalia beside the table of the comet's daily motion. Additional early annotations in other hands – the star names on the planisphere in French, a note on the facing page partly Dutch and partly Flemish – place the book around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; until about 1960 it was in a monastery library. Gingerich imagines it migrated to the Low Countries by the same Jesuit hands that brought the Wittich Copernicus to Liège. ‘This extraordinary volume has changed hands again, to an anonymous American collector who must have paid close to a million dollars for it.’ Gingerich, who had examined over a hundred copies of the Astronomicum Caesareum without finding one associated with Tycho, took this to be the copy Tycho retained when he gave Wittich his (the Chicago copy, with Tycho's presentation inscription; Tycho later complained it had cost him 20 florins). It is distinct from both the Chicago copy and the copy Tycho inscribed at Wittenberg on 14 June 1599, now at Gotha (Prandtl Band VI). Neither the monastery, the Belgian owner nor the American buyer is named.

Handwriting in the digitised volumes

An automated survey of the facsimile images of 29 digitised volumes locates handwriting and classifies it by kind (marginal notes, underlining, corrections, ownership inscriptions, stamps): 13,510 images examined, 1,023 of them carrying handwriting of some kind. It is not a leaf-by-leaf examination except where a record says so, and it attributes no hand. The Prague volumes carry, besides whatever Tycho wrote, the hands of earlier owners and the accession notes of the Jesuit houses, 1636–1675 (the Clementinum, Chomutov, Krumlov). Only the most informative images of each volume are listed, by image number, so that the facsimile can be opened at them; no reading of the annotations is offered here. The Uppsala volume’s facsimile is not online.

Notes
Marked Tychoniana, not his: a post-Tycho 1606 imprint in the Bibliotheca Tychoniana (Prandtl's Kepler-volume evidence). Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 (no. VII of the seven found since 1902, Sign. XIV J 199): Kepler's De stella nova (Prague 1606) and De Jesu Christi vero anno natalitio (Frankfurt 1606), ‘Ex bibliotheca Tychoniana’ on the first title; he took the two tracts, printed five years after Tycho's death, as proof that the family and Kepler kept the library together after 1601 and 1604 and added to it. The inference is not followed here: the volume is a post-Tycho imprint that the Jesuits marked as Tychoniana.

Severinus Pauli[?] (Leipzig, c.1583) → Christiern Jensen (Christiernus Joannis) of Copenhagen, 1620 → Henrik Hielmstierne (bookplate No.1661, Tuscher) → Royal Library, Copenhagen
Sources
Norlind 1970
Notes
Fincke, Geometria rotundi (1583), the Royal Library’s second copy of LN 599, in the Hielmstierne Sammelband Hielmst. 1661a 4°, bound with Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum (Strasbourg 1588), the work of Tycho’s rival. It is not Tycho’s copy: two early owners precede Hielmstierne — a Leipzig owner of about 1583 (‘Severinus Pauli[?] … Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]’ on the flyleaf) and Christiern Jensen of Copenhagen, 1620 (on the title page) — and the volume carries no mark of Tycho’s. A facsimile is on Early European Books (ProQuest).

Hielmst. 1226 4° — Copenhagen, Royal Library

examined and ruled outvol-s-mort-kb-flemlose
Examination
Norlind 1970, p. 346 (a work-level inference from the dedication; the copy carries no Tycho mark)
Marks securing the identification
No Tycho mark: the only marks are eighteenth-century Hielmstierne -- the Tuscher bookplate (1743-51) and the Bibliotheca Regia Hafniensis stamp. It is nonetheless the sole surviving copy of the edition (unicum, L. Nielsen).
Contents
  1. Flemløse, Peder Jacobsen, Ægloga de eclipsi solari anno 1574 ... futura (1574) (no. 90)
Catalogue record of the holding library
catalogue record — Royal Danish Library, catalogue record; the record as of 27 August 2026

Sources
Norlind 1970
Notes
The Royal Library’s Hielmst. 1226 4° is the only known copy of Flemløse’s Aegloga (1574). It is not Tycho’s: the full scan shows eighteenth-century Hielmstierne provenance and no Tycho mark, and none of the Prague catalogues — Kleinschnitzová, Šolc, Prandtl — lists the work. Tycho’s library went to Prague; this copy did not. A facsimile is on Early European Books (ProQuest), reached through the Royal Library’s electronic record; outside the library’s licence the page opens on a ProQuest login.

6Concordance of the catalogues

The concordance aligns each entry with the numbers under which the earlier catalogues list it: Prandtl’s Verzeichnis A (the works) and Verzeichnis B (the bound volumes, Bände I–XXIX), Kleinschnitzová’s FK numbers and the shelfmarks she recorded, Šolc’s numbers, the page of Norlind’s Bilaga I, Zinner’s number where given, the VD16 number, the National Library’s record number, and the letter in Tycho’s correspondence that attests the book. Sort by any column to read the concordance from any catalogue’s side. Prandtl’s A 6 (an Archimedes of Basel 1548, his Band IX) answers to no edition and is read here as a misdating of the Hervagius Archimedes of 1544 in Band VIII; it has no entry.

Below the table the concordance is read from the earlier catalogues’ side: every number of Prandtl’s Verzeichnis A and B, every volume and item of Kleinschnitzová, Šolc’s additions, every entry of Norlind’s Bilaga I and every record of the National Library’s former-owner index under Brahe, each answered by the entry or volume it stands for here, or by the reason it has none; and the register of the entries and records this edition has retired, with the reason and the record that absorbed them.

Prandtl’s misprints and slips, as read against Prusík 1901 and Kleinschnitzová 1933
  • A15 'FERNETIUS / Fernetii' for Fernelius (inherited from Studnicka).
  • A27 Band XV constituents printed '(23, 10, 27)' for (28, 10, 27).
  • A30 Band XIX constituents printed '(30, 24)' for (30, 25).
  • A26 and A27 are one book (14 H 190); Band XV has two constituents.
  • A6 / Band IX is a doublet of A5 / Band VIII (Prusik's '1548').
  • A44 'Tubingae' for Oppenheim (Koebel) 1518.
  • A52 'libri tres' for libri tredecim; XXIII is a Sammelband, not an Einzelband.
  • A58 'Wittenberg' for Leipzig (Camerarius, Valentin Papst 1556).
  • XVI: Crusius inscription placed 'auf dem Titelblatt von 55' and dated 1673; it stands on the title of 54 (first in the volume) and is dated 5 August 1654, 1673 being the Chomutov catalogue entry.
  • XXII 'Einzelband' (a Sammelband of four Rantzau pieces); IV, XXVIII describe states that no longer existed in 1932 (the manuscript removed before 1901; the Christmann an adligat of Scheiner 1631 by 1901).
  • XXV: Per Hierta had died in 1924.

Šolc 2002, the titles beyond Kleinschnitzová

Šolc numbers nothing: he files his additions under her numbers and shelfmarks, and his total — about 110 titles in 50 volumes (p. 329) — is a round figure.

Entries and records retired

The keys this edition has retired, with the reason and the record that absorbed them; a retired key keeps its page, which says so and points on.

KeyWhat it wasRetiredReasonAbsorbed in
e-mort-frederiksborg-agrippaHeinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim, Opera, tomus I (Lyon, ca. 1550, 8vo)28 September 2026The same volume as Prandtl A no. 48 / Band XX (Prandtl 1932 lists Band XX with Mortensen); provenance and notes folded into the Prandtl-numbered entry.Agrippa von Nettesheim, Heinrich Cornelius, Opera, tomus primus (c. 1550)
e-mort-rohsska-prachtband(unidentified — a gilt-supralibros Prachtband), A Tycho gilt-supralibros Prachtband (title not identified)8 October 2026The same volume as Prandtl A no. 57 / Band XXV (the Zwinger Theatrum humanae vitae XVIII at the Röhsska museum): Mortensen 1955 pp. 28–30 names the title, and the survivor s-mort-rohsska-prachtband already pointed to the Prandtl-numbered entry. The 'title not identified' record was a seed artefact that the merge of announced but never removed.Zwinger, Theodor, Theatri humanae vitae volumen decimum-octavum [the last tome, volumina XVIII–XXIX: 33 books, pp. 3251–4373 and the index] (1587)
e-ghost-albategnius-arabical-Battani (Albategnius), De motu stellarum — a corrected/Arabic edition Tycho sought (1598-1600)18 October 2026A better, Arabic text of al-Battani that Tycho sought in 1598–1600 and is not documented as having received; no printed Arabic al-Battani existed. The Nuremberg edition of 1537 he owned is Alfraganus, Rudimenta astronomica Alfragani. Item Albategnius astronomus peritissimus de motu stellarum ....
e-ging-apianus-cosmographia-1561Petrus Apianus, Cosmographia (1561 edition)18 October 2026A duplicate of Apianus, Petrus, Cosmographia (per Gemma Frisium) (1553) (Band II): Gingerich’s ‘1561 edition’ is the year stamped on that volume’s binding, not an edition.
e-kl-27bFederico Commandino, Federici Commandini Urbinatis Liber de horologiorum descriptione18 October 2026Commandino’s Liber de horologiorum descriptione is the second part of the Rome imprint of 1562 that carries Ptolemy’s De analemmate (Ptolemaeus, Claudius (ed. Federico Commandino), Liber de analemmate, a Federico Commandino instauratus; eiusdem Commandini Liber de horologiorum descriptione (1562), Kleinschnitzová 27:1); Šolc 2002 (p. 331) itemised it as a title, as he did the other parts of works retired on 18 October 2026. Neither Kleinschnitzová nor the library’s record lists it as a separate piece.
e-letter-braun-theatrumGeorg Braun & Frans Hogenberg, Theatrum urbium / Civitates orbis terrarum (the city-atlas; sought the further volumes)18 October 2026The fourth part of the Civitates orbis terrarum that was at Hven in December 1588 was Rantzau’s loan (Norlind 1926, p. 218, among the loans; Opera omnia VII, 386; Rantzau’s own copy is at Augsburg, Gebele 1926), and Norlind found no evidence that Tycho owned parts I–III; a borrowed book is outside this catalogue.
e-letter-munoz-novastellaJerónimo Muñoz (Munosius), Libro del nuevo cometa / De nova stella (Spanish, Valencia 1573)18 October 2026No document attests the book as Tycho’s: he asked Hagecius for Muñoz’s Spanish tract on the new star on 25 January 1590 (Opera omnia VII, 224); Hagecius answered on 1/11 June 1590 that he had his own copy, the author’s gift, and no one to translate it (VII, 251: ‘MUNNOSIJ libellum de nova stella Hispanico idiomate, ab ipsomet olim mihi missum et donatum, habeo, qui tamen eum Latinum faciat, habeo neminem’) and sent nothing; Tycho withdrew the request on 3 August 1590 (VII, 270), and the Progymnasmata say he never saw the text (III, 80). The store had read Hagecius’s letter as a gift.
e-norlind-hipparchus-aratiHipparchus (ed. princeps, Petrus Victorius), In Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III18 October 2026The same object as Hipparchus (ed. Petrus Victorius), the copy annotated by Joseph Justus Scaliger, In Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III (the Greek editio princeps, with Scaliger’s annotations) (1567) — the Victorius Hipparchus of 1567 with Scaliger’s annotations, requested in August 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, 102), acknowledged in March 1599 (VIII, 151) and still with the heirs when Kepler asked Jørgen Brahe for it in November 1624 (KGW XIX, no. 7) — entered twice; Norlind’s record and the Ripensis story move to the surviving entry.
e-orphan-wroclaw(unspecified), [Tychoniana reported at Wrocław University Library, Głombiowski 1955 — no title establishe18 October 2026The Wrocław ‘Tychonianum’ of Głombiowski 1955 is the Mechanica of 1598 that Tycho inscribed for Jakob Monau — an outgoing presentation copy carried in the census of that edition, not a book of the library.

7Holdings by institution

Where the located volumes are today. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds 51 of the 72 volumes — those the Clementinum college itself received as a gift, inscribed in 1642, and those gathered there from the other Jesuit houses after 1773; the remaining 21 are in 14 institutions in 8 countries and, for 2 of them, in private hands. The table counts only volumes identified as Tycho’s own; the map plots the institutions that hold them, so the privately held volumes are not on it.

Works are the itemised constituents of the volumes; a volume is digitised when a facsimile of it is linked. The road is the route by which the holder’s volumes came (§9):

  1. 0 Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges
  2. I The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773
  3. II The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601)
  4. III The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague)
  5. IV Rudolfine-imperial absorption
  6. V Attrition / loss
  7. VI Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik
  8. VIII With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604)
  9. U Route out of the library unknown

8The ownership marks

Tycho’s books are recognised by the marks his binders and his own hand put on them. The bindings form a datable sequence. In the student years the name was stamped on the boards — TVCHO BRADE / ANNO 1561 on the volume now at Helsingør, TY BRAD 1563 on the Uppsala Sammelband, TYCHO / BRAHE 1567 on the Strahov Euclid — or the initials alone with the year, T. B. 1560 (18 J 318) and 1567 (10 G 47); all of these are earlier than Hven. From 1576, when Uraniborg was furnished, the gilt cipher T.B.O. (Tychonis Brahe Ottonidis — Prusík 1901, p. 198) stands on brown leather with the year beneath it, 1576 on most of the books, then 1580, 1582 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 81) and 1583 (Gingerich 2002); where these bindings were made is not settled — Prandtl places a binder on Hven (1932, p. 9), Kleinschnitzová argues a Copenhagen workshop from the stamps shared with Vedel’s bindings (1933, p. 82); she also recorded Danish waste in two boards — a Danish print, an arithmetic she supposed, with a Dutch gospel print in the T.B.O. 1576 binding of 14 A 66 (no. 34), and a Danish manuscript fragment of the seventeenth century in the rebinding of 40 F 39 (no. 14). From 1588 the presentation bindings carry the gilt portrait-and-arms supralibros, Prandtl’s Prachtband (1932, p. 11); one of them, the Strahov Opus palatinum, was struck after 1599 by a Prague binder of the Rudolfine circle (Voit 2020). Books received ready-bound, and gifts, may carry only his handwritten initials or a purchase-note. The four periods are Prandtl’s (Verzeichnis B, 1932, pp. 13–14), after Prusík (1901, p. 198 n.); the date ranges are this catalogue’s, from the dated stamps, and are the scale used in the volume records.

The dies of period 4 are dated by the presentation copies of De mundi (1588): the Sascerides copy, Royal Danish Library LN 428 4° ex. 1, its dedication dated 20 March 1588 (Norlind 1970, p. 122; the census of De mundi); the Scultetus copy at Görlitz, portrait and arms, dedication dated 8 May 1588 (Norlind 1970, p. 124); the Maestlin copy in the British Library, dedication dated 14 May 1588 (Norlind 1970, p. 122).

36 of the 72 volumes carry no binding period in their record: books in another owner’s binding or rebound after they left the library, manuscripts, bindings stripped of their covering, and bindings not described at first hand.

Recognition checklist

  • An oval gilt portrait medallion on the upper board, with the distich ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei…’, in two sizes — about 76 × 58 and 58 × 43 mm, as measured in the table below — indicates a presentation binding of period 4, Prandtl’s Prachtband (1932, p. 11).
  • The arms oval on the lower board, with ‘Arma genus, fundi pereunt; durabile virtus…’, accompanies the portrait.
  • The gilt cipher T.B.O. on brown calf with a rhomboid arabesque and the year beneath indicates period 3; the same cipher with no year reported is Prandtl’s period 2.
  • Handwritten ‘T. B.’ initials or a purchase-note on the title-page mark gifts and copies received ready-bound.
  • The Jesuit accession inscription ‘A. 1642 / Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana’, or a Chomutov, Krumlov or professed-house catalogue entry (Chomutov 1645–1675, two of them Crusius’s gifts of 1654), indicates the Jesuit road — the Clementinum, or a Jesuit house whose library came to it after 1773.

A caution. The Clementinum’s inscription Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana is not by itself proof of Tycho’s ownership: the Jesuits went on adding to the Tychoniana after his death. Sign. 14 J 199, two Kepler tracts of 1606 bound together, carries the inscription. Kukula (1906–07, p. 25) and Prandtl (1932, p. 16) read it as a sign that the heirs and Kepler kept the library together and added to it; Kleinschnitzová excluded it from her census because Tycho died in 1601 (1933, p. 83). It is recorded here among the volumes marked Tychoniana but not his. Conversely, a volume bearing only the Jesuit inscription and no binding-stamp may still be Tycho’s where its imprint predates 1601: on that ground Kleinschnitzová admitted the plain-bound Clementinum volumes (1933, p. 83).

9Acquisition and dispersal

How the books came to Tycho, and by what roads they left the library — a few in his own lifetime, the rest after 1601. The acquisition channels are reconstructed from the correspondence and from the purchase-notes and dedications on the surviving copies. The roads of dispersal are the routes by which the volumes reached their present holders, each with the marks it leaves on a book; the chain of custody of every located volume is set out station by station, each step with the record that documents it, and where the record is silent the gap is stated as a gap. The figure reads the chains as one descent, from the library to the 15 institutions and the private hands that hold its volumes today.

Acquisition channels

How the books came to Tycho, as far as the correspondence and the purchase-notes and dedications on the copies show it; an entry is assigned to a channel only where a document names the route, so most entries carry none.

ChannelMechanismAgentsEntries assigned
Frankfurt book fairStanding orders through the biannual Willer catalogues, executed by correspondents who bought at the fair to order.Johannes Maior, Heinrich Brucaeus, Cunradus Aslachus, Herwart von Hohenburg, Paul Hainzel2
Procured by a correspondent or agentBooks bought to order or procured on request by a correspondent and sent on — Johannes Maior's parcel from Augsburg (June 1584), Paul Hainzel's comet tracts (March 1579), Heinrich Brucaeus's sendings from Rostock (March 1586, June 1584) — as distinct from purchases made at the Frankfurt fair itself (AQ-FAIR). Norlind grouped the four men as the intermediaries of Tycho's purchases (1970, p. 333); the channel is split so that a book bought at the fair and a book found for him by a friend are not one thing.Johannes Maior, Paul Hainzel, Heinrich Brucaeus9
Absorbed scholar-librariesThe pursuit of a dead scholar’s whole working library — Ambrose (1575), Brechtalius (1576), Dudith, Wittich (1589–1598); only the Wittich pursuit succeeded, in the annotated De revolutionibus.Thaddaeus Hagecius, Jakob Monau, Longomontanus0
Gift of an author or correspondentPresentation copies from authors and correspondents.Heinrich Rantzau, Giordano Bruno, Johannes Kepler, Joseph Scaliger, Bartholomaeus Pitiscus, Thaddaeus Hagecius26
Manuscript copying and transmissionManuscript copies made of texts he could not buy, and the search of other libraries for them (Vedel).Anders Sørensen Vedel, Thaddaeus Hagecius1
Direct purchaseBooks bought outright, often with an autograph purchase-note.6
Borrowed, not owned outside the catalogueSome fifty mathematical titles lent from the Duke of Bavaria’s library through Herwart in the Prague years — used, never owned, and so outside this catalogue.Herwart von Hohenburg

The roads of dispersal

The routes by which the located volumes passed from the library to their present holders, each named for the custody that determined it. The table gives each road’s diagnostic marks and present holders and the number of volumes on it; the account of each road follows the table, and the chain of custody of every volume stands in the table after that.

Every located volume is assigned to one road; the counts sum to the 72 volumes identified as Tycho’s. Road V has no located volume by definition, and the 107 titles without a located copy (§13) are not its measure: a title stands there because no copy has been identified, not because one is known to be lost.

The roads in detail

0 — Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges 4 volumes

Books that left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: the Apianus he gave Paul Wittich at Hven on 29 October 1580, the Apianus at Gotha in which he wrote a dated motto for Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxe-Weimar on leaving Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 — his own book given at parting, as the Gotha library reads the entry, or the duke’s book in which he wrote, as Norlind thought more likely —, the Calvin–Theocritus Sammelband dedicated to his cousin Hans Lindenov in exile, and — if Walde and Mortensen are right against Norlind — the Sammelband of 1563 that carries Vedel’s name. These volumes left the library before it was dispersed and reached their holders by roads of their own.

I — The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773 51 volumes

Tycho's son-in-law Frans Gansneb Tengnagel — a Catholic convert who ran the posthumous editions — had intended to continue Tycho’s work and died in 1622 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76); the heirs, pressed by the lawsuit over the unpaid purchase price, parted with their possessions piecemeal, the earliest dated step out of the library being of 1623 (p. 76); a part of the library came as a gift to the Jesuit Collegium Caesareum at the Clementinum in Prague (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76, after Volf). The volumes so given — twenty-three survive — carry on the title ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A° 1642’, in most cases with ‘Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana’ and ‘Musaei Mathematici’, and were shelved as the separately kept Musaeum Mathematicum, whose books are known by the red-brown double lines on their white spines (p. 78). A larger group came to the Jesuit college at Chomutov (Komotau), apparently in the same way (p. 76); a single volume each reached the college at Krumlov — by exchange in 1654 from Andreas Scherhackl of Budějovice, who had owned it since 1623 — and the professed house on Prague’s Malá Strana (pp. 76 and 78); the suppression of the Society in 1773 and the secularisation of the monasteries brought these fragments together again in the Clementinum (p. 78) — nineteen volumes of Chomutov provenance by 1933 (p. 81). Šolc's accounts of 1999 (§ 2.533, printed p. 150) and 2006 (printed p. 192 (scan 6)) give the nineteen the Chomutov inscription ‘Collegij Societis JESU Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A.’ with a year between 1671 and 1675 — the 1645 entry of 44 F 38 and Crusius's gifts of 1654 lie outside that range — and add that four further Tychonic volumes reached the Clementinum itself as gifts (‘Stiftungen’) of private persons whose names stand on their title pages; he names neither the donors nor the volumes. The store's Crusius volumes (5 G 92, 5 J 103) were gifts to the Chomutov college, not to the Clementinum, so they are not Šolc's four; which four he means is open (see lead-crusius-layer). The National Library’s provenance survey of its Jesuit stocks (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30) registers 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions, seven of them given to the college before 1600, and among them ‘minimálně čtyři knihy z pozůstalosti Tychona Brahe’, all with the supralibros ‘TBO 1576’ on the front board and the Chomutov inscription on the title; its authors connect the college’s unusual holding of mathematics and astronomy with P. Jan Jüngling (1705–1775), keeper of the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766, and suppose these books to have been duplicates of the Clementinum college’s library. The Museum itself was removed after 1773 to the lodging of its last keeper, Joseph Stepling, and returned only after his death in 1778, a custody in which losses occurred, at Karel Rafael Ungar's cataloguing of the 1780s the Tycho volumes were then distributed among the University Library's subject departments, predominantly department 14 (Šolc 2006, printed p. 192 (scan 6)) — he does not say what the first element of a present shelfmark denotes —, and the librarians of the Clementinum later broke up some of Tycho's Sammelbände and bound his books with others' (p. 80), which is why some of his volumes now hold works that were never his. In the chains of custody the Mathematical Museum is named as a station only where the volume itself carries the words (‘Musaei Mathematici’, ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae’ or the Museum's spine marking); the college alone is named otherwise. Gingerich's 2002 survey of the Clementinum volumes counts the marks as follows: sixteen carry the initials 'T.B.O.' tooled on the binding, six the gilt supralibros portrait, twelve the initials written in by hand, and two are author presentations (Bruno and Scaliger). Clear marginalia in Tycho's hand appear in only a few — among them the Ziegler In C. Plinii of 1531, in its Martianus Capella section, and Bartholomaeus Scultetus's Cometae of 1577. Šolc's own later wording (2006, p. 192) is ‘věnováno’ — donated — for the harder-to-sell, mostly astronomical remainder, with the Vitellio–Dürer volume reaching the Jesuits ‘probably by sale’ in 1636; the Handbuch's ‘gekauft’ (Faltysová 1999, § 1.13, after Tobolka) is the other reading, and neither cites a document.

II — The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601) 4 volumes

During the lawsuit over the purchase price the heirs parted with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library with them: ‘so manches Werk wanderte auch in Privatbesitz’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76). The volumes placed here are those whose first recorded owner after Tycho is a private collector of the seventeenth century; what else left by this road is untraced. Since 20 October 2026 the road also carries the Strahov Euclid of 1558 (AV II 2), formerly on a road of its own (VII): it passed from the heirs to Gabriel Crusius — his graphite ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ on the title, the formula his gift volumes at Chomutov carry in ink — and from him by private hands to Jan Josef Klauser (1705–1771), whose library Strahov bought in 1775; it carries no Jesuit inscription. The Ramus AG XIV 7 began the same way, Crusius giving it to the Chomutov college on 5 August 1654. Kleinschnitzová's 2 A 8 (e-kl-43), inscribed by Andreas Scherhackl of Budějovice in 1623 and given by him to the Krumlov Jesuits by exchange in 1654, belongs here too, not on the Jesuit road: its first owner after the heirs is a private man.

III — The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague) 1 volume

The 1648 Swedish capture of Prague carried off Rudolfine/Bohemian holdings, including Tycho material, to Sweden. The first Tycho items documented on this road are not books of the library: two manuscripts — a parchment copy of the star catalogue and a Solis et Lunae motus diarii of 1598–99 — and a printed book in a presentation binding, from Rudolf II’s collection at the Castle, shipped with the Castle’s books in 1648–49 and entered in the Stockholm royal library’s catalogue of 1650–51 under Frans Tengnagel’s name, all three untraced (Veselá 2025, p. 142). The Castle was the one Prague collection the Swedes confiscated systematically; the Old Town Jesuit college and the university libraries were untouched, which is why the core of 1642 was never at risk (p. 256). The recataloguing at Stockholm in 1650–51 stripped the booty’s spine marks, and Vossius removed the royal library’s signatures from the books he took in 1654: a volume without a Swedish mark is not thereby excluded from this road (pp. 208–214, 228). The database of the Swedish book plunder (Knihovna AV ČR, searched in full on 19 October 2026: 4,367 records) holds no Tycho imprint from its Prague-Castle group of 79 records (47 under Rudolf II, 20 under Ferdinand III) and no book of Tycho's own; its three Tycho imprints came by other roads — Dudith's De mundi with the Dietrichstein library of Mikulov (Stockholm KB), Hermann Bulder's De mundi and Tycho's dedication copy of the Mechanica to Petr Vok with the Rožmberk library (Stockholm University Library; Copenhagen). Tengnagel's name returns nothing.

IV — Rudolfine-imperial absorption 0 volumes

Rudolf II had the instruments and the manuscript observations ceded to him by contract (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 75), and books may have passed into the court’s orbit with them; none is documented. No located volume is placed on this road: the one candidate, the Vienna manuscript of the Commentariolus, enters the record by an undocumented step and stands on the road of unknown route. Veselá reads the three Stockholm items — two manuscripts and a print — as Tycho’s personal gift to Rudolf II on his arrival in Prague, an inference she marks as such (2025, p. 142). The one catalogue of the Castle library, of 1636 (Riegger 1795, pp. 214–230), is Ferdinand III’s library and not Rudolf’s, whose books had largely gone to Vienna after 1612, and a Habsburg supralibros is not proof of Rudolf’s ownership: any claim that a book of Tycho’s passed through Rudolf’s hands has to pass that test (pp. 140, 150).

V — Attrition / loss

War, fire and untraced dispersal account for the gap between the library as it stood at his death and the remnant located today — no single catastrophe, but a long attrition that left no mark to search by. No located volume belongs here by definition, and the titles without a located copy are not its measure: a title is unlocated because no copy has been identified, not because one is known to be lost; the size of the loss is bounded only by the size of the library, which is itself disputed.

VI — Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik 4 volumes

Two volumes carrying the 1642 inscription are now at Strahov, not in the Clementinum: Rheticus–Otho's Opus palatinum (Σ V 5/a) and the Regiomontanus Ephemerides (DR VII 19). The documented route out of the Clementinum is the one Boldan & Vackářová describe for the Mathematical Museum's library: after the suppression of 1773 Karel Rafael Ungar screened the incoming Jesuit and monastic books for duplicates, the observatory director Antonín Strnad bought part of the surplus astronomical volumes for himself, and from his estate they passed to Strahov, which bought the substantial part of his library after his death in 1799 (Munzar 2001). Straka gave exactly this chain for the Regiomontanus in 1913 — Clementinum → Strnad → Strahov — though Strahov's present cataloguer notes that the volume appears in neither published catalogue of Strnad's library (Seydl 1939; Kouklová 1989). The spine is the test: the Mathematical Museum's books carry no ex-libris, only red lines and an abbreviated title on the spine, and Strnad's books his handwritten name or name-stamp. Seydl identified the Strahov volumes from Strnad's library by matching his own book-list, in two hands, against the Strahov volume catalogue (Hyklová 2017, p. 49) — the method behind the cataloguer's finding that the Regiomontanus is in neither list. The library's own record of DR VII 19 nevertheless places the volume in the Clementinum's Mathematical Museum before it came to Strahov, and Munzar and Pařez (2002, p. 369) supposed the Strahov purchases from the Clementinum stock were made ‘probably not before’ 1773. Two volumes show the same leakage from other Jesuit stocks. The Bianchini of Teplá, inscribed at the Clementinum in 1642, is now in the Premonstratensians' library there by an undocumented step. Heidenstein's De bello Moscovitico (Basel 1588), in Tycho's portrait-and-arms binding and catalogued at Chomutov in 1671, never reached the Clementinum at all: it is at the Biblioteka Kórnicka (Cim.Qu.2812), its route there — the volume carries older shelfmarks and stamps not yet identified — still to be established. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 81) supposed that the Chomutov stock reached the Clementinum only in part; the Kórnik volume is the first located proof of it.

VIII — With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604) 1 volume

The manuscript observations went a road of their own: Kepler received them under a contract with Tengnagel of 1604 and never returned them; after his death in 1630 his son Ludwig held them as a pledge against the court’s bond of 1633 and sold them to Frederik III of Denmark — in 1655 on Mortensen’s account (1955, pp. 31–32), ‘at the latest in the beginning of 1662’ on Dreyer’s (1890, Appendix, pp. 370, 373). A leaf of another man’s observations sewn into Tycho’s own codex travelled with them.

U — Route out of the library unknown 7 volumes

Volumes identified as Tycho’s by their marks that surfaced in the trade or in a later collection with no documented step between his library and their first recorded later owner. The chain of custody records the gap as a gap; the later stations are given with their sources.

The custody of the surviving volumes

For every located volume, one station per documented custodian, with the dates the record gives, the basis of each step and its source; a gap in the record is a station of its own, a contested step is marked. The volumes stand by road and, within the Jesuit road, by the house whose inscription they carry; the grade is that of the volume’s identification.

    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. The Jesuit college, Prague
    Mortensen 1955, p. 30, from Dr Teichl’s report of 1943: ‘Bogen … har tidligere tilhørt Jesuiterkollegiet i Prag’. The library’s own record names no former owner. — Mortensen 1955
  3. route unknown
    How the volume reached Vienna is not documented.
  4. Library of the Technische Hochschule, now TU Wien, Vienna, Tresor 7704 I
    Reported there to Mortensen in 1943 by Dr Teichl, formerly director of the National Library in Vienna (Mortensen 1955, p. 30). — Mortensen 1955

    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry.   3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) from 1671

  4. route unknown
    The volume did not come to the Clementinum with the Chomutov library after 1773; the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’ and the stamps on the title have not been identified.

1957:0030
Helsingør, Maritime Museum
AU
  1. route unknown
    The route out of Tycho's hands is undocumented. The two struck ownership lines on the forperm (the museum: ‘tico brade ven:’ and ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’; Thykier 2003: ‘Tyge Brahe’ and ‘tico brahe ven’) may mark a transfer in his lifetime or a later owner's cancellation; a third inscription in another hand reads ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part of the leaf (Thykier 2003) — the only name of a later owner the volume yields. The book was used as a herbarium by a hand other than Tycho's, one of whose plant names is unattested before c. 1623 (Thykier 2003, after Wagner and Baagøe), so it was in a plant-collector's hands after Tycho's death. It stands in no Prague catalogue and its first title carries none of the Jesuit, Chomutov or Crusius marks of the Bohemian roads; the remnant of a label on the spine with the shelfmark 204 records a library between Tycho and the Munich trade that no source names (Thykier: ‘formodentlig katalognummeret i Tychos eller et senere bibliotek’; the dossier of 20 October 2026). — Thykier 2003; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart)
  2. Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich by 1932
    Prandtl 1932, the captions of his plates (pp. 2–3: ‘Seinerzeit im Besitze des Antiquariats Weiss & Co., München’) and p. 3 (‘kürzlich von München aus nach Amerika verkauft’ — wrong about the first step, see the next station); the Verzeichnis B entry for Band II names no location. The volume is in none of the firm's four digitised catalogues (1926–1930). — Prandtl 1932
  3. Maggs Bros., London 1933–c. 1938
    Catalogue 582 (1933), item 155, p. 92, £125, with every copy-specific identifier (the stamps, the half-torn fly-leaf, the purchase note, the Helsingborg note) and Prandtl cited for ‘our volume’; Catalogue 600 (1934), item 260, £125; Catalogue 666 (c. 1938), still £125. The pencil ‘+125’ at the head of the front pastedown is this price. The firm's archive (British Library Add MS 89311) would name the seller. — Maggs 582 (1933); Maggs 600 (1934); Maggs 666 (c. 1938); New York Times Book Review, 28 May 1933
  4. Herbert Reichner, New York c. 1939–c. 1940
    Catalogue 1 ([1939]), item 72, probably $850 — Reichner was Prandtl's publisher in Vienna and emigrated to New York in 1938–39; the volume is in none of his Catalogues 2–9 (1940–48). — Reichner, Catalogue 1 ([1939])
  5. route unknown from c. 1940
    The buyer from Reichner is not recorded; no American auction appearance 1930–58 (American Book Prices Current); Rare Book Hub has no record. Mortensen (1955, p. 25) knew of no such volume in Denmark, which bounds nothing, since the Danish literature stayed silent until Norlind 1970. — Mortensen 1955
  6. Oscar Ekman, engineer, and Lia Ekman, Copenhagen until 1957
    The museum's report of its acquisitions of 1956–57 (Klem, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Thykier 2003 dates the gift to January 1957 and names Oskar Ekman alone): ‘en gave fra fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle, civilingeniør Oscar Ekman’. Oscar Ekman (b. Copenhagen 13 October 1885, owner of Nordisk Elektricitets Selskab from 1913, d. 16 September 1956) had been a life member of the museum's friends' society since 1944–45; Lia Ekman (née Pouplier, b. Hamburg 1894, d. 1965) remained one to her death. Their source for the volume is not recorded; the 1965 sale catalogue of their library (Bruun Rasmussen 186) printed it as a withdrawn show-piece. — Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957; Kraks Blå Bog 1937; Bogvennen 1966; Thykier 2003
  7. M/S Museet for Søfart (Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg), Helsingør, inventory 1957:0030 from 1957
    The Ekmans' gift of 1956–57 (Årbog 1957; the museum's record); restored 1957 by Birgitte Dall. Deposited at the Royal Library's Håndskriftafdeling in 1986 as Acc. 1986/116 (the Kronik of 1987; the department's newsletter of November 2001), lent from there to the Ole Rømer Museum's exhibition ‘Tycho Brahes mange ansigter’, 25 October – 31 December 2001; in the museum's own keeping again, confirmed 13 October 2026, the date of return unrecorded. — Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart); Magasin 1987; Royal Library, Håndskriftafdelingen, Aktuelt (November 2001); Björklund 1992; Museet for Søfart 2026; Thykier 2003

10Owners and custodians

Every person, house, firm and library through whose hands a surviving volume passed, from Tycho’s heirs to the holders today, in alphabetical order: the role, the dates the record gives, the volumes, and under each volume the basis of the step and its source. The names stand as the records give them — an owner not identified is listed as such, and the two American private collectors are two entries, not one. Where the Familia has the person, the name opens its record there.

11Chronology

The dated events in the history of the library: its formation, the acquisition campaigns, the marks, the exile, the dispersal, and the rediscovery of the surviving volumes by modern scholarship. Each event carries the source it rests on, in the short form used throughout this chapter; the full references are in the sources section.

DatePhaseEventSourceEntries
14 December 1546LifeTycho Brahe born at KnutstorpChristianson 2000
1560FormationProcures the Ephemerides of Stadius after the eclipse of 21 August — his first recorded bookDreyer 1890, p. 14Stadius, Johannes, Ephemerides novae et exactae
30 November 1560FormationThe Prague Ptolemy (Basel 1551) bought at Copenhagen for 2 thaler — by Tycho (Dreyer, Friis) or by Johannes Pratensis, whose name and 1561 binding it also carries (Boldan & Vackářová 2024)Dreyer 1890, p. 14; Friis 1868–69, p. 267; Studnička 1901, p. 39; Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 74; Boldan & Vackářová 2024, pp. 144–145Ptolemaeus, Claudius, Claudii Ptolemaei Pelusiensis Alexandrini omnia quae extant opera praeter geographiam (1551)
1562FormationTo Leipzig to read law; buys astronomical books and instruments with money accounted for to his tutorDreyer 1890, pp. 15–17
1563Formation‘Ty Brad 1563’ sammelband (later gifted to Vedel; now Uppsala)Prandtl 1932, Verz. B, Band III; Mortensen 1955, p. 27Garcaeus, Johannes, Tractatus brevis et utilis de erigendis figuris coeli (1556); Osius, Hieronymus, Historia excidii Hierosolymorum longe luctuosissimi, cuius exemplum & memoria his temporibus maxime videtur accommodata & necessaria. Item historia Ioseph filii Iacob versibus enarrata (1558); Camerarius, Joachim, In hoc libro haec insunt: Hippocomicus, quae est disputatio de curandis equis. Xenophontis liber de re equestri Latinus factus. Nomina equestria Graeca & Latina. Xenophontis libri de repub. Lacedaemoniorum & Atheniensium. Itemque de praefectura equestri, conversi in sermonem Latinum. Historia rei nummariae, sive de nomismatis Graecis & Latinis (1556); Script. Graeci
1567FormationThe Strahov Euclid (Basel 1558) bound with TYCHO / BRAHE 1567 stamped on the board — the latest of the three dated name-stamps of the student years (after TVCHO BRADE 1561 and TY BRAD 1563) and the only one in the spelling BRAHEPařez 2009; Strahov Katalog Tritius, record 993601Euclid (ed. Bartolomeo Zamberti and Campanus of Novara; comm. Theon, Hypsicles), Euclidis Megarensis mathematici clarissimi Elementorum geometricorum libri XV. Cum expositione Theonis in priores XIII a Barthol. Zamberto Veneto latinitate donata, Campani in omnes, et Hypsiclis Alexandrini in duos postremos (1558)
1575AcquisitionAn attempt to buy the books of Dr Ambrose, a citizen of Augsburg, failsMosley 2007, p. 175 (TBOO VII, 15.24–27; 84.1–2)
1576FormationGranted Hven; Uraniborg begun; the T.B.O. 1576 binding cohortPrandtl 1932, Heft 8; Norlind 1970, p. 335; Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 81
1576AcquisitionAn attempt, through Camerarius, to buy Brechtalius’s mathematical books: already soldMosley 2007, p. 175 (TBOO VII, 42.14–16)
May 1579AcquisitionMarks 13 titles in a Frankfurt fair catalogue for procurementMosley 2007, p. 167 (TBOO VII, 54.38–42); Norlind 1970, p. 333
October 1580AcquisitionGives Wittich the Apian Astronomicum Caesareum (departure gift)Mosley 2007, p. 176; Gingerich 2002, p. 327Apianus, Petrus, Astronomicum Caesareum (Ingolstadt 1540) — Tycho's presentation copy to Paul Wittich (1540)
1586The pressFirst book from the Uraniborg press: Morsing’s Diarium astrologicum for 1586, its dedication dated 1 January 1586 (the first imprints, the poems to Pratensis and Ulfeldt, are of late 1584)Nielsen 1921, pp. 178–179, 186; Christianson 2000, p. 377
1586The marksThe engraved portrait dated 1586, from which Mortensen derived the supralibros portrait stampMortensen 1931, p. 142
September 1587AcquisitionTycho learns of Wittich's death (from Rothmann)Mosley 2007, p. 175
1588AcquisitionBruno's Camoeracensis acrotismus received (author gift)Mosley 2007, p. 168; Šolc 2002, p. 331Bruno, Giordano, Camoeracensis acrotismus seu Rationes articulorum physicorum (Wittenberg, Z. Crato 1588) (1588)
20 March 1588The marksEarliest dated binding with the gilt supralibros portrait: the Sascerides De mundi (KB Copenhagen)Mortensen 1931, p. 142; Gigas 1900, no. 1, pp. 31–33
1589AcquisitionFirst attempt to buy Wittich’s library, through noble emissaries at Wrocław, failsMosley 2007, pp. 175–176 (TBOO VII, 166.10–17); Christianson 2000, pp. 223, 378
March 1592AcquisitionSeeks Rheticus’s and Copernicus’s papers from HageciusMosley 2007, p. 174 (TBOO VII, 333.39–334.1)
1595AcquisitionSecond attempt to buy Wittich’s library, through Hagecius and Monau, failsChristianson 2000, pp. 223, 378
21 March 1597ExileThe whole library inventoried on Hven (‘all the junker's books’)Friis (ed.) 1876, p. 263; TBOO IX, p. 146; Thoren 1990, p. 371
29 March 1597ExileTycho leaves Hven for the last time: 29 March on Dreyer’s reading of the observing ledger’s ‘29 Aprilis’ (Easter fell on 27 March), followed by Thoren; Nielsen keeps 29 AprilDreyer 1890, p. 238 n. 2; Thoren 1990, p. 371; Nielsen 1921, p. 204
2 June 1597ExileDeparts Copenhagen into exileChristianson 2000, p. 314
October 1597ExileAt Wandsbek with Rantzau; the travelling press prints the MechanicaDreyer 1890, pp. 253–260; Norlind 1970, p. 334
1598AcquisitionThird attempt, through Longomontanus and Monau: the library found intact; negotiation opensChristianson 2000, pp. 223, 314, 378Copernicus, Nicolaus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1566)
1598ExileWinter at WittenbergChristianson 2000, p. 300; Norlind 1970, p. 334
March 1598AcquisitionKepler's Mysterium cosmographicum arrives (with Ursus's tract)Mosley 2007, pp. 168–169 (TBOO VIII, 14.27–33; 46.37–40)Kepler, Johannes, Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum (Mysterium cosmographicum) (1596)
1599PragueEnters Rudolf II's service; assigned Benátky castleChristianson 2000, p. 300
1600PragueThe library, shipped up the Elbe and held at Magdeburg since 1599, reaches Prague in mid-NovemberNorlind 1970, p. 334 (TBOO VIII, 192; 305; 343)
16 May 1600AcquisitionAt Benátky, Baron Karl von Wartenberg shows Tycho the catalogue of the whole library of the late Andreas Dudith; Tycho keeps it to return on a visit to the baron's castle ‘seven miles’ away and asks Monau whether the heirs would let him see, and sell, the books he had markedTBOO VIII, 320.37–321.5 — Tycho to Jacob Monau, Benátky, 16 May 1600 (epistolarium brahe-t_16000516001); Mosley 2007, p. 175, nn. 281–282
14 June 1600AcquisitionMonau answers that Dudith's library ‘now hangs as if between heaven and earth’ — no longer the heirs', ‘not so much sold as pawned’ to another for a sum of money — and the pursuit ends; the Dudith copy of the De mundi that survives at Stockholm is Tycho's gift of 1588, not a purchaseTBOO VIII, 325.39–326.6 — Jacob Monau to Tycho, Wrocław, 14 June 1600 (epistolarium brahe-t_16000614001); Mosley 2007, p. 175, n. 283
October 1600AcquisitionMonau brings the Wittich De revolutionibus copies to PragueGingerich 2002, p. 325Copernicus, Nicolaus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1566)

12Definitions and conventions

How an entry is to be read — its status, its two grades, its units, its road — what each figure in this chapter counts, what each source attests, and what is known of the size of the library the figures describe.

How to read the entries

Status. Located: a physical copy identified as Tycho’s own survives and is recorded with its shelfmark. Attested, not located: a document names the book as Tycho’s, but no copy has been found; within this class, retired as unlocatable marks a mass-survival text whose copy would carry no known mark to search by. Disputed: ownership or identity is contested and the entry is kept out of the located count. Lost: a copy is recorded as destroyed, or as having vanished after being seen. Tychoniana, not his: a book that came down among the Tychoniana without having been Tycho’s — bound into one of his volumes after it left the library, or carrying the Clementinum’s Tychoniana note though printed after his death (Kleinschnitzová’s Kein Tychonianum); it belongs to the history of the Jesuits’ Tychoniana, not to his library, and carries no grade.

Grades. Two independent A–D scales are used. An entry’s confidence grades how securely the book can be asserted to have been Tycho’s: A, secure (a surviving copy with his marks, or an unambiguous document); B, probable; C, possible, resting on inference; D, doubtful. A surviving volume’s identification grades how securely that particular copy is his: A, his marks or hand on the copy itself; B, a catalogue or scholarly identification without a mark checked at first hand; C, circumstantial; D, doubtful. A located entry may still stand at C where the volume is identified by its marks but the text bound in it is not. The grades are never rounded or removed; the entries marked Tychoniana, not his, carry none.

Units. Entries count works, not volumes: every separately printed work, and every manuscript, bound in a volume identified as Tycho’s has an entry of its own — the works bound in after the volume left his library included, and so marked; a part of one imprint (a second title within the same edition) is not a separate entry. A Sammelband therefore holds several entries. Volumes count physical objects. No ratio of located to attested entries is a survival rate: a work enters the located tier because a copy was found, and most of that tier was compiled from the surviving Prague volumes in the first place.

Roads and custody. Each located volume is assigned to one road: the route by which it passed from the library to its present holder, named for the custody that determined it — a gift of Tycho’s lifetime, the Jesuit houses — the Clementinum’s own gift of 1642 and the colleges whose libraries it gathered after 1773, the imperial collections and the Swedish booty of 1648, the observation books, private hands of the seventeenth century; where no step out of the library is documented the road is recorded as unknown. Each volume carries a chain of custody: one station per documented custodian, with the dates the record gives, the basis of the step and its source. A gap in the record is a station of its own, route unknown; a contested step is marked disputed. Roads are counted in volumes, never in entries, and the counts sum to the volumes identified as Tycho’s. An acquisition channel — how a book came to Tycho — is recorded only where a document names the route; most entries carry none.

Numbers. Every entry carries a fixed number, assigned once in the alphabetical order of 19 October 2026 and never re-assigned: an entry added later takes the next free number, a retired entry keeps its number and is listed, with the reason, in the register of retired entries under the concordance. Every surviving volume likewise carries a volume number. Cite an entry as ‘Bibliotheca Tychoniana no. N’ with its record key, a volume by its number and shelfmark.

The other indexes. The concordance is read from both sides: by entry, and by each earlier catalogue’s own numbers — Prandtl’s, Kleinschnitzová’s, Šolc’s, Norlind’s and the National Library’s former-owner index — each number answered by an entry or by the reason it has none. The owners and custodians stand in an index of their own, each with the volumes that passed through their hands.

The roads

The codes used in the Road column of the holdings, in the volume records and in §9:

  1. 0 Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges
  2. I The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773
  3. II The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601)
  4. III The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague)
  5. IV Rudolfine-imperial absorption
  6. V Attrition / loss
  7. VI Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik
  8. VIII With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604)
  9. U Route out of the library unknown

The size of the library

The library’s original size is unresolved: the estimates run from Mortensen’s ceiling of 1,000 volumes to Christianson’s ‘over three thousand’, and the higher figure rests on a single shelf-number.

EstimateProposed byBasis
over 3,000 volumesChristianson (2000), pp. 102, 201, 404 n. 12the shelf-number 2781 that Studnička read in 1901 on the spine of the Gesner of 1565, now in Austin, where the spine shows no number; reported by Norlind
‘at best speculative’Gingerich (2002), pp. 323–324‘similar numbers are apparently not found in the other surviving volumes, so Norlind’s deduction is at best speculative’; nevertheless a library of 3,000 titles ‘would not be unreasonable’ beside Rantzau’s 6,000 and Dee’s about 4,000
at most 1,000 volumes (about 2,000 works)Mortensen (1955), p. 31what the circular Museum room at Uraniborg, 5 m across and also holding the great globe and the smaller instruments, could have held, and the argument that a larger library would have left more survivors: ‘Forsigtig tør man maaske sætte Antallet af Bind til højst 1000 svarende til omkring 2000 Skrifter’
about 5,000 volumesO. Walde (letter to Mortensen, 1938)the figure Mortensen printed without attribution in 1942, p. 25 (‘Tallet har vel naaet circ. 5000 Bd.’), gave in 1955, p. 31, as Walde’s estimate in a private letter of 1938, and judged probably too large (‘vistnok for stort’): it would need more room than the Museum had, and more books would have survived

Norlind himself wrote that it is impossible to form any estimate of the library’s size, crediting the 2781 inference to Studnička (Norlind 1970, p. 335).

What each source attests

The two tiers are built in opposite directions: the located tier works backwards, from a surviving volume to the entry it proves; the attested tier works forwards, from Norlind’s catalogue and Tycho’s letters to a book that has not been found.

The Clementinum count

Kleinschnitzová (1933) records 97 works in 47 volumes; Šolc (2002) extends this to about 110 titles in 50 volumes, counting the volumes his survey added and several bound-in parts as titles. This edition itemises 105 works in 51 National Library volumes. 94 of them carry her numbers — her 34:3, Ptolemy’s Centiloquium, being the Liber fructus appended to the Bonatus of 1550 and counted with it — and 11 stand beyond her list: the pieces the library’s own records add to her volumes (the Strabo of 14 F 8, Peurbach’s Tractatus of 7 B 22, Apianus’s Instrumentum of 14 A 63, the Grynaeus and the Erastus of 14 H 192), the three volumes Šolc found (XV K 22, XXXI H 26, XIV B 38) and the two incunables of 44 F 38. The works she marks Kein Tychonianum are entered as not his, the Apianus Cosmographia of 14 J 164 as disputed, and the parts of one imprint that Šolc counted as titles — Rantzau’s praedictiones, Commandino’s De horologiorum descriptione, the De regibus Bohemicis, the Maurolico dialogues, Brucaeus’s sine doctrine — are not counted.

13Desiderata

What remains to be found or resolved. 107 attested titles have no located copy: 59 carry a trace worth following (a title, an attestation, a last-known location), 42 are retired as unlocatable because the text survives in quantity and Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark to search by, and 6 are recorded as lost. The disputed identifications and the open questions attached to individual records follow. A scholar who can settle any of these is invited to write.
