VD16 A 3899; Zinner 3699; [7] leaves and 214 pages, octavo (VD16; the ‘4°’ at Norlind, p. 339, is an error). Written and printed while Aslakssøn was abroad as tutor to Otto Brahe (matriculated at Basel 1596/97). The book is dedicated to Tycho (Norlind, p. 339; Store norske leksikon), whence Norlind’s inference that it ‘har väl alltså befunnit sig i Tychos bibliotek’. The ownership rests on that inference alone: no copy with Tycho’s marks and no presentation copy is recorded in the inventories of Prandtl, Kleinschnitzová, Šolc or Mortensen, or in the trade. In the preface Aslakssøn declares for Copernicus, a position Tycho rejected, so that the dedication stands in tension with the book’s own position. The work is a ‘Mosaic physics’, a synthesis of astronomy and scripture on the three heavens (elemental or aerial, astronomical or sidereal, eternal or perpetual); Comenius later listed Aslakssøn among the Mosaic physicists who preceded him. Book III, De caelo perpetuo, was translated into English as ‘The Description of Heaven … Composed in Latine by Cunradus Aslachus, and conuerted into English by Raph [Ralph] Iennings’ (London 1623; EEBO A22193). Copies of the edition survive in Munich (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek), Vienna (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek) and Copenhagen (Royal Library); none is Tycho’s. The dedicatory epistle, read in the Munich copy, is addressed ‘Tychoni Brahe de Knudstrup, fundatori Arcis Uraniburgicae … sideralis scientiae scrutatori, instauratori, conservatori unico’, dated Basel, 16 November 1596, and signed ‘Cunradus Aslachus Bergensis’; it hails Tycho as ‘indefessus Caeli scrutator & Atlas’ and pays eyewitness homage to his celestial globe and astronomical instruments.
41Busch, Georg[Nova-1572 tracts] Von dem Cometen ... 1572 + the fuller Erfurt 1573 redaction1572, 4°CNorlind 1970, p. 341 (s.v. Busch, Georg); Zinner no. 2574; 2609-2614 (after Norlind)Norlind 1970 (p. 341): ‘Tycho måste ha ägt åtminstone tvenne upplagor av skriften’ — in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 279–288) Tycho writes that Busch published two German tracts on the new star; one, Norlind reasons, is among the editions Zinner 2574 and 2609–2613 (Augsburg and Erfurt, 1572–73), the fuller one Zinner 2614 (Erfurt 1573, 25 leaves). Busch’s tract on the comet of 1577 has its own entry.
49Carelli, Giovanni BattistaEphemerides ad annos XIX (1557-1575)Venice, 1557, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 342 (s.v. Carellus, Johannes Baptista); Šolc 2006Norlind (1970, p. 342), citing Dreyer, states that Tycho ‘skaffade sig under sin Leipzigvistelse’ this edition — acquired it during his Leipzig years — and cites it often in his earliest observation journal (Opera omnia X, 5 ff.). Dreyer’s sentence is narrower: ‘In his observations from 1563–64 he also mentions the Ephemerides of Carellus (Venice, 1557)’ (Tycho Brahe, Edinburgh 1890, p. 18, n. 1); the acquisition at Leipzig is Norlind’s inference. The edition is Venice: Vincenzo Valgrisi, 1557, 4to; its title runs ‘ad annos XIX’, 1557 to 1575, where Norlind prints ‘IX’. Three datings stand side by side: Šolc 2006 (printed p. 190 (scan 4)) places the Carelli ephemerides for 1557 with the Stadius among the tables Tycho ‘procured at once’ after the eclipse of 21 August 1560, unsourced; Norlind's Leipzig purchase is an inference from Dreyer p. 18 n. 1 (the citations in the observations of 1563–64); and the loci record of the Copenhagen years (after Christianson 2020, pp. 19–22) has the Carelli bought with Jens Nilsson in Copenhagen about 1561. Šolc's 1560 is not adopted.
50Carion, JohannLibellus de directionum significationibusBTycho’s correspondence, letter of 9 May 1586 (tekstnet.dk)Hagecius sent Tycho Carion’s De directionum significationibus in 1586; Hagecius to Tycho, 9 May 1586: ‘Mitto etiam tibi libellum de Directionum Significationibus’.
51Caselius, JohannesFriderico II. regi Daniae ad regni senatores epitaphios (a funeral oration)Rostock, 1588, 4°CNorlind 1970, p. 342 (s.v. Caselius, Johannes); TBOOCaselius wrote to Tycho in May 1588 that he was composing a laudatio of the late king and would send him a copy in June (Opera omnia VII, p. 121: ‘Iam optimo Regi vestro laudationem pango, cuius exemplum Iunio ad te mittam’); Norlind (1970, p. 342) lists the Rostock print of 1588 on that promise. No receipt is recorded and no copy located. The fourth piece of the Chomutov volume 14 A 63 (Kleinschnitzová 33:4) is a manuscript star table, not this oration.
53Chytraeus, DavidDe stella inusitata et nova ... et de comato sidere 1577Rostock, 1577BNorlind 1970, p. 342 (s.v. Chytræus, David); Zinner no. 2768 (after Norlind)Norlind: 'sannolikt denna upplaga... som Tycho ägde' — owned this Latin edition (not the German), per Prog. III,225-229 and comet-book IV,366-367. The ownership is inferred from the Progymnasmata citations (Norlind p. 342); no physical Tycho copy has been identified. Imprint: Rostock, 1577, 4to — the Latin edition (Zinner 2768 / Hellman 29), which Norlind argues Tycho owned in preference to the German (Zinner 2769 / Hellman 30).
54Chytraeus, DavidHistoria Augustanae confessionisFrankfurt, 1578, 4°CNorlind 1970, p. 342 (s.v. Chytræus, David)Norlind: 'Ägdes sannolikt av Tycho' — probably owned, per Tycho's letter to Landgrave Wilhelm Sept 1591 (Opera VI,243).
57Clavius, ChristophGnomonice (Gnomonices libri octo)Rome, 1581, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 342 (s.v. Clavius, Christophorus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 15 March 1586 (tekstnet.dk); Norlind 1926Brucaeus bought Tycho a copy of Clavius’s Gnomonices at Rostock in March 1586 (his letter of 15 March 1586: ‘emi et tibi Gnomonicen CLAVIJ Bambergensis’, valued at seven Joachimsthaler; Opera omnia VII, 100). The purchase was conditional: the bookseller had deposited the books with Brucaeus at the beginning of the winter and would take them back if Tycho did not want them or already had them (‘Emi autem hac conditione, ut si tibi forte non placerent, aut forte eosdem iam esses nactus, Bibliopola ad se recipiat … Iam enim libros ineunte hyeme apud me deposuit’, VII, 100); whether this copy reached Hven is not recorded (Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3). That Tycho had the work is his own statement to Rantzau of 22 February 1597: Clavius’s writings on Euclid, on Sacrobosco and on gnomonics ‘in promptu habeo, et iamdudum introspexi’ (VII, 381). In December 1584 the Rostock bookseller, back from Frankfurt without the books Tycho had ordered, had sold his one copy, valued at nearly five Joachimsthaler, to Heinrich Rantzau (Opera omnia VII, 88; Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3), so Tycho’s first order went unfilled.
58Clavius, ChristophIn Sphaeram Ioannis de Sacro Bosco commentarius, 4°ANorlind 1970, p. 343 (s.v. Clavius, Christophorus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 23 October 1594 (tekstnet.dk); TBOOCort Aslakssøn sent the commentary to Tycho in 1594 (Aslaksson to Tycho, 23 October 1594: ‘CLAVIJ hunc in Sphæram SACROBOSCI Commentarium ad te ablegavi ob tractatulum quendam de Nova Stella’), and Tycho received it. Tycho himself names it among the works of Clavius he has to hand, writing to Rantzau on 22 February 1597 (Opera omnia VII, 381: ‘ea nihilominus quae in Euclidem ingeniose et in Iohannem de Sacrobusco luculenter, et de Gnomonicis copiose conscripsit, in promptu habeo, et iamdudum introspexi’). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified: the one work of Clavius among the Clementinum volumes is the Apologia of 1588, bound after Maestlin’s Alterum examen (Kleinschnitzová 13:2, Sign. 14 G 30), not this commentary. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
64Copernicus, NicolausEpistola ad Bernardum Wapowski (the Letter against Werner), in a transcript, ManuskriptBNorlind 1970, p. 343 (s.v. Copernicus, Nicolaus)Norlind 1970, p. 343: the letter Copernicus wrote at the request of Bernard Wapowski, canon of Kraków, on Johann Werner’s De motu octavae sphaerae; the comet book quotes a passage from it, and Tycho says there that he owns the text in a second- or third-hand transcript (Opera omnia IV, 292). No manuscript from his library is identified; the surviving transcripts of the letter have not been examined for the question.
66Cramer, DanielIsagoge in Metaphysicam AristotelisHanau, 1594, 8°BNorlind 1970, p. 344 (s.v. Cramer, Daniel)Dedicated to Tycho on the title page; Cramer visited Hven in the summer of 1592; Tycho is praised in an epigram on p. 13 and his world-system is named on pp. 217–218. Norlind (p. 344): the book ‘bör alltså ha funnits i biblioteket på Hven’ — must therefore have been in the Hven library. The ownership rests on the dedication alone; no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Norlind (p. 344) transcribes the dedication ‘Ad Tychonem Brahe, Danum, virum nobilem et in astronomia facile principem’. Imprint: Hanau (Hanoviae), 1594, octavo.
69Digges, ThomasAlae seu scalae mathematicae (on the radius/cross-staff)Londini, 1573, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 344 (s.v. Diggesæus, Thomas); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 8 December 1576 (tekstnet.dk)Brucaeus asked Tycho in December 1576 to send him ‘the noble Englishman’s book on the radius’, Digges’s Alae seu scalae mathematicae of 1573 (Opera omnia VII, 44; Norlind 1926, no. 7), which implies that Tycho owned it. Norlind 1970 lists Digges only as discussed in the Progymnasmata (III, 167–203).
70Dresser, MatthäusHistoria LutheriLeipzig, 1598, 8°BNorlind 1970, p. 344 (s.v. Dresserus, Matthias)A parcel of nine copies of the Historia Lutheri reached Tycho from Wittenberg with two letters for Rosenkrantz; he forwarded it and kept one copy to read at leisure (‘behåller han ett exemplar av boken för att i lugn och ro kunna studera den’; Tycho to Rosenkrantz, September 1598, Opera omnia VIII, 115). Dresser is not named in the letter; the identification is Norlind’s. The book was printed at Leipzig; only the parcel came from Wittenberg. Tycho’s copy has not been identified.
71Du Chesne, Joseph (Quercetanus)Ad Iacobi Auberti Vindonis de ortu et causis metallorum ... brevis responsioLugduni, 1575, 8°BNorlind 1970, p. 359 (s.v. Quercetanus, Josephus)Quercetanus (Joseph Du Chesne), Ad Iacobi Auberti … brevis responsio (Lyon 1575, 8vo): a Paracelsian book Tycho owned only briefly. Its preface is dated 1 April 1575, and he gave the copy to Thaddaeus Hagecius at their meeting in Regensburg in the autumn of that year; in August 1585 he asked Hagecius for another copy, unable to recall author or title (Tycho to Hagecius, August 1585, Opera omnia VII, 95). The work is identified from Hagecius’s marginal note ‘Libellus est Josephi Quercetani’ on Tycho’s letter (autograph in Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek), not from the book; Norlind gives the title as ‘med största sannolikhet’ (Norlind 1970, p. 359). The copy passed into Hagecius’s library; a copy recovered from it would carry his marks, not Tycho’s. Status attested, passed on, since 20 October 2026: the copy left the library in his lifetime as a gift to Hagecius (road 0), which is why no copy is sought — not a mass-survival text retired as unlocatable.
79Euclid (ed./comm. Christoph Clavius)Elementorum libri XV (with Clavius' commentary)CNorlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Euclides)Norlind: 'Någon av de tre första upplagorna (1574-91) har Tycho sannolikt ägt' — probably owned one of the first three editions. The Euclid found at Strahov (AV II 2, stamped TYCHO BRAHE 1567; Pařez 2009) is the Basel 1558 Zamberti–Campanus edition and is entered separately; no copy of a Clavius edition has been located.
80Everaert, Martin (Everhardus)Ephemerides novae et exactae 1590-1610 ex novis tabulis BelgicisLeiden, 1597, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Everartus, Martinus)Dedicated to Christian IV. Tycho received the tables at Wandsbek on 7 May 1598 (Tycho to Rosenkrantz, May 1598, Opera omnia VIII, 61), perhaps brought by Longomontanus (Tycho to Longomontanus, March 1598, Opera omnia VIII, 35), and criticised them sharply in the same letter. No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
90Flemløse, Peder JacobsenÆgloga de eclipsi solari anno 1574 ... futuraHafniæ, 1574, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 346 (s.v. Flemlöse, Peder Jacobsen)That Tycho owned the work is well founded: the Aegloga is dedicated to him (17 October 1574), and Flemløse came to Hven early in 1578 as one of his very first pupils (Norlind 1970, p. 346). This copy, however, is not demonstrably Tycho’s. The only surviving copy known (a unicum, according to L. Nielsen as cited by Norlind 1970, p. 346) is KB Hielmst. 1226 4, an eighteenth-century Hielmstierne Danica acquisition carrying no mark of Tycho’s. No Prague or Clementinum copy is known: the work appears in none of Kleinschnitzová, Prandtl or Šolc, and the Czech National Library’s index of former owners records no copy of Brahe’s. Norlind uses no verb of ownership: he infers only that a copy was ‘högst troligt’ on Hven, from the dedication, not that the Copenhagen copy is Tycho’s. The copy is therefore rejected as Tycho’s, while ownership of the work is retained at grade C. Status attested, B, since 20 October 2026: the work-level ownership is sound on the dedication; the Royal Library's copy, judged in its own volume record, is not shown to be his.
107Gessner, ConradThierbuch (German, transl. C. Forer)Zürich, 1563, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Gesner, Conradus)Norlind: ‘Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch’ — Tycho, who also had Gessner’s Thierbuch. The book is attested only by Tycho’s own letter to Landgrave Wilhelm of September 1591, which places the Oryx description on fol. 68 (Opera omnia VI, 244). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Whether his copy was the 1563 or the 1583 edition is unrecorded; Norlind holds it immaterial, the two editions being in his words identical: Zurich, Christoph Froschauer, 1563 (VD16 G 1728), reissued 1583 (VD16 G 1729), folio. It is a different book from the surviving Gessner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zurich 1565; Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 46; now at the University of Texas at Austin). The only Thierbuch physically traced in Tycho’s orbit is Landgrave Wilhelm’s own Kassel copy, not Tycho’s, destroyed in an air raid in September 1941.
113Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Apodixis physica et mathematica de cometisGörlitz, 1581, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2979 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933A copy was sent to Tycho by Scultetus in Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581, Opera omnia VII, 64). Tycho discusses the work in his book on the comet (Opera omnia IV, 293–295). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified, and the work belongs to the Hagecius gap: Tycho owned at least four works of Hagecius, each documented by a letter, and not one survives in the Clementinum. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78) remarked on the absence: among the Clementinum Tychoniana there is not a single work of Hagecius, though his long friendship with Tycho and Norlind’s list make it likely that Tycho had many if not all of his works, and none of the Clementinum’s Hagecius copies carries a provenance note pointing to him. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 80) names the mechanism by which such a copy could lose its provenance: composite volumes from Tycho’s library were broken up and rebound with pieces of other provenance (5 G 42, 14 J 164, 19 G 20, XII A 12), and Richard Kukula, director of the university library 1897–1918, had old Sammelbände dissolved as a matter of principle, among them, to judge by its modern binding, the Scultetus of 14 F 284. Whether Tycho’s Hagecius copies were lost or survive unrecognised remains an open question. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds three copies of the Görlitz 1581 edition — in a Luther convolute, in a convolute from the Jesuit college at Litoměřice, and as the host volume (record 000030653) of the Hagecius composite owned by the Jesuit college at Chomutov — and none bears a Tycho mark.
114Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Descriptio cometae qui apparuit 1577Prague, 1578, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2824 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933Sent to Tycho by Paul Hainzel in Augsburg (Hainzel to Tycho, March 1579, Opera omnia VII, 50). Tycho discusses the work in his book on the comet (Opera omnia IV, 261–296). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified, and the work belongs to the Hagecius gap: the receipt is documented by letter (Norlind, p. 349), yet no Hagecius copy of Tycho’s survives in any inventory, an absence Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78) remarked on herself. Imprint: Prague, Jiří Melantrich z Aventinu, 1578, 4to (Zinner 2824; Hellman 48), issued with the Spongia contra … Hannibalis Raymundi. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds two copies — 14 K 191, and a second (record 000030662) bound as the second tract in the Hagecius composite from the Jesuit college at Chomutov (host volume, record 000030653) — and neither bears a Tycho mark.
115Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae ... apparitioneFrankfurt am Main, 1574, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2673 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933; Dreyer 1890; Mosley 2007Norlind: ‘Måste Tycho ha ägt’ — Tycho must have owned it, since the Progymnasmata treat the work at length (Opera omnia III, 19–43). Hájek sent Tycho a copy with many manuscript corrections and additions in his own hand, hoping that Tycho would print the revised text or take selections into his own account of the nova; Tycho discussed the revised text in the Progymnasmata and did not print it (Dreyer 1890, p. 58 n. 2; Mosley 2007, p. 124 n. 42; Opera omnia VII, 99). Tycho’s copy, which would carry Hájek’s autograph corrections, has not been identified. The National Library of the Czech Republic’s two copies of the Frankfurt 1574 edition — one inscribed for the Chomutov Jesuit college in 1671 (‘Collegij Soctis IESV Commotonij Ao. 1671’, record 000154680), one stamped ‘REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN.’ (record 000014579) — have no earlier owner in the library’s records.
116Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Responsio ad ... Hannibalis Raimundi scriptumPrague, 1576, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2736 (after Norlind)Two copies reached Tycho: one sent by the author in August 1576 (Hájek to Tycho, Opera omnia VII, 38), a second in Maior’s parcel of June 1584 (VII, 83). A reply to Hannibal Raimundus of Verona, who held that the star of 1572 was not new. Neither copy is located. The National Library’s copy of the work, the first tract (record 000030657) of a Hájek composite from the Chomutov Jesuit college (record 000030653), carries no Tycho mark in the library’s record.
118Heerbrand, JakobDisputatio de adiaphoris et calendario Gregoriano (resp. Corbinus)Tübingen, 1584, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Heerbrandus, Jacobus); Zinner no. 3137 (after Norlind)Sent to Tycho by Maior June 1584 (Opera VII,83).
119Hegelund, Jens Pedersen (Johannes Hegelius)Themata pro disputatione quarta psychologiae (praes. Jacobus Cocus)Wittenberg, 1599, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hegelius, Iohannes)Dedicated to Tycho by the author, a son of Tycho’s friend Bishop Peder Jacobsen Hegelund of Ribe; Norlind: ‘har säkerligen befunnit sig i hans bibliotek’ — certainly in his library. The author enrolled at Wittenberg in November 1598, some months before Tycho and his sons.
124Hipparchus (ed. Petrus Victorius), the copy annotated by Joseph Justus ScaligerIn Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III (the Greek editio princeps, with Scaliger’s annotations)Florence (Giunta), 1567, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hipparchus Bithynus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 17 April 1599 (tekstnet.dk); Kepler, GW XIX (1975)Hipparchus’s commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus in the Greek editio princeps of Petrus Victorius (Florence 1567), Scaliger’s own copy, annotated in his hand. Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, formerly in Tycho’s service on Hven, met Scaliger in Holland and reported that he owned the Greek text. Tycho asked in August 1598 for the book or for transcripts of the passages he needed (Opera omnia VIII, 102); Scaliger sent excerpts, acknowledged in March 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 151); and in April 1599 Tycho thanked him for two books granted him (‘pro utroque autem libro mihi tam benigne concesso’), of which the Hipparchus is the one identified. Norlind (1970, p. 362) considers that the other may be the Cyclometrica elementa duo of 1594 with Scaliger’s dedication, now Sign. 14 A 59 (Prandtl A 42). That Tycho had the annotated book itself Kepler states to Herwart von Hohenburg in January 1603: Scaliger had once sent Tycho his Hipparchus with his own notes, and it was still in the possession of the heirs (Norlind 1970, p. 350, citing the letter as Caspar nr. 242, p. 354). On 16 November 1624 Kepler asked Tycho’s son Georg Brahe for ‘Hipparchum de fixis graecè, ist ein klains folium, vnd vil drinnen manu Scaligerj’ (KGW XIX, no. 7, pp. 202–203), so the annotated book was still with the heirs two years after Tengnagel’s death. Whether Kepler obtained it is not recorded, and no copy has been traced since.
125Horst, Dethard (Horstius)Prognosticon de eventu belli Turcici1601ATycho’s correspondence, letter of 18 April 1601 (tekstnet.dk)The Prognosticon reached Tycho as a gift through Georg Rollenhagen in April 1601; the letter of 18 April 1601 calls it ‘prognosticon de eventu belli Turcici, sane gratissimum’. It was among the last books to enter Tycho’s library. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
127Jöstel, MelchiorLunae deliquium ad hunc Christi annum 1599Wittenberg, 1599, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 350 (s.v. Jœstelius, Melchior); Zinner no. 3817 (after Norlind)Jöstel was Tycho’s collaborator in Prague, and the eclipse times in the tract were computed by Tycho’s lunar theory. Norlind: ‘Att Jöstelius’ skrift ingått i hans bibliotek är otvivelaktigt’ (that Jöstel’s tract entered his library is beyond doubt). The discrepancy at the eclipse of 31 January 1599 forced Tycho to revise his lunar theory, delaying the Progymnasmata.
129Kepler, JohannesProdromus dissertationum cosmographicarum (Mysterium cosmographicum)Tübingen, 1596, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 350 (s.v. Kepler, Johannes); Zinner no. 3664 (after Norlind)Kepler to Tycho, Graz, 13 December 1597 (Opera omnia VIII, 14–15), sent no copy of the Mysterium cosmographicum (Tübingen 1596), supposing that Tycho already had one: ‘Exemplaria non dubito, quin antea habeas: quare facile patior, ut difficultas transmittendi per tantum intervallum a mittendo me avocet’. Tycho to Kepler, Wandsbek, 1 April 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, 44), replied that he had seen and read the book before: ‘Librum tuum, quem Prodromum vocas Dissertationum Cosmographicarum, iam ante videram et … perlegeram’. So already Norlind 1970, p. 350. How and when his copy reached him is not recorded; no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
135Liddel, Duncan[Themata][Helmstedt], [1595]BNorlind 1970, p. 351 (s.v. Liddelius, Duncanus)Norlind: ‘Tycho har ägt ett exemplar, ty han citerar’ — Tycho owned a copy, since he cites its proposition 2 in a letter to Cramer of September 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 185), where Liddel, in a section ‘Parerga mathematica’, names Tycho in connection with the new world-system in terms that leave the reader unsure whether Tycho was its author. Title and imprint are Norlind’s conjecture, bracketed by him and unverified (‘Omöjlig att belägga’); the tract is not the Themata de melancholia (Helmstedt 1596) that P. J. Anderson’s Liddel bibliography (1910) lists as no. 4, and Anderson did not know it.
137Lycosthenes, ConradProdigiorum ac ostentorum chroniconBasel, 1557, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 352 (s.v. Lycosthenes, Conradus); Zinner no. 2177 (after Norlind)Norlind: 'Endera av upplagorna ägdes av Tycho (sannolikt den latinska)' — owned (probably the Latin ed.); to Brucaeus Nov 1588 (Opera VII,155) Tycho writes he leafed through the whole book.
140Maestlin, MichaelAusführlicher und gründlicher Bericht von der Jahrrechnung (de emendatione Calendarii)Heidelberg, 1583, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 352 (s.v. Mæstlinus, Michael); Zinner no. 3087 (after Norlind)Brucaeus sent Tycho 'Maestlini de emendatione Calendarii' in June 1584 (Opera omnia VII, 86). Whether the parcel held the Heidelberg edition of 1583 (Zinner 3087) or its reprint of 1584 within the Nothwendige und gründtliche Bedenckhen von dem allgemeinen römischen Kalender (Heidelberg 1584; Zinner 3144) cannot be decided; Norlind takes the former as the likelier. Against the Gregorian reform.

Offusius, Iofrancus)Norlind 1970, p. 355: Tycho received a copy of the printed book from Hagecius at their meeting at Regensburg in November 1575 (Opera omnia VII, 184; II, 421) and was particularly taken with its section on the planets’ influence at their varying distances from the earth; in May 1588 he wrote to Hagecius that he could no longer find the book in his library and asked him to procure another copy (VII, 121; Hagecius’s answers of November 1588 and May 1589, VII, 147 and 184). A book that left the library, or was mislaid in it, in Tycho’s own lifetime. Norlind adds that a copy stood in Queen Christina’s library which he could not find among the Reginenses in the Vatican — a lead he did not pursue, and one worth the question, since books from Prague reached her library in 1648.

Paracelsus, Theophrastus)The only authority is Joachim Morsius, who in 1625 — in the dedication to the pseudo-Paracelsian lion-prophecy — reported on Cort Aslakssøn’s word that Tycho had owned a copy, and who further supposed that the manuscript was by then in Prague with Tycho’s heirs. Norlind relays both. No inventory and no Clementinum catalogue records it, and no copy has been identified: the ownership is attested at second hand only and remains unverified. Status attested, not located, since 20 October 2026: no one contests the ownership — Norlind relays only Morsius's report — so the Definitions' 'disputed' does not fit.

Thorndike (History of Magic and Experimental Science VI, p. 84) held that neither Tycho nor Hagecius owned a copy. Norlind shows that Thorndike misread the three passages of the correspondence on which he relied (Opera omnia VII, 120, 147 and 212), which concern Apianus and Pena and not this book, and so defends Tycho’s ownership against Thorndike’s denial. The Czech National Library holds the work as the fourth tract of a Hagecius composite volume from the Jesuit college at Chomutov; its record notes no mark of Tycho’s.
185Ptolemaeus, ClaudiusAlmagest (old Venetian edition, c. 1515)Venetiis, 1515, 2°ANorlind 1970, p. 358 (s.v. Ptolemæus, Claudius); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 20 January 1587 (tekstnet.dk); Fund og Forskning 1965Tycho states that he owns an old Venetian Almagest, some seventy years old in 1587 (letter of 20 January 1587: ‘vetus quoddam exemplar Almagesti, ante annos proxime 70. It is distinct from the Ptolemy volumes among the Clementinum copies — the Opera (Basel), the Geographia (Cologne 1597) and the De analemmate (Rome 1562). Norlind identified the edition in print (Fund og Forskning XII, 1965, p. 156, ‘Efterslæt’): the Latin Almagest printed at Venice in 1515 (Petrus Liechtenstein; Gerard of Cremona’s version), whose prefatory life of Ptolemy — ‘indledningen til en oversættelse af Almagesten, trykt i Venedig 1515, som Tycho Brahe har ejet og nævner i et brev’ — is the source of the royal descent and the physical description of Ptolemy in Tycho’s elegy In effigiem Cl. Ptolemaei (Epistolae astronomicae, 1596, p. 239). No copy of the Venice Almagest with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

Two copies of the 1590 edition in the Royal Library, Hielmst. 547 2° and Hielmst. 146 2°, examined in facsimile, descend from Henrik Hielmstierne and bear neither a mark of Tycho’s nor the bound-in transcript. No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
194Regiomontanus, JohannesDe cometae magnitudine longitudineque ... problemata XVINürnberg, 1531, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 360 (s.v. The tract was also reprinted within Regiomontanus’ Scripta (Nuremberg 1544), a volume Norlind likewise places in Tycho’s library.

234Ursus, Nicolaus Reimers (Bär)De astronomicis hypothesibus, seu de systemate mundanoPrague, 1597, 4°ANorlind 1970, p. 365 (s.v. Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus); Zinner no. 3739 (after Norlind); Jardine et al. 2005; Jardine & Segonds 2008; Švédská knižní kořist (database)Norlind records that Tycho received the book (‘erhöll boken’). It was printed ‘Absque omni privilegio’; in it Ursus denies having stolen the system, dedicates the work to Landgrave Moritz, prints a laudatory letter from Kepler (Graz, 15 November 1595), and violently attacks Tycho and Rothmann. Tycho lent his copy, with the offending passages marked, to Holger Rosenkrantz in 1598 and complained that it was not returned (Opera omnia VIII, 126). Jardine, Launert, Segonds, Mosley and Tybjerg (2005, pp. 98–103) found the Royal Library’s copy from the Rosenkrantz sale of 1695 unmarked; the copy now in the Danish National Library of Science and Medicine, 4° Astr. 8050, perhaps transferred from the Royal Library between 1918 and 1926, is inscribed ‘Donum Autoris’ on the title and carries sixteen clear marginal marks, all against passages insulting to Tycho and all but two of them in the dedication to Landgrave Moritz or in the invective poem that follows it. They argue that this is the copy prepared for Lange and lent to Rosenkrantz. The identification rests on the pattern of the marks, not on a mark of ownership; the hand of the marks has not been compared with Tycho’s or with those of his assistants. A book lent out of the library in 1598 and never returned is a survivor of the library’s lifetime, not of its dispersal. The Czech National Library holds a copy of the Prague 1597 edition, 14 J 81/adl.2, bound second in a re-bound convolute after della Faille’s Theoremata (Antwerp 1632); its record, recatalogued under Kukula, carries no provenance. Jardine and Segonds restate the identification in 2008: the copy is the one Caspar Lehmann obtained from Ursus himself and sent through Rollenhagen in the spring of 1598; Tycho had the marks made for Erik Lange’s testimony and lent the volume to Holger Rosenkrantz, who did not return it despite the demands of 9 September 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, p. 112) and 5 December 1598 (pp. 125–126); their ‘about a dozen’ marked passages answers to the twelve puncta Lange attested, the article of 2005 counting sixteen clear marks and two doubtful (2008, pp. 175, 195–196, 243 n. 3). Three copies of the book reached Tycho in the spring of 1598 — from a student of Helmstedt, from Lehmann through Rollenhagen, and from Hagecius (pp. 157 n. 3, 191–192). A second surviving copy of the book Jardine and Segonds call rare: Västerås Stadsbibliotek, from the Olomouc Jesuit college (‘Collegij Olomu. Soctis JESV Catalogo inscriptus an: 1604’), through the Stockholm royal library of 1650–51, in a parchment binding cut from a coloured Hebrew manuscript (the Swedish-booty database, record SJ 203; Gawryś, Slavica Arosiensia III, no. 213). Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
235Ursus, Nicolaus Reimers (Bär)Fundamentum astronomicum, id est nova doctrina sinuum et triangulorumStrasbourg, 1588, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 365 (s.v. Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus); Zinner no. 3316 (after Norlind); Jardine & Segonds 2008; Balsem 2020Ursus set out in this book a world-system that, in Norlind’s words, differs only slightly from Tycho’s. Tycho held that Ursus had taken it from a sketch seen during his stay at Uraniborg in the autumn of 1584, in Erik Lange’s company, and pressed the charge of plagiarism in the correspondence with the Landgrave and Rothmann printed in 1596; Norlind, with Dreyer, holds the charge probably unwarranted. Tycho received several copies: one sent by Rantzau (Tycho to Rantzau, December 1588; Opera omnia VII, 387), a second probably from Christian Ripensis, which may be the other copy Tycho mentions in that letter, and one from Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg (Tycho to Rothmann, February 1589; Opera omnia VI, 179). Rollenhagen sent a copy to Rantzau on 16 October 1588 (Landesarchiv Schleswig-Holstein, Breitenburg-Archiv Abt. 127.21, Hss. 293, p. 552); Tycho already had one from elsewhere, ‘aliunde’ (to Rantzau, 21 December 1588, Opera omnia VII, p. 387) (Jardine & Segonds 2008, pp. 120–121). A copy with a Prague provenance of 1595 — ‘Daniel Muller à Mollenberg, '95 Prag’ on the title, ‘Raymari’ on the fore-edge, interleaved and annotated in a hand the Kepler-Kommission declared in 1964 not to be Kepler's — is at Leiden, 538 E 2, from Isaac Vossius's library; Balsem declines to call it Swedish booty for want of any trace of Christina's shelfmark on its ruined spine (2020, p. 37 and Cat. Math. 730). Not Tycho's copy, but a Prague copy of the year of the quarrel.
238Viète, François (Vieta)Two tracts newly published in 1600 (‘libelli duo’), one of them probably the Apollonius Gallus1600ATycho’s correspondence, letter of 26 April 1600 (tekstnet.dk)Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho from Munich two booklets Viète had just published, without naming them (Herwart to Tycho, 26 April 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 305: ‘libelli duo, quos … FRANCISCUS VIETA, nuper in lucem prodire voluit … his iunctos ad te mitto’); Tycho acknowledged receipt in his letter to Herwart of 28 August 1600. Norlind (1970, p. 208) identifies one of them from Kepler’s letter to Herwart of July 1600 (Caspar no. 168), which reports that Kepler had seen at Tycho’s Viète’s ‘Opus de aequationibus’: not the De aequationum recognitione, printed only in 1615, but the Apollonius Gallus of 1600, whose second appendix (problems I and IV) determines a planet’s apogee and eccentricity from three observations. On 8 November 1600 Herwart described Viète’s Canon mathematicus under the title ‘Francisci Vietaei opera Mathematica’ and offered to procure it if Tycho wished (Herwart to Tycho, 8 November 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 386: ‘Quod si eum desideres, curabo omnino, ut habeas’) — an offer, not a sending, and not the Opera of 1646. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
241Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-KasselObservations of the comet of 1577 (sent to Tycho)CTycho’s correspondence, letter of 11 June 1588 (tekstnet.dk); Schrimpf & Verbunt 2021Wilhelm IV’s observations of the comet of 1577 reached Tycho through the Rothmann and Kassel correspondence (Tycho to Rothmann, 11 June 1588: ‘Recensui etiam in hoc libro... Observationes’) and were collated into his comet book, the Progymnasmata; they were not held as a discrete Wilhelm IV codex. Wilhelm IV’s own observation manuscripts survive at the Universitätsbibliothek Kassel — Landesbibliothek und Murhardsche Bibliothek, in the ‘2 Ms. astron.’ series (the observation corpus 1–7; the star catalogue 2 Ms. astron. 74; the handbook 2 Ms. astron. 5; Schrimpf and Verbunt 2021), with Wilhelm’s correspondence at the Hessisches Staatsarchiv, Marburg; those are Wilhelm’s copies, not Tycho’s. Status attested since 20 October 2026: nothing is contested — the observations reached Tycho and were collated into the comet book; no discrete codex was ever held.
246(eight unidentified authors)[Eight unidentified Tycho-owned books, superexlibris and autograph marginalia, found in a Prague monastery, 1943]BMortensen 1955Felix Mainx reported to Mortensen that in 1943 he had found, in a Prague monastery library, eight further books, not further specified, bearing Tycho’s superexlibris and many autograph marginalia; he intended to describe the find in a later paper (Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘otte andre ikke nærmere angivne Bøger, som foruden Tycho Brahes Superexlibris havde mange egenhændige Marginalnoter’). The books have not been traced since.
250(ancient geographers, ed. David Hoeschel)Geographica — ancient minor Greek geographers, newly first-published (incl. Scylax of Caryanda)Augsburg, 1600BTycho’s correspondence, letter of 8 September 1600 (tekstnet.dk)Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho a newly published edition of the ancient minor Greek geographers with his letter of 8 September 1600 (‘veteres quosdam Geographos nunc primum in lucem editos’), that is, Hoeschel’s Geographica (Augsburg 1600). The book was Tycho’s own.
253Typus pompae funebris 5. Junii anno 1588 habitae Rodtschildii in exequiis Friderici II Daniae regis, opera et consilio Henrici Rantzovii efformatus (Frans Hogenberg and Simon Novellanus, twenty engravings)1588, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 364 (s.v. Typus pompæ funebris 5. Junii Anno 1588 …)Norlind 1970, p. 364: twenty engravings of the funeral procession of Frederik II at Roskilde on 5 June 1588, made at Rantzau’s instance and dedicated to Christian IV. Tycho acknowledged the gift to Rantzau in December 1588 — ‘delineationem exequiarum ac sepulturae regiae Hamburgi per te aeneis figuris procuratam’ (Opera omnia VII, 386). A print series from the Rantzau connection rather than a book of the study; no copy with a mark of Tycho’s is known.

Tycho owned a single copy and therefore sent Cramer a transcript (Tycho to Cramer, September 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 186)). Norlind could not trace the print itself. No copy of the programme is traced, and a copy of Tycho’s would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

36Brasch, MartinCarmen epicum de Varadino (manuscript poem)1600CNorlind 1970, p. 340 (s.v. Brasch, Martinus)Brasch sent the manuscript poem, which celebrates Melchior von Roedern’s defence of Grosswardein (Várad) in 1598, to Tycho twice: in August 1600, when it was lost in transit (Opera omnia VIII, 337), and as a replacement in September 1600 that ‘probably reached’ him (Opera omnia VIII, 380; Norlind p. 340); von Roedern died on 20 September 1600. No surviving manuscript codex has been located in any catalogue. Martin Brasch the Younger also published a printed Varadini Hungariae propugnaculi... anni 1598 (1598) on the same subject — plausibly the same matter in print beside an authorial manuscript redaction of 1600, though no source collates the two. The first copy never arrived, the replacement only ‘probably’ did, no codex survives, and no ownership mark that could be looked for attaches to the item; the entry therefore rests on the correspondence alone. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique manuscript sent and probably received, not a mass-survival text — the class retired as unlocatable does not fit it.

The extant Copenhagen University Library copy is not Tycho's: it is the author's dedication copy to Jacob Ulfeldt. Tycho's copy (ex-Rostgaard) is lost. The earlier witness is Oluf Bang, Samling af nyttige Materier, 7. Stykke (1745), p. 531, from which Mortensen (1955, pp. 30–31) takes the copy: in Rostgaard's library at his death in 1745, bequeathed to the University, and not found there.

Mortensen (1942, pp. 14–15) dates the note 5 April 1592 at Uraniborg and gives its text in Høst's Danish rendering (Chronos 1822, p. 24): ‘Private og indvortes Ulykker lettes ikke ved Omskiftelse af Sted og Himmelegn; thi, hvorsomhelst nogen maatte gaa hen, bringer han sig selv med. Men offentlige Elendigheder undgaaes ofte ved at forandre Sted’.
154Methodius (pseudo-)Revelatio (Revelationes Methodii) — a manuscript copy made for Tycho1600BTycho’s correspondence, letter of 10 December 1600 (tekstnet.dk)Herwart had the Revelatio ascribed to Methodius transcribed for Tycho because the volume that contained it was too bulky to send, and despatched the copy from Munich with the Alphonsine tables (Herwart to Tycho, 10 December 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 393: ‘METHODIJ uti fertur Revelationem, quam describi curavi, cum liber, cui inserta fuerat, ob molem transferri nequeat’). The transcript is not among the Clementinum volumes and has not been identified at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, or the Austrian National Library; the text survives in many copies, and a transcript without Tycho’s own mark cannot be told from them. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique transcript made for Tycho and sent, not a mass-survival text.

Paulus Alexandrinus); Zinner no. 3309 (after Norlind); Šolc 1999; Šolc 2006; Collijn 1933 (as Kleinschnitzová printed it)A book by another author that Tycho owned (Paulus Alexandrinus, edited from Heinrich Rantzau’s library, Wittenberg 1588), in its original Tychonic binding. Reported by Isak Collijn to Flora Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78 n. 1) as a Tychonianum in the Landesbibliothek Dresden, the companion to the Waldstein (Mnichovo Hradiště) copy of Tycho’s own De nova stella, which, as a copy of one of Tycho’s own works, lies outside this library. The volume is lost: Norlind (1970, p. 356) records the Dresden library’s own communication that the copy ‘gått förlorat under senaste världskrig’ — was lost in the Second World War. Šolc still lists the volume in Dresden — ‘befand sich … in der Sächsischen Landesbibliothek Dresden’ (1999, § 2.533, printed p. 150) and, in the present tense, ‘se nachází v Zemské knihovně v Drážďanech’ (2006, p. 192) — and nowhere mentions the loss Norlind reports from the library itself; neither text cites a sighting. The entry keeps ‘lost’ on Norlind's report; a question to the SLUB (its war-loss records, and whether a Paulus Alexandrinus, Wittenberg 1588, in a Tychonic binding has since been acquired) would close it.
213Scaliger, Joseph JustusDe emendatione temporum (revised ed.; Leiden, Plantin 1598)Lugduni Batav., 1598, 2°ANorlind 1970, p. 362 (s.v. Scaliger, Joseph Justus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 14 March 1598 (tekstnet.dk); Walde 1938; Norlind 1926; Mortensen 1955Sought in 1584 through Johannes Maior, Tycho’s agent at the Frankfurt fairs; the first edition of 1583 then reached Tycho twice in June 1584, from Maior at Augsburg on 8 June (Maior to Tycho, 8 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 83: ‘Inprimis autem mihi curae fuit SCALIGERI de emendatione temporum’) and from Heinrich Brucaeus at Rostock on 12 June (Brucaeus to Tycho, 12 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 86: ‘Mitto IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM de emendatione temporum’). One of the two copies survives: Prague, National Library, Sign. 19 A 46, initialled ‘T. B.’ on the title-page; Kleinschnitzová (no. 41, p. 92) could not say which: ‘Dürfte das von Brucaeus oder Major an Brahe gesandte Exemplar sein.’ The entry concerns the revised edition of 1598, which Tycho acknowledged to Scaliger from Wandsbeck on 14 March 1598 (Tycho to Scaliger, 14 March 1598: ‘redintegratum de Temporum Emendatione... primum accepi’); Norlind (1926, no. 28) read the copy as the author’s gift, Walde (1938, p. 14 n. 2) as an ordinarily procured copy, the letter containing no thanks. A copy of this edition from Tycho’s library was found by Walde in the summer of 1937 in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg: white parchment with Tycho’s portrait on the upper and his arms on the lower board, both blind-stamped, and the decor usual on his bindings; not bound on Hven, which he left in 1597, perhaps at Wandsbeck in 1598; many marginalia in several hands, photographs of which Hans Ræder judged not to be Tycho’s; no dedication; the only later note ‘M. Braunhardt i Gotha 1761 … Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’, which Walde could not explain (a person named Oppel, or the town of Oppeln near Neisse, where Tycho’s great globe was found in 1632). Mortensen cited the find in 1955 without the title; nothing later is recorded of the volume, and Norlind’s catalogue of 1970 does not include it. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

Six folio leaves of excerpts from Proclus’s commentary on the first book of Euclid, published by Studnička as Tycho’s autograph (1901, 1903). Dreyer denied that the hand is Tycho’s and found no sign that the manuscript had ever been his (Opera omnia I, p. 317); Norlind (1970, p. 340) reports both views. Status disputed, D, since 20 October 2026: no ownership mark; Dreyer denied hand and ownership (Opera omnia I, p. 317) and Šíma & Valeška give the hand to a professional writer — a contested identification, by the Definitions disputed.
61Copernicus, NicolausCommentariolus (De hypothesibus motuum coelestium ... commentariolus) — manuscript, ManuskriptCNorlind 1970, p. 343 (s.v. Copernicus, Nicolaus); Walde 1938; Jardine & Segonds 2008; Vackářová 2026A manuscript of the Commentariolus in the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Vienna, attributed to Tycho’s library by Norlind. Tycho owned the text: Hagecius gave him a copy at Regensburg in 1575, and he printed it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia II, 428). Whether the Vienna manuscript is that copy rests on Norlind’s attribution and on the Uraniborg-circle contents of the same Sammelhandschrift; the volume carries no mark of his, and its catalogue record names no former owner, so both the entry and the identification of the copy are graded C. Walde (1938) showed the Vienna manuscript to have been Longomontanus’s gift to the amanuensis Johannes Eriksen at Benátky on 18 July 1600 and left open whether it passed from Eriksen to Tycho; Eriksen’s books otherwise went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty. The witness therefore belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho’s own shelves. Jardine and Segonds note the copy that came from Hagecius (2008, p. 187 n. 4). The National Library's account of 2026 adds two points to the Regensburg gift: that the original Hájek exemplar is untraced (the same object as Norlind's ‘Tycho's exemplar not located’ if the Regensburg transfer was a gift), and the conjecture that it was Tycho who had Copernicus's name — absent from the anonymous letter as it circulated — set at the head of the transcripts he distributed (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 22 (scan 22); ‘zřejmě’, her conjecture, not a documented fact). The three surviving transcripts she names (Vienna, Stockholm, Aberdeen; p. 20) are those the history essay already records. Status disputed since 20 October 2026: the witness belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho's shelves (Walde 1938 against the transfer), and a located C with the ownership in doubt is the Definitions' disputed, not located.
88Fincke, ThomasGeometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel 1583)Basileæ, 1583, 4°CNorlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Fincke, Thomas)Thomas Fincke, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel: S. Henricpetri, 1583), dedicated to Frederik II. Both copies in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, have been examined in digital reproduction, and neither bears any mark of Tycho’s ownership. The first copy (LN 599 4, ex. 1) carries the autograph ‘Horrebow’ (the eighteenth-century family of Danish Royal Astronomers) on the title page and royal-cipher and BRH stamps, in an eighteenth-century marbled-board binding. The second (Hielmst. 1661a 4, ex. 2) is a contemporary Sammelband (Fincke 1583 with Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum, Strasbourg 1588) in limp vellum, inscribed ‘Severinus Pauli[?] … Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]’ (mottoes ‘Superna curato, Humana contemnito’ and ‘Mens generosa ultra polos’) and ‘Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620’ (motto ‘Ex uno omnia’), later Hielmstierne’s. Norlind nonetheless placed the book in Tycho’s library — ‘fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg’ (Bilaga I, p. 346) — but his whole basis is Fincke’s printed praise of Tycho in the preface, a compliment present in every copy rather than a mark in any copy. No inventory, inscription or ownership mark attests Tycho’s ownership, and neither surviving Copenhagen copy is his.

O.’; the mathematical fragment MS XII A XII; the Sacrobosco compendium MS VII E XXIX, formerly bound in 14 F 16) and sixteen printed works in four groups by binding — plain (14 A 59, 1 H 56, 14 F 16, 14 J 164, 14 J 192, 14 B 16, 5 B 70, 5 C 31), brown leather with ‘T. B. O.’ (14 H 190, 14 H 225, 14 J 190, 14 K 70), and the Prachtbände in white (14 J 176, 14 G 30) and brown leather (8 H 39, 12 H 10). Prusík held that Tycho bound his books more richly as his means grew, the conjecture Kukula repeated and Bargum answered.

The Prague binderies of the 1580s–1610s in the Strahov holdings: the Master with the Eagle (at least 40 volumes) and the ‘Knihvazač rudolfínského okruhu II’ (about 70 volumes), the latter's work reaching Strahov by several routes — Pontanus's gifts of 1595, the sixteen books of the imperial councillor Franz Gottfried Troilo von Lessoth, Pavel Pistorius z Lucka — and not only by purchase (p. 118); the second version of Lohel's supralibros lent only to this binder in 1605–1615 (p. 119); the title inscription ‘Liber Monast: B. V. M. Montis Syon vulgo Strahow 1608’ (p. 119, n. 23).
    Contributes The binder of the Opus palatinum in his Strahov context; the dated parallel for the Mechanica's title inscription.
    Available online Strahov Library — Bibliotheca Strahoviensis 14 (PDF, 5 MB)
  111. Voit 2023
    Petr Voit, Boj o volnou plochu (Praha 2023), pp. 209 and 560 — cited by the Strahov catalogue record of the Opus palatinum (Σ V 5/a) beside Voit 2020, pp. 250–252. Not read.
    Contributes A second published treatment of the Opus palatinum binding, as the holding library cites it.
  112. Volf 1932
    Josef Volf, ‘Tycho Brahe a jeho hvězdářská pozůstalost’, Říše hvězd 13 (1932), no. 1, pp. 1–9, and no. 2, pp. 21–29 (with a German summary); first printed in Český bibliofil (1931), not seen. From the Bohemian chamber records: the instruments and the manuscript observations bought for Rudolf's collections, ‘kdežto knihovna zbyla dědicům’; the 4,000 thaler of September 1603; the rescript of 9 July 1609; the heirs assigned from 1623 to the arrears of the towns Žatec, Kadaň, Rakovník and Chomutov, with payments until 1654; the heirs turned Catholic, and ‘putuje část slavné bibliotéky Brahovy s nádhernými vazbami a se supralibros do klementinské knihovny jako dar’; Rudolf Tycho Gansneb Tengnagel, captain of the Malá Strana from 1642, gave his share of the debt to the Dominicans of St Giles (Ferdinand III's assurance of 14 March 1643 for 22,534 fl.), Sophie Brahe hers (9,942 fl.) to the Kadaň Franciscans; iron instead of money in 1672; debts still claimed in 1685 and 1688; the Czechoslovak restitution claims of the 1920s against Vienna, with the documents.
    Contributes The Czech archival account of the estate; the Clementinum transfer called a gift.
    Available online Říše hvězd archive (part 1: RH-1932-01.pdf)
  113. Walde 1920
    Otto Walde, Storhetstidens litterära krigsbyten: en kulturhistorisk-bibliografisk studie, II (Uppsala, 1920), p. 329: the first report of the Uppsala volume of 1563 (Prandtl’s Band III) with Vedel’s name on the first title. Cited here after Mortensen 1942 (p. 25) and Mortensen 1955 (p. 27, n. 4).
    Contributes The first report of the Uppsala volume of 1563.
  114. Walde 1938
    Otto Walde, ‘Några böcker från Tycho Brahes krets’, Nordisk tidskrift för bok- och biblioteksväsen 25 (1938), pp. 11–17. The Braunsberg find: in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg a copy of Scaliger's De emendatione temporum in the revised Leiden edition of 1598, bound in white parchment with Tycho's arms on the lower and his portrait on the upper board, both blind-stamped, with the decor usual on his bindings; not bound on Hven, perhaps at Wandsbeck in 1598; many marginalia in several hands, photographs of which Hans Ræder judged not Tycho's; no dedication; the later note ‘M. Braunhardt i Gotha 1761 … Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’. Also the Uppsala volume of 1563 given to Vedel and the Glareanus Vedel bought in 1564, now in Prague; the 2781 spine number and its uncertainty; and the books of Johannes Eriksen Hamburgensis, Tycho's amanuensis, which went into Queen Christina's library with the Prague booty (a Pitiscus bought at Prague on 14 August 1601, now at Hanover; two chemical manuscripts at Leiden; a Lull of 1593 at Västerås) — and, apart from them, the Vienna Commentariolus manuscript, Longomontanus's gift to Eriksen at Benátky on 18 July 1600, whose supposed passage to Tycho and with his papers to Vienna Walde doubted.
    Contributes The identity of the Braunsberg volume and the Eriksen provenance of the Vienna Commentariolus.
    Available online Projekt Runeberg — p. 11
  115. Zeeberg 1993
    Peter Zeeberg, Den praktiske muse: Tycho Brahes brug af latindigtningen (Studier fra Sprog- og Oldtidsforskning 321; Copenhagen: Museum Tusculanum, 1993); pp. 14–17 on the first prints of the Uraniborg press, the poem to Erik Lange of 27 November 1584 and the dating of the poems.
    Contributes The first item printed on the Uraniborg press, from Tycho's own observation protocol.
  116. ZfB 1906–07 (binding note)
    ‘Ein Bucheinband Tycho Brahes’, Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde 10 (1906/07), Heft 1, Chronik, pp. 42–43, with three facsimile plates of the two supralibros (signed ‘—W—’ in the contents). The Munich antiquarian bookseller Ludwig Rosenthal had sent the volume: the eighteenth volume of Zwinger's Theatrum humanae vitae (Basel 1587) in wooden boards covered in brown leather, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames, the innermost with fourteen portrait medallions of scholars, four gilt rosettes, and the gilt portrait and arms medallions with their distichs; a manuscript note inside the board called it a ‘Schweizer Ledereinband mit Blinddruck und Goldmedaillons’, and the writer supposed it made at Basel for Tycho. The volume is the one now at the Röhsska museum, Göteborg.
    Contributes The 1906 description and the Rosenthal step in the provenance of the Röhsska volume.
    Available online Internet Archive
